teile.einleitung: The safety pin is a bent wire pin whose point disappears into a cap. In this way you can pin fabric together without pricking yourself. It was invented in 1849 by the American Walter Hunt, supposedly in just a few hours.
wichtigste: The safety pin is bent from a single piece of wire.
A cap over the point protects against pricking, which is where the name comes from.
At the bend it has a coil that works like a spring.
Walter Hunt invented the safety pin in 1849.
Hunt sold the rights to his invention to pay off debts.
In sport it is often used to pin on your race number.
With a safety pin you can quickly fix a pair of trousers with a broken button.

abschnitte.text: A **safety pin** is usually made of a single piece of steel or brass wire. One end is ground to a point, and at the other there is a small metal **cap**. In between, the wire is bent into a coil that works like a **spring**. If you squeeze the pin together and hook the point into the cap, the spring force holds it in place. Because the point is covered, you do not prick yourself.

The American **Walter Hunt** patented the safety pin in the USA in **1849**. According to legend, he bent it from a piece of wire in a few hours while thinking about his debts. To pay them off, he sold the rights for a small sum. The company that bought them later made a lot of money with it. Hunt also invented other things, including an early sewing machine.

The idea was not completely new. More than 3,000 years ago people in Europe already wore so-called **fibulae**. These were clothing pins made of bronze, often finely decorated, that held clothes together. They also had a spring coil and a kind of holder for the point. Fibulae are often found in excavations, including in Switzerland.

Safety pins are little all-rounders. Runners use them to pin their **race number** to their shirt. If a button or a hem comes loose, the pin holds the clothing together until it can be mended. In the past they were also used to fasten cloth nappies on babies. In some first aid kits they are used to fasten bandages.

Every year countless safety pins are made worldwide, today mostly by machines in factories. In the 1970s they became an ornament of the **punk** movement. The safety pin is regarded as an example of a simple, brilliant invention that has hardly changed in over 170 years. In German it is sometimes also called “Sicherheits-” or “Wäschenadel”, which means laundry pin.

begriffe.erklaerung: A protective right that allows an inventor to be the only one to use or sell an invention.
A springy part that jumps back into shape after being squeezed.
A clothing pin from ancient times that held clothes together.
A long, thin thread of metal.

gewusst: Walter Hunt sold the rights to the safety pin for little money, and others became rich from it.
More than 3,000 years ago there were already clothing pins with a spring that were similar to the safety pin.
The shape of the safety pin has hardly changed since 1849.

teile.einleitung: Deep-sea mining means extracting raw materials such as metals from the floor of the deep sea, several thousand metres down. The most sought-after are manganese nodules, ore crusts and deposits at hot springs. So far there is no commercial mining yet, but there is fierce debate around the world about whether it should be allowed.
wichtigste: Deep-sea mining is the extraction of raw materials from the seabed at great depth.
Manganese nodules contain valuable metals such as manganese, nickel, cobalt and copper.
The largest known manganese nodule fields lie in the Clarion-Clipperton Zone in the Pacific.
Manganese nodules grow only a few millimetres in a million years.
The seabed outside national areas is regarded as the common heritage of mankind.
The International Seabed Authority ISA, based in Kingston, Jamaica, regulates mining there.
Sediment clouds from mining could spread far with the currents and cover living things.

abschnitte.text: The **deep sea** begins below about 200 metres, where hardly any light reaches. But many deposits of raw materials lie much deeper still, often at 4000 to 6000 metres. In deep-sea mining, remote-controlled machines are meant to drive over the seabed and collect raw materials. These are then pumped through long pipes to a ship on the surface. So far, such machines have only been used in tests.

The best known are **manganese nodules**, lumps about the size of a potato that lie loose on the seabed. They contain manganese, nickel, cobalt and copper. On the slopes of underwater mountains there are **cobalt-rich iron-manganese crusts**. At hot springs, the black smokers, **massive sulphides** form with copper, zinc and sometimes gold. Many of these metals are needed for batteries, electric cars and electronics.

The largest known field of manganese nodules is the **Clarion-Clipperton Zone** in the Pacific between Hawaii and Mexico. It covers several million square kilometres. There are other deposits in the Indian Ocean and the Pacific. Massive sulphides are found mainly along the mid-ocean ridges, where new crust is formed.

A country's **exclusive economic zone** reaches up to 200 nautical miles from the coast, and there it decides about the raw materials itself. According to the UN Convention on the Law of the Sea of 1982, the seabed beyond that is regarded as the **common heritage of mankind**. Here the International Seabed Authority ISA in Kingston, Jamaica, grants exploration licences. The rules for actual mining have been negotiated there for years but are not yet finished.

Many animals live in the deep sea that no human has ever seen, such as sea cucumbers, sponges and strange crustaceans. Some live directly on the nodules and would have no habitat without them. Mining creates **sediment clouds**, which can spread far with the currents and cover living things. Because manganese nodules grow only a few millimetres in a million years, the damage would practically never disappear. That is why more than 30 states (as of about 2025) and many experts are calling for a pause until the consequences have been better researched.

Switzerland has no sea, but it is involved through companies and research. The Switzerland-based company **Allseas** converted a ship with which a test mining of manganese nodules was carried out in the Pacific in 2022. Swiss researchers also study the deep sea and the effects of human interference. Swiss consumers, too, face the question of where the metals in mobile phones and batteries come from.

begriffe.erklaerung: The dark, cold part of the sea below about 200 metres.
A metal-rich lump that grows on the seabed over millions of years.
A hot spring on the seabed from which dark, mineral-rich water pours out.
Fine mud and dust that settles on the bottom.
A measure of length used at sea; one nautical mile is 1852 metres.

gewusst: A manganese nodule the size of a potato can be several million years old.
We know less about the floor of the deep sea than about the surface of the Moon.
On research voyages in the Clarion-Clipperton Zone, thousands of animal species have been discovered that were previously unknown.

teile.einleitung: Mirror neurons are special nerve cells in the brain that become active not only when you do something yourself but also when you watch someone else doing it. They were discovered in monkeys in the 1990s. Many people suspect that they help us to imitate others and to feel with them, but exactly this is disputed among researchers.
wichtigste: Mirror neurons fire both when you carry out an action yourself and when you watch it.
They were first discovered in macaques, a group of monkeys.
They were discovered by Giacomo Rizzolatti's research group in Parma, Italy.
The first mirror neurons were found in the premotor area F5.
They were first described in the 1990s.
According to widespread hypotheses they support imitation and empathy.
In humans their role is disputed, because direct measurements of single cells are rare.
In humans Broca's area is regarded as a possible counterpart to area F5.

abschnitte.text: **Neurons** are nerve cells that pass on signals in the brain. **Mirror neurons** are such cells with a special property. They become active when an animal reaches for a nut itself, but also when it only watches someone else reaching for a nut. So the brain in a way mirrors the action it observes. That is where their name comes from.

At the beginning of the 1990s the research group around **Giacomo Rizzolatti** at the University of Parma in Italy studied the brains of **macaques**. They wanted to find out which cells are active when grasping. To do this they measured the signals of single nerve cells in the **premotor area F5**, a region that plans movements. Surprisingly, some cells also fired when the monkeys were only watching. This discovery was published in the following years and became known worldwide.

Many researchers suspected that mirror neurons help with **imitation**, for example when a child copies a movement. Other hypotheses link them with **empathy**, that is, feeling with others. They could also play a role in understanding other people's intentions and in learning language. In humans **Broca's area**, which is important for language, is regarded as a possible counterpart to area F5.

In monkeys single cells could be measured directly, but in humans this is only rarely possible. Usually methods such as brain imaging are used, which only show larger regions. Whether these regions really contain mirror neurons cannot be said for certain in this way. Some researchers think the role of mirror neurons in empathy or language is greatly exaggerated. That is why research on this has still not been concluded.

When you watch a player shoot at a football match, your own leg may twitch. When you watch dance or sport, your brain activates regions that are also responsible for your own movements. Babies imitate facial expressions from an early age. Researchers are still investigating whether mirror neurons play the main role in this.

begriffe.erklaerung: A nerve cell that passes on signals in the body and the brain.
A group of monkeys that includes the rhesus monkey.
The ability to put yourself in other people's shoes and feel with them.
An assumption that has to be tested through research.
A region in the human brain that is important for speaking.

gewusst: Mirror neurons were discovered rather by chance, when researchers were actually studying grasping movements.
In monkeys some mirror neurons even fire when they only hear the sound of an action, such as a nut being cracked.
Despite their great fame, it is still unclear how important mirror neurons really are for compassion.

teile.einleitung: An inactivated vaccine is a vaccine that contains no pathogens that can multiply. It consists of killed pathogens or only of individual parts of them. From it, the immune system learns to recognise the real pathogen without you becoming ill.
wichtigste: Inactivated vaccines contain killed pathogens or only parts of them.
The hepatitis A vaccine contains whole inactivated viruses.
Jonas Salk developed the inactivated polio vaccine, which was approved in 1955.
A toxoid is a detoxified bacterial poison that still produces immunity.
Usually several doses and boosters are needed, because the immune response is weaker.
The TBE vaccine against a tick-borne disease, which is important in Switzerland, is an inactivated vaccine.
In Switzerland, adults between 25 and 65 are recommended a booster against tetanus and diphtheria about every 20 years.

abschnitte.text: With a vaccination, the body is given a harmless “wanted poster” of a pathogen. In an **inactivated vaccine**, the pathogens are killed, also called **inactivated**, or only individual fragments are included. So the pathogens cannot multiply in the body. The opposite is a live vaccine with weakened but living pathogens, for example against measles. Inactivated vaccines are usually also suitable for people with a weakened immune system.

Some inactivated vaccines contain **whole pathogens** that have been made harmless, for example with formaldehyde, such as the hepatitis A and TBE vaccines. Others contain only one protein from the surface of the pathogen. Since the 1980s the hepatitis B vaccine has been produced by genetic engineering with yeast cells that make such a virus surface protein. A **toxoid** is a detoxified bacterial poison, as in the vaccine against tetanus and diphtheria. In **conjugate vaccines**, sugar substances from the bacterial coat are coupled to a carrier protein.

Because the pathogens do not multiply, the immune response is weaker than with a live vaccine. That is why several doses are usually needed, weeks or months apart. Later the protection slowly wears off, so there are **booster vaccinations**. Inactivated vaccines often contain an enhancer, a so-called adjuvant, so that the immune system reacts more strongly. After the vaccination your arm may hurt or you may feel tired for a short time; this is a normal reaction.

At the end of the 19th century, researchers developed the first vaccines from killed bacteria, for example against cholera and typhoid. A great success was the polio vaccine of **Jonas Salk**, which was approved in the USA in 1955. Polio, also called infantile paralysis, had previously paralysed many children. Salk did not patent his method, so that as many people as possible could benefit from it. Thanks to vaccinations, polio has now disappeared in most countries.

The **Federal Office of Public Health** publishes the Swiss vaccination schedule every year. Many basic vaccinations for children are inactivated vaccines, for example against tetanus, diphtheria, whooping cough and polio. The **TBE vaccine** protects against an inflammation of the brain and its membranes that is transmitted by ticks. In Switzerland it is recommended for almost everyone from about six years of age who spends time outdoors in nature. Whether a vaccination is needed is best discussed with your doctor.

begriffe.erklaerung: A substance that prepares the immune system for a pathogen.
Killed, so that a pathogen can no longer multiply.
A detoxified bacterial poison that still gives protection.
A later vaccination that strengthens the protection again.
An additive that strengthens the effect of a vaccine.

gewusst: Tetanus bacteria live in soil, which is why the vaccination is also important after injuries while gardening.
When asked who owned the patent, Jonas Salk is said to have replied that you could not patent the sun either.
The flu vaccine is adapted anew every year, because flu viruses keep changing.

teile.einleitung: Participant observation is a research method in which researchers live for a long time with the people they are studying. They take part in their everyday life, observe closely and write everything down. In this way they get to know a culture or group from the inside.
wichtigste: In participant observation, researchers live for a long time with the people they study.
It is used mainly in ethnology and sociology.
The ongoing records are called field notes.
A key informant explains connections and arranges contacts.
The danger of losing distance is called “going native”.
In covert observation, the people observed do not know that they are being studied.
Classic fieldwork often lasts at least a year.

abschnitte.text: In **participant observation**, researchers move in with a group of people for a long time. They eat, work and celebrate with them and often learn the language. At the same time they observe closely how the people live and what is important to them. This method is part of **fieldwork**, that is, research on the spot instead of at a desk.

One of its founders is considered to be the Polish-British ethnologist **Bronisław Malinowski**. During the First World War he lived for a long time on the Trobriand Islands near New Guinea. Instead of only reading reports, he took part in village life himself. His book of 1922 about the islanders' exchange trade became a model for **ethnology**.

The method is not only used in distant countries. The American sociologist **William Foote Whyte** lived for several years in an immigrant neighbourhood in Boston. His study **Street Corner Society** of 1943 described the life of young men in this neighbourhood. Today schools, hospitals, clubs or companies are also studied in this way.

Researchers constantly write **field notes** about everything they see and hear. A **key informant** is a person from the group who explains connections and arranges contacts. Classic fieldwork often lasts at least a year. That way you experience a whole yearly cycle with festivals, work and seasons.

Anyone who identifies too strongly with the group may lose their scientific distance; this is called **going native**. That is why **reflexivity** is important: researchers question their own influence and their role. In open observation everyone knows that research is being done, in covert observation they do not. The covert form is controversial because the people were unable to give their consent.

begriffe.erklaerung: Research directly on the spot, where the people live.
The science that compares the cultures and ways of life of people.
The records that researchers make during fieldwork.
A person from the group who explains a lot to the researchers.

gewusst: Malinowski was not actually meant to stay long during the First World War, but because of the war his stay became much longer.
Swiss ethnologists also do research in this way, for example in mountain villages or in cities such as Zurich.
As well as their field notes, some researchers also keep a personal diary about their feelings in the field.

teile.einleitung: The second is the basic unit of time. It is about as long as it takes to say the German word “einundzwanzig” (twenty-one) or to clap your hands once. Today it is measured with atomic clocks more precisely than any other quantity.
wichtigste: The second is abbreviated to “s”.
A minute has 60 seconds, an hour 3,600 and a day 86,400 seconds.
On a clock the thin, fast hand shows the seconds.
One heartbeat of an adult at rest lasts about a second.
The fastest people run 100 metres in less than 10 seconds.
In a countdown you count seconds backwards.
Since 1967 the second has been defined with the help of atoms.

abschnitte.text: The second is one of the seven base units in the International **System of Units** (SI). Other units of time are calculated from it: 60 seconds make a minute, 60 minutes an hour. For very short times it is divided further, for example into milliseconds (thousandths) or microseconds (millionths). A blink of an eye, for example, lasts only about a third of a second.

The name comes from Latin. The hour was first divided into 60 small parts, called “first diminished parts”, which became the minute. These were divided again into 60 parts, the **second** diminished parts, in Latin “secunda”. The division into 60 goes back to the ancient Babylonians, who calculated with the number 60.

In the past a second was the 86,400th part of a day, but the Earth does not turn quite evenly. That is why a new definition has applied since 1967: a second is the time in which a **caesium atom** oscillates 9,192,631,770 times. Such **atomic clocks** are wrong by less than a second in millions of years. In Switzerland the Federal Institute of Metrology METAS in Bern-Wabern runs atomic clocks for the official Swiss time.

In sport hundredths of a second often decide between victory and defeat. In Berlin in 2009 Usain Bolt ran the 100 metres in 9.58 seconds, which is still the world record. At ski races and the Olympic Games the times are often measured by Swiss timing companies. They use light barriers, which are more accurate than any hand-held stopwatch.

In a single second light travels almost 300,000 kilometres, but sound in the air only about 340 metres. That is why you can estimate the distance of a thunderstorm: about three seconds between lightning and thunder correspond to one kilometre. To keep clocks in step with the Earth's rotation, a **leap second** has been added now and then since 1972. Experts have decided to abolish these leap seconds by 2035 at the latest.

begriffe.erklaerung: A unit from the International System of Units, which is used almost everywhere in the world.
A very accurate clock that counts the oscillations of atoms.
An extra second that is added so that clocks match the Earth's rotation.
A thousandth of a second.

gewusst: A hummingbird can beat its wings dozens of times in a second.
A year has over 31 million seconds.
Anyone who is 1 billion seconds old has already lived almost 32 years.

teile.einleitung: A low-pressure area, or low for short, is an area in which the air pressure is lower than in the surroundings. Lows often bring clouds, wind and rain and so determine a large part of our weather. On German-language weather maps you can recognise them by a large T.
wichtigste: In a low-pressure area, the air pressure is lower than in the surroundings.
In the northern hemisphere, the air turns anticlockwise around a low.
Lows often bring clouds and precipitation, because the air rises and cools.
A typical low of the middle latitudes has a warm front and a cold front.
The Icelandic Low in the North Atlantic has a strong influence on the weather in Europe.
The Genoa Low often brings heavy precipitation to the south side of the Alps.
The names of the high and low-pressure areas in Central Europe are given by the Free University of Berlin.

abschnitte.text: The air presses down on the Earth with its weight; this is called **air pressure**. Where the air pressure is lower than all around, a low-pressure area forms. The lowest pressure at its centre is called the **central pressure**. Air pressure is measured in hectopascals; at sea level it is on average about 1013 hectopascals. The opposite of a low is a **high-pressure area**, which usually brings fine weather.

In a low, air flows from all sides towards the centre and rises there. As it rises it cools, and the **water vapour** it contains turns into tiny droplets. In this way clouds form, and soon rain or snow falls. Because of the Earth's rotation, the air does not flow straight to the centre but turns **anticlockwise** in the northern hemisphere. In the southern hemisphere it is the other way round.

A typical low of the middle latitudes forms where warm and cold air meet. A **warm front** with long-lasting rain and a **cold front** with showers, thunderstorms and wind develop. In summer, a **heat low** sometimes forms over land that has warmed up strongly. Tropical storms such as hurricanes are also especially strong low-pressure areas over warm seas.

The **Icelandic Low** is almost always in the North Atlantic and often sends lows towards Europe. For Switzerland, the **Genoa Low** over northern Italy is also important. It often brings heavy rain and snow to Ticino and the southern valleys. Because the lows usually come from the west, bad weather often reaches Switzerland first in the Jura and in western Switzerland.

Especially strong lows can cause **hurricane-force storms**. On 26 December 1999, the storm **Lothar** swept across Switzerland and blew down millions of trees in the forests. Burglind in January 2018 also caused great damage. That is why weather services such as MeteoSwiss give early warnings of storm lows.

Since the 1950s, highs and lows in Central Europe have been given names by the **Free University of Berlin**. Since 2002, members of the public have been able to buy a weather sponsorship and so give a low a name. The money supports weather observation at the university. In the past, lows only got female names; today female and male names alternate every year.

begriffe.erklaerung: The weight of the air pressing on a surface.
The unit in which air pressure is measured.
The boundary between a warm and a cold air mass.
The lowest air pressure at the centre of a low.
A very strong storm with wind speeds of about 118 kilometres per hour or more.

gewusst: On German-language weather maps a low is often marked with a T (for “Tief”), while in English an L for “low” is used.
A barometer shows falling air pressure, which often means that rain is on the way.
In just a few hours, the storm Lothar blew down about as much timber in Switzerland as is normally harvested in several years.

teile.einleitung: The Sphinx Observatory is a research station high up on the Jungfraujoch in the Bernese Alps. At around 3,570 metres above sea level, researchers there measure the weather, the air and the Sun's radiation. At the same time the viewing terrace of the Sphinx is a popular destination for tourists from all over the world.
wichtigste: The Sphinx Observatory stands at around 3,570 metres above sea level on the Jungfraujoch.
It was opened in the 1930s.
From the Jungfraujoch a lift goes up through the rock to the Sphinx.
It is named after the rock on which it stands.
Above the station there is less atmosphere with little water vapour, ideal for measuring sunlight.
The University of Liège has been measuring the make-up of the atmosphere there with spectrometers for decades.
MeteoSwiss runs an automatic weather station on the Sphinx.
Together with Empa and the PSI, aerosols and greenhouse gases, among other things, are measured.

abschnitte.text: The **Jungfraujoch** is a saddle between the mountains Jungfrau and Mönch on the border between the cantons of Bern and Valais. The **Sphinx** is a rocky peak above the saddle on which the observatory was built. It lies at around **3,570 metres** above sea level. All around stretch glaciers, among them the Great Aletsch Glacier, the longest in the Alps. The region is part of the UNESCO World Heritage Site Swiss Alps Jungfrau-Aletsch.

Since 1912 the **Jungfrau Railway** has run through a long tunnel in the Eiger and Mönch to the Jungfraujoch. Its terminus at 3,454 metres is regarded as the highest railway station in Europe. From the saddle a fast **lift** carries visitors and researchers more than 100 metres up through the rock to the Sphinx. Only thanks to the railway did research at this height become possible all year round.

Soon after the railway opened, scientists began doing research on the Jungfraujoch. In 1931 the **High Altitude Research Station Jungfraujoch** was set up there. The Sphinx Observatory was opened in the 1930s and later extended with a dome for astronomical observations. In the past, for example, cosmic rays from space were studied there. Today the focus is on researching the atmosphere.

On the Sphinx **MeteoSwiss** runs an automatic high-altitude weather station. Empa and the Paul Scherrer Institute PSI measure, among other things, **aerosols**, that is tiny floating particles, and **greenhouse gases** such as carbon dioxide and methane. Because the station often lies above the polluted air of the valleys, it shows the make-up of the air over the whole of Europe. That is why it belongs to a worldwide network of measuring stations for monitoring the atmosphere.

Above the Sphinx there is much less air than in the lowlands, and the air contains little **water vapour**. This is ideal for studying sunlight precisely. The **University of Liège** in Belgium has been measuring there for decades with spectrometers which gases occur in the atmosphere. These long series of measurements show, for example, how greenhouse gases or substances that damage the ozone layer are changing.

Besides the research, the Sphinx has a large **viewing terrace**. From there, in clear weather, you can see far across the Alps and sometimes as far as the Vosges and the Black Forest. Every year hundreds of thousands of visitors come up to the Jungfraujoch. In this way tourism and top research meet at the Sphinx.

begriffe.erklaerung: A building from which the sky, the weather or the air are observed and measured.
The layer of air that surrounds the Earth.
Tiny particles such as dust, soot or droplets that float in the air.
A measuring device that splits light into its colours in order to identify substances.
A gas such as carbon dioxide that holds back heat in the atmosphere.

gewusst: On the Sphinx Saharan dust is measured, which is sometimes blown as far as the Alps.
Jungfraujoch station is regarded as the highest railway station in Europe.
The observatory is called the Sphinx because the rock on which it stands has that name.

teile.einleitung: Thomas S. Kuhn was an American physicist, historian of science and philosopher. He wondered how science actually makes progress: does knowledge grow slowly bit by bit, or are there great upheavals? His book about “scientific revolutions” is one of the most widely read books about science of all.
wichtigste: Thomas S. Kuhn lived from 1922 to 1996 and was American.
He obtained his doctorate in physics at Harvard University.
In 1957 his first book, about the Copernican Revolution, came out.
In 1962 he published “The Structure of Scientific Revolutions”.
In it he described how one paradigm is replaced by a new one.
Later he partly replaced the ambiguous term paradigm with “disciplinary matrix”.
From 1979 he taught at MIT until his retirement.

abschnitte.text: Thomas Samuel Kuhn was born in Cincinnati in the USA in 1922. He studied physics at **Harvard University** and wrote his doctoral thesis in that subject there. Even while studying he was fascinated by the history of science. He later taught at Berkeley, at Princeton and, from 1979, at the **Massachusetts Institute of Technology** (MIT). He died in 1996 in Cambridge in the state of Massachusetts.

Kuhn's first book came out in 1957 and dealt with the **Copernican Revolution**. In it he showed how people learned that the Earth goes round the Sun and not the other way round. This change took many decades and was not only a question of astronomy. Religion, philosophy and people's view of the world also played a part. This experience shaped Kuhn's later ideas.

In 1962 “**The Structure of Scientific Revolutions**” came out. The book was originally published in a series called the “International Encyclopedia of Unified Science”. It was translated into many languages and sold millions of copies. People outside science, for example in business and politics, also took up Kuhn's terms. As a result, expressions such as “paradigm shift” have entered everyday language.

According to Kuhn, a **paradigm** is the shared way of thinking of a group of researchers, that is, their basic assumptions, methods and models. In calm times, researchers carry out **normal science**: they solve puzzles within this framework. If more and more contradictions appear, which are called anomalies, the field gets into a crisis. Then a new paradigm can replace the old one, as with Copernicus or with Einstein's theory of relativity. Kuhn called this upheaval a scientific revolution.

Critics accused Kuhn of using the word paradigm with very many meanings. That is why he later introduced the term **disciplinary matrix**, which includes everything that a scientific community shares. An important part of it is **exemplars**, that is, model examples. These are concrete problems with solutions from which students learn a subject, for example the swinging pendulum in physics. Anyone who has solved many such examples sees new problems through the eyes of their subject.

Kuhn's ideas changed the way people think about science. He showed that researchers too work in communities and are shaped by habits. Some philosophers criticised him because his view made progress look too much like a change of fashion. Nevertheless, his book is still required reading in the history and philosophy of science today, including at Swiss universities.

begriffe.erklaerung: The shared way of thinking and the models of a group of researchers.
When an old basic idea is replaced by a completely new one.
Everyday research that solves puzzles within the existing framework.
A result that does not fit the current theory.
When a professor retires from their post.

gewusst: Thanks to Kuhn, the word “paradigm shift” became so well known that it now appears in advertising and politics.
Although Kuhn was a physicist, he became famous mainly as a philosopher and historian.
Kuhn said that an idea sometimes only wins through once a new generation of researchers has grown up.

teile.einleitung: The Swiss Greenland Expedition of 1912 was a research journey in which a small group of Swiss men crossed the huge Greenland ice sheet from west to east. It was led by the Zurich geophysicist Alfred de Quervain. To this day names such as Schweizerland in East Greenland recall this adventure.
wichtigste: The leader of the expedition was the Swiss geophysicist Alfred de Quervain.
The crossing party travelled from the west coast to the east coast of Greenland.
The route over the ice sheet was about 650 kilometres long.
Dog sledges were used for transport.
The goal was the place Angmagssalik on the east coast, which is now called Tasiilaq.
The expedition gave the landscape Schweizerland its name.
A high mountain was named after the naturalist François-Alphonse Forel.
De Quervain described the journey in the book “Quer durchs Grönlandeis” (Across Greenland's Ice).

abschnitte.text: **Alfred de Quervain** (1879 to 1927) was a Swiss geophysicist, meteorologist and earthquake researcher from Zurich. He was especially interested in weather and climate at great heights and in polar regions. As early as 1909 he had made a first journey to West Greenland. From this came the plan to cross the whole ice sheet.

The expedition consisted of two parts. One group stayed on the west coast and made scientific measurements there, for example of weather and glaciers. The **crossing party** with de Quervain consisted of four men. It wanted to cross the **ice sheet** from west to east and observe weather, altitude and snow on the way.

abschnitte.titel: With dog sledges over the ice
abschnitte.text: In the summer of 1912 the men travelled over the ice with **dog sledges**. The route was about 650 kilometres long and led over heights of well over 2,000 metres. Cold, storms and crevasses made the journey dangerous. After several weeks they reached the east coast and finally the place **Angmagssalik**, now called Tasiilaq. This was one of the first crossings of Greenland.

On the way down to the east coast the researchers saw a wild mountain landscape, which they called **Schweizerland** (“Switzerland land”). They named one of the highest mountains after the naturalist **François-Alphonse Forel** from Vaud, who is regarded as the founder of the study of lakes. Mont Forel is over 3,000 metres high and is one of the highest peaks in Greenland. These names are still on the maps today.

Alfred de Quervain described the journey in the book **“Quer durchs Grönlandeis”**, which inspired many people. The measurements provided valuable data about the weather and ice in the interior of Greenland. The expedition started a long tradition of Swiss polar research. To this day Swiss scientists study the Greenland ice, for example to understand climate change.

begriffe.erklaerung: A huge layer of ice that covers almost a whole country, as in Greenland or Antarctica.
A research journey into a little-known, often dangerous area.
A researcher who studies the Earth with the methods of physics, for example earthquakes or weather.
A deep crack in the ice of a glacier.

gewusst: In Greenland there is a landscape called Schweizerland, named by Swiss researchers.
The place Angmagssalik, which the expedition reached, is now called Tasiilaq.
A mountain over 3,000 metres high in Greenland bears the name of a researcher from Lake Geneva.

teile.einleitung: The gambler's fallacy is a widespread error of thinking about chance. Anyone who falls for it believes that after a long run of bad luck an event is now “due”. But coins, dice and roulette balls have no memory.
wichtigste: In the gambler's fallacy you believe that independent random events will even out in the short term.
In European roulette the chance of red is always 18/37, no matter what came before.
In 1913 black came up 26 times in a row at the casino in Monte Carlo, and many players lost a lot of money on red.
The probability of throwing heads five times in a row with a fair coin is 1/32.
Lottery numbers are never “overdue”, because every draw is independent.
The law of large numbers is often misunderstood here.
The opposite error, believing in a lucky streak, is called the hot hand fallacy.

abschnitte.text: The **gambler's fallacy** is a belief that random events must soon even themselves out. If black comes up five times at roulette, many people think red is now “due”. But every spin is **independent** of the ones before. The ball does not know where it landed before.

A European **roulette** wheel has 37 pockets: 18 red, 18 black and the green zero. So the chance of red on every spin is 18/37, just under 49 per cent. In 1913 black came up 26 times in a row at the casino in **Monte Carlo**. Many players bet more and more money on red, because they thought it simply had to come. They lost huge sums, which is why the error of thinking is also called the Monte Carlo fallacy.

With a fair **coin** the chance of heads on every throw is 1/2. Throwing heads five times in a row has the probability 1/2 × 1/2 × 1/2 × 1/2 × 1/2, that is **1/32**. That is rare, but if the first four throws were heads, the chance for the fifth is still exactly 1/2. The rare run does not make the next throw less likely. In the same way, after four daughters a fifth child is not more likely to be a son.

The **law of large numbers** says that with very many throws the proportion of heads gets close to a half. Many people misunderstand this and believe that chance must actively correct differences. In truth, earlier differences are not evened out but simply diluted by the huge number of further throws. After 10 throws you can still have clearly more heads than tails; after a million throws such a difference hardly matters any more.

Some people play lottery numbers that have not been drawn for a long time, because they are supposedly **overdue**. Others avoid numbers that have just been drawn. Both make no sense, because every draw is independent of earlier ones. The opposite error is the **hot hand fallacy**: you believe that someone who has scored several times is on a lucky streak and will go on scoring. In real games of chance that is not true either.

Our brain is constantly looking for **patterns**, even where there are none. We also often imagine chance to be more even than it really is. Real random sequences surprisingly often contain long runs. Anyone who knows about the gambler's fallacy is less easily tempted into risky bets. Games of chance are built so that in the long run the casino always wins.

begriffe.erklaerung: A number between 0 and 1 that shows how likely an event is.
Two events do not influence each other.
A wrong line of thought that leads to a wrong result.
The rule that with very many attempts the frequency gets close to the probability.

gewusst: In the famous game in Monte Carlo in 1913, black came up 26 times in a row.
A coin has no memory; even after ten heads the chance of tails is exactly 1/2.
Real chance forms long runs more often than most people expect.

teile.einleitung: Tiktaalik was a prehistoric fish that lived about 375 million years ago. It had features of fish and at the same time of animals with four legs. That is why it is a famous example of how life came from the water onto land.
wichtigste: Tiktaalik was found in 2004 on Ellesmere Island in northern Canada.
The fossils are about 375 million years old.
Tiktaalik shows the transition from fish to land vertebrates.
Unlike typical fish, it had a movable neck.
Its pectoral fins contained bones like an upper arm, an ulna and wrist-like parts.
It probably had gills and lungs.
In the language of the Inuit, the name means “large freshwater fish”.

abschnitte.text: For a long time researchers searched for a fossil that stands between fish and the first four-legged animals. The palaeontologist **Neil Shubin** and his colleagues considered which rocks such an animal would have to be in. They chose layers from the late **Devonian** on **Ellesmere Island** in the Canadian Arctic. After several summers of searching, they found the first skeletons there in 2004. In 2006 they presented Tiktaalik to the world.

Tiktaalik had scales, gills and fins with fin rays like a fish. At the same time it had a flat head with eyes on top, similar to a crocodile. Unlike fish, it had a **movable neck**, so it could turn its head without moving its whole body. Its ribs were strong and could perhaps support the body out of the water. It probably breathed with gills and with simple **lungs**.

The pectoral fins are especially exciting. They contain bones that correspond to an **upper arm**, an ulna and a radius, as well as parts like a wrist. Tiktaalik could probably use them to prop itself up in shallow water, a bit like doing a press-up. The same sequence of bones is still found today in the arms of humans and in the legs of frogs or cats.

Tiktaalik lived in shallow rivers and swamps in a warm climate. At that time Ellesmere Island lay close to the equator, because the continents have moved since then. In the shallow, often low-oxygen water it was useful to be able to gulp air. Tiktaalik was a predator and probably hunted other fish.

Tiktaalik is not a direct ancestor of all land animals but a close relative of these ancestors. However, it shows very clearly how features developed step by step. Neil Shubin wrote the book “**Your Inner Fish**” about it. In it he explains that our bodies still contain many traces of our fish past. That is why Tiktaalik is often shown in school books as an example of evolution.

begriffe.erklaerung: A petrified remain of a living thing from ancient times.
A geological period from about 419 to 359 million years ago.
A living thing that combines features of two groups of animals.
Animals with a backbone and four limbs, also called tetrapods.

gewusst: The researchers predicted in advance in rocks of which age they would find such an animal, and they were right.
The name Tiktaalik was chosen by Inuit elders from Nunavut.
In Poland, footprints of four-legged animals have been found that are even older than Tiktaalik.

teile.einleitung: A scientific theory is a well-tested explanation for many observations in nature. Unlike in everyday life, it is not just a guess but is supported by many experiments and measurements. Famous theories such as the theory of evolution or plate tectonics have changed our picture of the world.
wichtigste: A scientific theory is a well-tested explanation for many observations.
The theory of evolution explains the variety of living things through change and natural selection.
Alfred Wegener presented the theory of continental drift in 1912.
Plate tectonics explains earthquakes, volcanoes and mountain ranges such as the Alps.
In the 16th century Nicolaus Copernicus argued that the Earth moves around the Sun.
According to germ theory, tiny pathogens cause many diseases.
The Big Bang theory explains the origin of the universe from a very hot and dense state.

abschnitte.text: In everyday life people say “That's just a theory” and mean a guess. In science, **theory** means something completely different: a well-tested explanation that brings together many observations. An idea that has not yet been tested, on the other hand, is called a **hypothesis**. A good theory also allows predictions that can be checked.

It starts with observations and questions, from which a hypothesis arises. Researchers test it with **experiments** and measurements, often independently of one another in many countries. If the explanation survives all the tests, it becomes an accepted theory. The philosopher Karl Popper stressed that it must be possible to disprove a theory; this is called **falsifiability**.

In the 16th century **Nicolaus Copernicus** put forward the theory that the Earth moves around the Sun and not the other way round. In 1912 the German researcher **Alfred Wegener** presented the idea that the continents move. This later developed into **plate tectonics**, which explains earthquakes, volcanoes and mountain ranges such as the Alps. The Big Bang theory describes how the universe came into being from a very hot and dense initial state.

Charles Darwin's **theory of evolution** explains the variety of living things through change and natural selection over a long time. According to **germ theory**, tiny pathogens such as bacteria are the cause of many diseases. Researchers such as Louis Pasteur and Robert Koch confirmed it in the 19th century. Since then, doctors have washed their hands thoroughly before operations.

At the beginning of the 19th century the English naturalist **John Dalton** founded modern **atomic theory**. It says that all substances are made of tiny particles, atoms. In Bern in 1905, while working at the patent office, **Albert Einstein** developed the special theory of relativity. So theories can also arise in quite unexpected places.

begriffe.erklaerung: A well-tested explanation for many observations.
An idea that still has to be tested.
A planned test to check an idea.
A theory must be stated in such a way that it could be disproved by observations.

gewusst: Alfred Wegener's idea of moving continents was laughed at for a long time and only accepted decades after his death.
A scientific theory is never finally proved, but it can be confirmed again and again.
Albert Einstein developed some of his most famous ideas while he was working at the patent office in Bern.

teile.einleitung: Statistical significance is a tool with which researchers check whether a result is probably real or could have come about just by chance. It is used in almost all sciences, from medicine to particle physics.
wichtigste: A result is called significant if it can hardly be explained by chance.
In many fields a significance level of 5 per cent applies.
The null hypothesis usually states that there is no difference or effect.
A type I error means rejecting the null hypothesis although it is true.
A type II error means missing an effect that is really there.
Significant does not automatically mean important or meaningful.
In particle physics 5 sigma is required for a discovery.

abschnitte.text: Imagine a coin shows heads ten times in a row. Is it a trick coin, or was it chance? A **statistical test** answers exactly such questions. If a result is very unlikely when only chance is at work, it is called **significant**. The word comes from the Latin significare, which means to show something.

You start with a **null hypothesis**, that is the assumption that there is no effect. In a test of a medicine, for example, it says that the medicine works no better than a placebo. Then you calculate the **p-value**, the probability of such a clear result if the null hypothesis is true. If this value is below the significance level, usually 5 per cent, you reject the null hypothesis. This limit was made well known by the British statistician Ronald Fisher in the 1920s.

A test can also be wrong. In a **type I error** you reject the null hypothesis although it is true, so you see an effect that does not exist. In a **type II error** you miss an effect that is really there. The probability of discovering a real effect is called the **power** of the test. Larger samples increase the power.

If you carry out 20 independent tests at the 5 per cent level and none of the effects exists, you still expect on average one falsely significant result. That is why you have to be stricter when doing many tests. In the **Bonferroni correction** you divide the level by the number of tests. With 10 tests and an overall level of 5 per cent, the threshold for each single test is 0.005.

abschnitte.titel: Significant is not the same as important
abschnitte.text: A very large study can detect even tiny differences as significant. If a medicine lowers blood pressure by only 0.5 mmHg, that may be significant but hardly matters medically. That is why you always look at the **effect size** as well. Particle physics is especially strict and requires **5 sigma**, a probability of error of about one in 3.5 million. This threshold was reached in 2012 at CERN in Geneva with the discovery of the Higgs boson.

begriffe.erklaerung: The assumption that there is no effect or difference.
The probability of getting such a clear result by chance alone.
A limit fixed in advance, usually 5 per cent, from which a result is called significant.
The probability of discovering an effect that is really there with a test.

gewusst: The well-known 5 per cent limit is an agreement and not a law of nature.
Some journals have restricted the reporting of p-values because they are often misunderstood.

teile.einleitung: Ticinosuchus ferox was a predatory reptile that lived about 240 million years ago in the Triassic period. Its skeleton was found on Monte San Giorgio in Ticino, one of the most famous fossil sites in the world. The name means roughly “wild crocodile from Ticino”.
wichtigste: Ticinosuchus was found on Monte San Giorgio in the canton of Ticino.
It belongs to the archosaurs related to crocodiles.
The animal was about 2.5 metres long.
The palaeontologist Bernhard Krebs described it in 1965.
Ticinosuchus was probably a predator that hunted on land.
The find is remarkable because the site consists of marine deposits.
The species name “ferox” means “wild”.

abschnitte.text: Ticinosuchus was about **2.5 metres** long, so longer than an adult human is tall. It walked on four legs that stood more under its body than splayed out to the sides as in a lizard. This meant it could move around fairly well on land. It had a long tail and a powerful head with pointed teeth. On its back it had rows of small bony plates, like those of modern crocodiles.

Ticinosuchus belongs to the **archosaurs**, a large group that also includes dinosaurs, pterosaurs, birds and crocodiles. Within this group it is on the side of the crocodile relatives. But it was not a crocodile in today's sense; it was an early relative. In the Triassic there were many such animals, which were often the largest predators on land. The dinosaurs only later became the dominant land animals.

**Monte San Giorgio** is in southern Ticino on Lake Lugano, near the border with Italy. Its rock layers contain very well-preserved fossils from the Middle Triassic, especially fish and marine reptiles. Since 2003 the mountain has been a **UNESCO World Heritage Site**. In the 20th century the University of Zurich carried out large excavations there, during which Ticinosuchus was also recovered. Many finds can be seen in the museum in Meride and in the Palaeontological Museum in Zurich.

abschnitte.titel: A land animal in the sea?
abschnitte.text: The rocks on Monte San Giorgio are deposits from a shallow sea basin. That is why it is surprising that an animal that lived on land was found there. Experts think that the dead body was washed into the sea from a nearby shore. On the low-oxygen seabed it hardly decayed and was covered by mud. In this way the skeleton was preserved almost completely.

The palaeontologist **Bernhard Krebs** described Ticinosuchus scientifically in 1965. He chose the name from “Ticino”, the Italian word for the canton, and the Greek “suchos” for crocodile. The skeleton is one of the best examples of an early crocodile relative from Europe. It helps researchers understand how the archosaurs developed in the Triassic.

begriffe.erklaerung: A petrified remain or a trace of a living thing from ancient times.
A geological period from about 252 to 201 million years ago.
A group of reptiles that includes crocodiles, dinosaurs and birds.
An expert who studies fossils and prehistoric life.

gewusst: Ticinosuchus was already alive before the great dinosaurs ruled the Earth.
Birds are distantly related to Ticinosuchus, because they also belong to the archosaurs.
Over the years, thousands of fossils have been found on Monte San Giorgio.

teile.einleitung: Cones are the woody seed structures of conifers such as firs, spruces, pines or larches. The seeds ripen between their scales. What is fascinating is that cones open and close all by themselves, depending on whether the weather is dry or damp.
wichtigste: Cones grow on conifers and carry the seeds under their scales.
In dry weather a cone opens its scales so that the winged seeds can fly away.
To open and close, the cone needs nothing but a change in humidity.
The scales bend because two layers of tissue swell to different degrees.
The cones of the silver fir stand upright on the branches.
Most of the cones on the floor of Swiss forests come from the spruce.
Squirrels like to get the seeds out of the cones.

abschnitte.text: A cone is a seed structure, that is, the part of a **conifer** in which the seeds develop. It consists of an axis around which many woody **scales** are arranged in a spiral. Under each scale there are usually two seeds, each with a small wing. Depending on the type of tree, it takes from a few months to two years for a cone to ripen.

When the air is dry, the scales spread apart and the seeds can fall out. In rain or fog they close again, because wet seeds would not fly far. This works because each scale consists of **two layers** that swell to different degrees when damp. The cone needs no energy and no living cells for this; even a cone that has fallen off still moves.

In everyday German almost all cones are called “Tannenzapfen” (fir cones), but that is usually wrong. The **silver fir** carries its cones upright at the top of the crown. When they are ripe, the scales fall off one by one, and only the spindle stays on the branch. The **spruce**, on the other hand, has hanging cones that fall to the ground whole. That is why almost all the cones you find in a Swiss forest are spruce cones.

The seeds in the cones are nutritious and popular with many animals. The **squirrel** gnaws off the scales and leaves behind a frayed spindle. Mice, on the other hand, gnaw the cones neatly and smoothly. The **common crossbill** is a bird with a crossed beak, which it uses to skilfully get seeds out of the cones. Woodpeckers also wedge cones into cracks in trees to peck them open.

Researchers have taken the movement of cones as a model; this is called **biomimetics**. This led to the idea of fabrics that open small air holes when you sweat and close again as they dry. Building fronts that open by themselves depending on the weather are also being developed on this principle. Some people even use cones as simple weather indicators.

begriffe.erklaerung: A tree with needles instead of broad leaves, for example spruce, fir or pine.
A woody plate on the cone under which the seeds lie.
The central axis of a cone on which the scales sit.
Technology that copies ideas from nature.

gewusst: A cone can still open and close even after years if you alternately make it wet and let it dry.
You almost never find whole silver fir cones on the ground, because they already fall apart on the tree.
The cones of some pine species in North America only open after a forest fire, because of the heat.

teile.einleitung: T cells are white blood cells and are among the most important fighters in our immune system. They recognise cells that have been infected by viruses or have turned into cancer cells, and they help to get rid of them. They are named after the thymus, the organ in which they mature.
wichtigste: T cells are a group of white blood cells, the lymphocytes.
They mature in the thymus, which shrinks over the course of life.
Helper T cells carry the marker CD4 on their surface.
Cytotoxic CD8 T cells kill infected or abnormal body cells.
A T-cell receptor recognises a small piece of protein that is presented on an MHC molecule.
HIV mainly attacks CD4 helper T cells.
In 2025 the Nobel Prize in Medicine was awarded for discoveries about regulatory T cells.

abschnitte.text: T cells are **lymphocytes**, a type of white blood cell. They come from stem cells in the bone marrow and then travel to the **thymus**, an organ behind the breastbone. After that they patrol through the blood and lymph and stay in lymph nodes and the spleen. They belong to the acquired immune defence, which can remember particular pathogens.

In the thymus, the young T cells learn to tell foreign from self. In **negative selection**, T cells that react strongly to the body's own substances are removed. This prevents them from attacking the body itself. Only a small part of the cells passes this strict test. In children the thymus is large; later it shrinks and is partly replaced by fat.

Every T cell carries a **T-cell receptor**, which, like a lock, only fits one particular key. Body cells show small pieces of protein on their surface on so-called **MHC molecules**, rather like identity cards. If such a piece comes from a virus, the matching T cell recognises the danger. Then it multiplies strongly and forms a whole army of identical cells.

**Helper T cells** with the marker CD4 pass on commands to other defence cells, for example to the B cells, which make antibodies. **Cytotoxic T cells** with CD8 kill infected cells directly. Regulatory T cells put the brakes on the immune system so that it does not overreact. Memory T cells stay in the body for years and react much faster the next time they meet the same pathogen. This is also what makes many vaccinations work.

**HIV** mainly destroys helper T cells and so weakens the whole immune system. In **CAR T-cell therapy**, T cells from cancer patients are given a new receptor against tumour cells in the laboratory and returned to the body. In 2025 Mary Brunkow, Fred Ramsdell and Shimon Sakaguchi received the Nobel Prize in Medicine for their research on regulatory T cells. These cells help to prevent the immune system from attacking the body itself.

begriffe.erklaerung: A group of white blood cells that includes T cells and B cells.
An organ behind the breastbone in which T cells mature.
A feature by which the immune system recognises something foreign.
A protein on the cell surface that shows small pieces of protein like an identity card.
A disease in which the immune system attacks the body itself.

gewusst: There are so many different T-cell receptors in the body that almost any imaginable pathogen can be recognised by some T cell.
The letter T in the name stands for thymus.
For a long time the thymus was thought to be a useless organ, until its task was discovered in the 1960s.

teile.einleitung: Toblerone is a famous chocolate from Bern with pieces in the shape of triangles. It was invented in 1908 by Theodor Tobler and Emil Baumann and contains nougat made of honey and almonds. With its typical shape it is one of the best-known Swiss products in the world.
wichtigste: Toblerone was invented in Bern in 1908.
It was invented by Theodor Tobler and Emil Baumann.
The pieces are shaped like triangles.
The name contains the Italian word “torrone”, a nougat made of honey and almonds.
For a long time the Matterhorn was shown on the packet, and a bear is hidden in the mountain.
Since 2023 Toblerone has been partly produced in Slovakia.
It comes with milk, dark and white chocolate.

abschnitte.text: Toblerone is a **milk chocolate** with small pieces of honey and almond nougat. Typical features are the **triangles** in a row and the triangular box. As well as the classic milk chocolate, there are varieties with dark and with white chocolate. The bars range from tiny ones to bars weighing several kilograms.

Theodor Tobler ran a chocolate factory in Bern that his father had founded. In 1908, together with his cousin **Emil Baumann**, he developed the new chocolate. The name is a mixture of **Tobler** and the Italian word torrone. Torrone is a sweet nougat made of honey, almonds and egg white. In 1909 Tobler patented the production method in Bern.

It is often said that the shape is reminiscent of the **Matterhorn**. According to another story, the inventors were inspired by dancers who formed a pyramid in a show. In any case, the Matterhorn was shown on the packaging for a long time. Hidden in the picture of the mountain is a **bear**, the heraldic animal of the city of Bern.

The Tobler company later merged with Suchard and today belongs to the American food group **Mondelez**. Toblerone is still produced in **Bern**. Since 2023, however, part of the production has been done in Bratislava in **Slovakia**. Because the chocolate is therefore no longer made only in Switzerland, the Matterhorn was not allowed to stay on the packet under the Swissness rules. Since then the packet has shown a generic mountain.

Toblerone is sold in very many countries and is a popular **souvenir** from Switzerland. Travellers buy it especially often in duty-free shops at airports. In 2016 a change caused a stir when the gaps between the triangles were made bigger in Great Britain to save weight. After protests from customers, the old shape was later brought back.

begriffe.erklaerung: A sweet mixture made, for example, of honey, sugar and nuts or almonds.
An Italian nougat made of honey, almonds and egg white.
Swiss rules that set out when a product may be described as Swiss.
An animal that is shown on the coat of arms of a city or country.

gewusst: A bear was hidden in the Matterhorn on the old Toblerone packet, and many people only discovered it after years.
Toblerone was one of the first chocolates whose production method was protected by a patent.
The inventor Theodor Tobler was the son of the company's founder, Jean Tobler.

teile.einleitung: A stethoscope is a device that doctors use to listen to sounds inside the body, for example your heartbeat. It is one of the best-known tools in medicine. With it you can also hear how the air flows in the lungs.
wichtigste: With a stethoscope you listen to the heart, lungs and intestines.
Listening in this way is called auscultation.
It was invented in 1816 by the French doctor René Laënnec.
A stethoscope consists of a chest piece, tubes and earpieces.
It does not amplify sounds electrically but carries the sound along.
A stethoscope is often also used when measuring blood pressure.

abschnitte.text: The stethoscope is a listening device for examining the body. The name comes from Greek: stethos means chest and skopein means to look at. Doctors often wear it around their neck. Listening with a stethoscope is called **auscultation** in technical language.

At the front is the **chest piece**, usually with a thin membrane and a small funnel. When it is placed on the skin, the membrane vibrates with the sounds inside the body. The sound travels through the **tubes** to the ear tubes with soft earpieces. Because hardly any sounds from outside get in, you hear the quiet sounds much more clearly.

At the heart you hear the **heart sounds**, which are made when the heart valves close. It sounds a bit like “ba-boom”. In the lungs you hear the rushing of the air you breathe, and with pneumonia often crackling or rattling too. On the tummy, a gurgling sound shows that the intestines are working.

In 1816 the French doctor **René Laënnec** in Paris wanted to examine a young patient. At that time doctors put their ear directly on the chest, which made him feel uncomfortable. He rolled a sheet of paper into a tube and suddenly heard the heart much more loudly. From this he developed a wooden listening tube, and later tubes and two earpieces were added.

When **measuring blood pressure**, a cuff is put around the upper arm and pumped up. With the stethoscope in the crook of the elbow you hear when the blood starts to flow again and when the knocking disappears. This gives the two values of blood pressure. Today there are also automatic devices for this that do not need a stethoscope.

As well as classic stethoscopes, there are **electronic stethoscopes**, which can amplify and record sounds. This means heart sounds can be saved or sent to other experts. Despite ultrasound and other modern devices, the stethoscope remains important. It is cheap, ready to use quickly and needs no electricity.

begriffe.erklaerung: Listening to sounds inside the body with a stethoscope.
A valve in the heart that makes sure the blood flows in only one direction.
A thin, vibrating disc that picks up sound.
The pressure with which the blood pushes against the walls of the blood vessels.

gewusst: The first stethoscope was simply a rolled-up sheet of paper.
Many doctors warm the chest piece in their hand before listening, because otherwise it feels cold on the skin.
Vets also use stethoscopes, even on elephants.

teile.einleitung: The Nobel Prize is regarded as the most important award in the world for science, literature and peace. For its size, Switzerland has produced a particularly large number of Nobel Prize winners.
wichtigste: The very first Nobel Peace Prize went in 1901 to Henry Dunant from Geneva, together with Frédéric Passy.
The International Committee of the Red Cross in Geneva received the Nobel Peace Prize three times.
In 1919 Carl Spitteler became the first Swiss writer to receive the Nobel Prize in Literature.
In 1920 Charles-Édouard Guillaume received the Nobel Prize in Physics for the alloy Invar.
The Basel chemists Paul Müller and Tadeus Reichstein received the Nobel Prize in Medicine.
Researchers at the IBM laboratory in Rüschlikon won the Nobel Prize in Physics in 1986 and 1987.
In 1996 Rolf Zinkernagel received the Nobel Prize in Medicine for research on the immune system.

abschnitte.text: The Nobel Prize goes back to the Swedish inventor **Alfred Nobel**, who had invented dynamite. In his will he decided that his fortune should be used for prizes. Since 1901 prizes have been awarded every year for physics, chemistry, medicine, literature and peace. A prize for economics was added later. The prizes are presented each December in Stockholm, and the Peace Prize in Oslo.

In 1901 **Henry Dunant** from Geneva, together with the Frenchman Frédéric Passy, received the very first Nobel Peace Prize. Dunant had the idea for the Red Cross after seeing the misery of the wounded after the Battle of Solferino in 1859. The **International Committee of the Red Cross** in Geneva later received the Nobel Peace Prize three times, in 1917, 1944 and 1963. This makes it one of the most honoured organisations.

In 1919 **Carl Spitteler** from Liestal became the first Swiss writer to receive the Nobel Prize in Literature. He was honoured above all for his great epic poem “Olympian Spring”. In 1946 Hermann Hesse also received the Nobel Prize in Literature. Hesse was born in Germany but lived for a long time in Ticino and was a Swiss citizen.

Swiss researchers were especially successful in chemistry and medicine. The Bern surgeon Theodor Kocher received the Nobel Prize in Medicine in 1909 for his work on the thyroid gland. The Basel chemist Paul Müller was honoured in 1948 for discovering the effect of **DDT** against insects, which at the time helped against diseases such as malaria. Tadeus Reichstein received the prize in 1950 for research on hormones such as **cortisone**. Rolf Zinkernagel showed how immune cells recognise cells infected by viruses and received the Nobel Prize in Medicine for it in 1996.

**Charles-Édouard Guillaume** from Neuchâtel received the Nobel Prize in Physics in 1920 for the metal alloy Invar, which hardly expands when heated. Invar was important for accurate clocks and measuring instruments. At the IBM research laboratory in Rüschlikon, Heinrich Rohrer and Gerd Binnig invented the **scanning tunnelling microscope**, with which individual atoms can be made visible; for this there was a Nobel Prize in 1986. A year later Karl Alexander Müller received the prize for high-temperature superconductivity. In 2019 the Geneva astronomers Michel Mayor and Didier Queloz were honoured for discovering the first planet orbiting a Sun-like star.

begriffe.erklaerung: A famous prize that Alfred Nobel's foundation awards every year for great achievements.
A mixture of two or more metals with new properties.
A state in which a material conducts electricity with no resistance at all.
A microscope that can scan individual atoms with a fine tip.

gewusst: Two Nobel Prizes in Physics in two years running went to the same laboratory in Rüschlikon on Lake Zurich.
The Red Cross in Geneva has won the Nobel Peace Prize three times in all, more than any other organisation.
At the time of his Nobel Prize, Henry Dunant was poor and was living in Heiden in the Appenzell region.

teile.einleitung: Carrying capacity is a term from ecology. It states how many living things of one species a habitat can feed in the long term. It is abbreviated with the letter K, and it helps us understand why animal populations do not grow endlessly.
wichtigste: The carrying capacity K is the maximum population size that a habitat can feed permanently.
In logistic growth, the growth curve has an S shape.
The population grows fastest at half the carrying capacity.
Pierre-François Verhulst set up the logistic growth equation in 1838.
Once a population has reached the carrying capacity, its growth is zero.
Competition for food is a density-dependent factor.
On St Matthew Island, a reindeer population collapsed after greatly exceeding the carrying capacity.

abschnitte.text: Every habitat has only limited **resources** such as food, water, shelter and space. The **carrying capacity** K is the largest number of animals of one species that it can support in the long term. If more animals live there, food becomes scarce and the population decreases again. A meadow, for example, can only feed a certain number of cows without being grazed bare. That is why on Swiss Alpine pastures it is set out how many animals may graze in summer.

At first a small **population** grows quickly, because there is enough food for everyone. The closer it gets to the carrying capacity, the more slowly it grows. The curve therefore looks like an S lying on its side; this is called **logistic growth**. The Belgian mathematician **Pierre-François Verhulst** described this growth with an equation in 1838. The curve is steepest exactly at half the carrying capacity, that is, at K/2.

The equation for growth is: growth = r · N · (1 − N/K). Here N is the number of animals and r is the growth rate. With r = 0.5 per year, N = 200 and K = 1000, this gives 0.5 · 200 · 0.8 = 80 animals of growth per year. If N reaches exactly the value K, the bracket becomes zero and the population stops growing. With K = 800 animals, the population grows fastest at 400 animals.

Some factors have a stronger effect the more densely the animals live. Such **density-dependent factors** include competition for food, diseases that spread more easily in large groups, or predators. Other factors, such as a harsh winter or a flood, affect all the animals, no matter how many there are. They are called density-independent. Together they determine how large a population really becomes.

abschnitte.titel: The reindeer of St Matthew Island
abschnitte.text: In 1944, 29 reindeer were released on remote **St Matthew Island** in the Bering Sea. There were plenty of lichens there and no wolves. By 1963 the population had grown to about 6000 animals, far more than the island could feed in the long term. The lichens were grazed bare, and after a harsh winter the population collapsed to a few dozen animals. The example shows what happens when a population far exceeds the carrying capacity.

Fishing and hunting use the idea of carrying capacity to manage resources sustainably. If you keep a population at about half the carrying capacity, you can let the most grow back and harvest the most. The carrying capacity of the whole Earth for humans is also discussed. It depends greatly on how much food, energy and space each person needs.

begriffe.erklaerung: The largest number of living things that a habitat can feed permanently.
All the living things of one species that live together in an area.
Growth that is fast at first and then levels off at an upper limit.
An influence that becomes stronger the more animals live in a small space.

gewusst: The term carrying capacity was originally used for pastures and herds of livestock.
Experts later determined the causes of the reindeer deaths on St Matthew Island from the bones that were found.
In the laboratory, bacteria in a Petri dish often show a very neat S-curve.

teile.einleitung: The range is a simple measure from statistics that shows how far apart the values of a data set are. It is calculated by subtracting the smallest value from the largest. In this way you can see at a glance whether numbers are close together or widely spread.
wichtigste: The range is the largest value minus the smallest value of a data set.
It shows how far apart the values are.
For the numbers 4, 11, 7, 2 and 9 the range is 11 minus 2, that is 9.
For temperatures of -5, 3, 8 and -2 degrees the range is 13 degrees.
If all the values are the same, the range is 0.
If you know the range and the smallest value, you can work out the largest.
A larger range means that the values are more spread out.

abschnitte.text: The **range** is a **measure of spread**, which means it describes how different values are. In a data set you look for the **maximum**, the largest value, and the **minimum**, the smallest. Then you calculate maximum minus minimum. The result always has the same unit as the data, for example degrees, centimetres or marks. A range is never negative.

For the numbers 4, 11, 7, 2 and 9 the largest value is 11 and the smallest 2, so the range is 9. Four children are 142, 155, 149 and 160 centimetres tall; the range is 160 minus 142, that is 18 centimetres. With temperatures you have to watch out for **negative numbers**: from -5 to 8 degrees is 13 degrees. If all the values are the same, the range is 0.

You can also turn the calculation round. If a data set has a range of 20 and a smallest value of 15, the largest value is 15 plus 20, that is 35. If, on the other hand, you know the largest value, you subtract the range. Such tasks help you understand what the range actually means.

The marks of class A have a range of 2, those of class B a range of 3.5. It follows that the marks in class B are more **spread out**. But the range does not tell you whether class B is better or worse. For that you need an **average** such as the mean or the median. That is why the range is often used together with such averages.

The range is very easy to calculate and easy to understand. Its drawback: it depends on only two values, the largest and the smallest. A single **outlier**, for example a very unusual measurement, can make it much bigger. That is why experts also use other measures, for example the interquartile range or the standard deviation.

In the weather forecast people talk about the range between the lowest and the highest temperature of a day. In deserts it can be several dozen degrees between day and night. It also gives a quick overview of prices, sports results or people's heights. In German the same word, “Spannweite”, is also used for the width of wings, for example of birds or aircraft.

begriffe.erklaerung: A list of values, for example measurements or marks.
The largest value of a data set.
The smallest value of a data set.
How much values differ from one another.
A value that differs greatly from all the others.

gewusst: A range can never be less than zero.
A single wrong measurement can double the range of a whole series of measurements.
Two classes can have the same average mark but quite different ranges.

teile.einleitung: A bull is an adult male of the cattle family. Bulls are big and strong and can weigh more than a tonne. In Switzerland, people often call a bull “Muni” in Swiss German.
wichtigste: An adult male of the cattle family is called a bull.
Cattle can hardly see the colour red.
In a bullfight, the bull is provoked by the movement of the cloth, not by its colour.
The red cloth in a bullfight is called a muleta, and the bullfighter is a matador.
Bullfights are especially well known in Spain.
The eyes of cattle are on the sides of their head.
The German saying “Das ist für ihn ein rotes Tuch” (that is a red cloth to him) means: that makes him very angry.

abschnitte.text: A bull is a fully grown **male of the cattle family**. It is usually bigger and much more muscular than a cow, with a powerful neck and a broad forehead. A large bull can weigh more than a tonne. In many breeds bulls have horns, but there are also hornless breeds.

The eyes of cattle are **on the sides of the head**. This means they can see almost all the way round themselves without turning their head. Only directly behind them can they see nothing. Cattle see fewer colours than we do; they can hardly make out **red**, but they react very sensitively to movement.

Bullfights are especially well known in **Spain**, but they also take place in Portugal, southern France and Latin America. The **matador** waves a red cloth called the **muleta**. What provokes the bull is the movement of the cloth, not its colour. Bullfights are very controversial because the bull is injured and often killed, and animal fights of this kind are banned in Switzerland.

In Swiss German the bull is called **Muni**. At the Federal Wrestling and Alpine Festival, the winner traditionally receives a live bull as a prize, the **Siegermuni** (winner's bull). Usually, though, the wrestling king lets the bull go on living on a farm. In Valais there are also the well-known fights of the Hérens cows, in which the cows measure their strength without any people taking part.

The German saying “Das ist für ihn ein **rotes Tuch**” (that is a red cloth to him) means that something makes him very angry. “To take the bull by the horns” means to tackle a difficult problem bravely. On the stock exchange, the bull stands for rising prices. In the sky there is also the constellation of Taurus, the Bull, with the bright red star Aldebaran.

Bulls can be very strong and sometimes unpredictable. That is why on farms they often wear a **nose ring**, by which they can be led safely. When hiking, you should cross pastures with cattle calmly and keep your distance. This is especially important when dogs are with you or when there are calves in the pasture.

begriffe.erklaerung: Large hoofed animals with horns that are kept as farm animals.
The Swiss German word for a bull.
The bullfighter who waves the red cloth in a bullfight.
The red cloth used in a bullfight.

gewusst: A bull would also charge at a blue or green cloth if it were moved.
The winner's bull at the Federal Wrestling Festival is always given its own name.
The famous bronze statue “Charging Bull” on Wall Street in New York shows a bull ready to attack.

teile.einleitung: Significant figures are the digits of a number that really say something about its accuracy. In the sciences they show how precisely a measured value is known. Anyone who uses them correctly gives results neither less nor more precisely than they really are.
wichtigste: Significant figures are the meaningful digits of a number.
Zeros at the start of a number, as in 0.0705, are not significant, but zeros between other digits are.
The number 0.00450 has three significant figures, because the zero at the end counts.
When multiplying, the result follows the number with the fewest significant figures: 2.5 × 3.42 gives 8.6.
