When adding, the number of decimal places counts: 12.11 + 0.3 gives 12.4.
0.0346 rounded to two significant figures gives 0.035.
Exactly counted numbers such as 25 pupils have an unlimited number of significant figures.

abschnitte.text: Every **measurement** is only possible up to a certain accuracy. The **significant figures** of a number are all the digits you know for certain, plus the last, slightly uncertain digit. If you measure 12.3 centimetres with a ruler, the value has three significant figures. If you write 12.30 centimetres instead, you claim to have measured to a tenth of a millimetre. That is why it is important not to simply write down as many digits as you like.

All digits except zero are always significant. **Leading zeros** at the start, as in 0.0705, do not count; they only show the position of the decimal point. Zeros between other digits always count, so in 0.0705 the zero between 7 and 5 does. Zeros at the end after the decimal point also count, which is why 0.00450 has three significant figures. With 1.20 × 10³ in **scientific notation** you can see at once that there are three.

When **multiplying and dividing**, the result has as many significant figures as the least precise value. So 2.5 × 3.42 = 8.55 becomes 8.6, because 2.5 has only two significant figures. When **adding and subtracting**, on the other hand, the decimal places count. So 12.11 + 0.3 = 12.41 becomes 12.4, because 0.3 is only precise to tenths. A result can never be more precise than the measured values it is calculated from.

When rounding to two significant figures, 0.0346 becomes 0.035. In physics the **measurement uncertainty** is often given as well. A measured value of 9.8123 m/s² with an uncertainty of 0.02 m/s² is written as (9.81 ± 0.02) m/s². The last digit of the measured value matches the position of the uncertainty. More digits would only seem more precise.

Not every number is a measured value. If you count 25 pupils in a class, this number is **exact**. Such numbers have an unlimited number of significant figures and do not limit the accuracy of a calculation. The same applies to fixed conversions, for example that a metre has exactly 100 centimetres.

In chemistry, physics and engineering everyone has to know how reliable a number is. A calculator often shows ten digits, but most of them are meaningless. Anyone who pays attention to significant figures avoids **false precision**. This is important, for example, for doses of medicine, in construction or in laboratory experiments at school.

begriffe.erklaerung: A digit that says something about the accuracy of a number.
The range in which the true value of a measurement probably lies.
Writing a number as a factor times a power of ten, for example 1.20 × 10³.
When a number is given with more digits than are really known.

gewusst: The numbers 1200 and 1.20 × 10³ are the same size but reveal different amounts about accuracy.
A calculator knows nothing about significant figures; it simply shows all the digits.
Counted things such as apples in a basket are as precise as you like.

teile.einleitung: A transformer is a design for artificial neural networks with which computers process language and other data. It was presented in 2017 in the research paper “Attention Is All You Need”. Almost all modern AI language models that write or translate texts are based on this idea.
wichtigste: The transformer architecture was presented in 2017 in the paper “Attention Is All You Need”.
Its heart is self-attention.
Attention is calculated from three vectors: query, key and value.
A transformer processes all positions of a sequence at the same time, that is, in parallel.
If you double the length of the input, the computing effort of full self-attention roughly quadruples.
BERT uses only the encoder of a transformer, GPT only the decoder.
Transformers are found in chatbots, translation programs and many other AI applications.

abschnitte.text: A transformer is a type of **neural network**, that is, a computer program that learns from many examples. It was described in 2017 by a research team at Google in the paper “Attention Is All You Need”. Originally it was meant to translate texts from one language into another. It soon turned out that it is also useful for writing texts, images, music and even proteins.

A transformer first breaks a text down into small pieces called **tokens**, such as words or parts of words. Each token is turned into a long list of numbers, a **vector**. Similar words are given similar lists of numbers. In addition, each token is given information about its position in the sentence, so that the order is not lost.

The heart of it is **self-attention**: each word looks at which other words in the sentence are important for it. For this, each token forms three vectors: query, key and value. The query of a word is compared with the keys of all the words, and the better they match, the more weight their value gets. So that the numbers do not get too large, they are divided by the square root of the vector length, so for length 64 by 8.

Older **recurrent networks** read a text word by word, one after another, which was slow. A transformer, on the other hand, processes all positions of a sequence at the same time. This suits graphics processors perfectly, because they carry out many calculations in parallel, and it made it possible to train huge models. One disadvantage is that every word is compared with every other word: with twice the length of text, full self-attention needs about four times as much computing work.

The original transformer consists of an **encoder**, which understands the input, and a **decoder**, which produces the output word by word. Google's BERT model from 2018 uses only the encoder and is good at understanding texts. The GPT models use only the decoder and specialise in continuing texts. The name GPT stands for “Generative Pre-trained Transformer”, and chatbots such as ChatGPT are also based on it.

begriffe.erklaerung: A computer program built roughly on the model of nerve cells that learns from examples.
A small piece of text, for example a word or part of a word, that a language model processes.
A list of numbers with which a computer describes something.
A method in which each word checks which other words are important for it.

gewusst: The title “Attention Is All You Need” is a play on a well-known song by the Beatles.
The paper from 2017 is one of the most frequently cited scientific works of recent years.
Large transformer models are trained in huge data centres with thousands of graphics processors.

teile.einleitung: A toaster is an electric kitchen appliance for toasting slices of bread. Glowing wires make the bread crisp and brown on the outside. What looks so simple is full of physics and chemistry.
wichtigste: You toast bread with a toaster.
In the toaster, wires get so hot that they glow.
Toasted bread is called toast.
A modern toaster makes the finished bread pop up.
With the dial you set how brown the bread will be.
If the bread stays in too long, it turns black and burns.
You must never poke around in a toaster with a fork, because you can get an electric shock.
Crumbs collect at the bottom, and you should empty them out now and then.

abschnitte.text: In a toaster, electricity flows through thin **heating wires**, usually made of a mixture of nickel and chromium. These wires resist the current and become so hot that they glow red. The heat radiates onto both sides of the slice of bread. The water in the bread evaporates at the surface, and the bread becomes crisp. A toaster uses about as much electricity as a hairdryer.

When toasting, sugars and proteins in the bread react with each other. This **Maillard reaction** produces the brown colour and the fine toasted flavour. The same reaction also creates the crust when baking bread or frying meat. If the bread gets too hot or is toasted for too long, it chars and turns black. It is better not to eat burnt parts.

With the **dial** you set the toasting time, that is, how light or dark the toast will be. When you push the lever down, a magnet or a catch holds the bread carriage in place. When the time is up, the toaster switches off the electricity and a **spring** makes the bread pop up. Older toasters used a bimetallic strip for this, which bends when warm. Today small electronics often control the time.

In the past, people toasted bread over a fire, for example on a fork. Electric toasters appeared at the beginning of the 20th century, once durable heating wires could be made. With the first devices you had to turn the bread by hand. Around 1920 the American Charles Strite invented the **pop-up toaster**, which ejects the bread by itself. When bread was later sold ready-sliced, the toaster spread to many households.

Inside a toaster there are parts carrying **electricity**, so you must never reach in with a fork or a knife. If a slice gets stuck, you first pull out the plug and let the appliance cool down. You should empty the crumbs in the **crumb tray** regularly, otherwise they can burn. A toaster does not belong under curtains or wall cupboards. Children should only use it if an adult has allowed it.

begriffe.erklaerung: A wire that becomes hot when electricity flows through it.
A chemical reaction that makes food brown and tasty when it is heated.
A small drawer at the bottom of the toaster that catches breadcrumbs.
When electric current flows through the body, which is dangerous.

gewusst: The heating wires in a toaster reach several hundred degrees.
There are toasters that toast pictures or patterns onto the bread.
In Switzerland, toast is often eaten as “Toast Hawaii”, topped with ham, pineapple and cheese and baked.

teile.einleitung: A start-up is a young company with a new idea that wants to grow quickly. Many start-ups fail, but some become world-famous companies.
wichtigste: A start-up is a young company with a new kind of business idea.
A minimum viable product is a first version with only the most necessary functions.
Business angels are private individuals who invest money and experience early on.
Risk capital or venture capital is provided by specialised funds in return for shares in the company.
The burn rate shows how quickly a start-up uses up its capital.
A start-up not listed on the stock exchange and worth over a billion dollars is called a unicorn.
For a limited liability company (GmbH) in Switzerland you need at least 20,000 francs of share capital.

abschnitte.text: A start-up is a **young company** that wants to put a new idea into practice, often with modern technology. It is typical for it to want to grow quickly and to take a high risk in doing so. Many famous firms such as Apple or Google began as small start-ups. In Switzerland many start-ups come out of universities such as ETH Zurich or the EPFL in Lausanne; they are then called **spin-offs**.

At the beginning there is an idea that is meant to solve a problem. Instead of developing for years, start-ups often first build a **minimum viable product**, MVP for short. This is a first version with only the most necessary functions. With it you test whether customers really want the product, and then improve it step by step.

abschnitte.titel: Where does the money come from?
abschnitte.text: The very first round of funding is called **seed funding**. Often family, friends or a **business angel** provide the first money. Later, specialised funds invest **risk capital**, also called venture capital, and get shares in the company in return. How quickly a start-up uses up its money is shown by the burn rate.

**Incubators** offer founders offices, advice and contacts, often over a longer time. An accelerator, on the other hand, is a limited, intensive programme of a few months, for which you often give up shares in the company. In Switzerland there are also support programmes from the Confederation, the cantons and the universities. Anyone who wants to found a GmbH needs at least 20,000 francs of **share capital**; for a public limited company (AG) it is 100,000 francs.

A start-up valued at over a billion US dollars but not yet on the stock exchange is called a **unicorn**. The name fits because such companies are as rare as mythical creatures. At some point investors want to turn their shares into money; this is called an **exit**. It happens through the sale of the company to another business or through a stock market flotation.

begriffe.erklaerung: Money that investors give young, high-risk companies in return for shares.
A private individual who puts their own money and knowledge into a start-up early on.
Money that founders must at least put in when starting a GmbH.
A company that grows out of a university or a larger company.

gewusst: Many famous firms such as Apple or Amazon were founded in a garage.
A large proportion of all start-ups give up again in their first few years.

teile.einleitung: The Swatch is a colourful Swiss plastic wristwatch that came onto the market in 1983. It was cheap and fashionable and helped the Swiss watch industry out of a severe crisis. Today the brand belongs to the Swatch Group in Biel, one of the largest watch companies in the world.
wichtigste: The first Swatch came onto the market in 1983 and was presented in Zurich.
The case of a classic Swatch is made of plastic.
The name combines “Second” and “Watch”.
Nicolas G. Hayek is regarded as the “father of the Swatch”.
Swatch watches are especially known for their bright colours and patterns.
New collections appear about every six months.
The Swatch helped to save the Swiss watch industry.

abschnitte.text: A **Swatch** is a light quartz watch with a plastic case. Compared with classic watches it consists of far fewer parts, only 51. The case is welded shut, so you cannot simply open it. This meant it could be produced in large numbers and at a low price.

In the 1970s, cheap **quartz watches** from Japan and other countries came onto the market. Many Swiss watch companies got into difficulty, and tens of thousands of people lost their jobs. This is known as the **quartz crisis**. The Swiss watch industry needed a new idea to become successful again.

Engineers at the company ETA in Grenchen, including Elmar Mock and Jacques Müller, developed the new plastic watch at the beginning of the 1980s. On 1 March 1983 the Swatch was presented in Zurich. At the same time, the businessman **Nicolas G. Hayek** brought the struggling watch companies together into a new group and made the Swatch famous around the world. That is why he is regarded as the “father of the Swatch”.

Swatch watches come in countless colours, patterns and designs, often created by artists. New **collections** appear about every six months. Many people own not just one Swatch but collect several. Rare models are traded among collectors for high prices.

In 1998 Hayek's merger of companies became the **Swatch Group**, based in Biel in the canton of Bern. It includes many well-known brands such as Omega, Longines, Tissot and Rado. Since the death of Nicolas G. Hayek in 2010, his children have continued to run the company. Today the Swatch is regarded as a symbol of Swiss inventiveness and design.

begriffe.erklaerung: A watch in which a tiny vibrating quartz crystal sets the beat.
A severe crisis of the Swiss watch industry in the 1970s and 1980s.
A series of new models that come out together.
The cover of a watch that protects the movement.

gewusst: In 1998 Swatch invented “Internet Time”, which divided the day into 1000 “beats” instead of hours.
A classic Swatch consists of only 51 parts.
In 2022 Swatch, together with Omega, brought out the MoonSwatch, and long queues formed outside its shops.

teile.einleitung: Diving means going below the surface of the water to explore the underwater world, do research or work. With a compressed air cylinder, divers can stay underwater for a long time. Important safety rules apply, because humans are not fish.
wichtigste: In scuba diving you usually breathe compressed air from a cylinder.
Fins on your feet help you move forward.
The mask makes sure that you can see clearly underwater.
A wetsuit made of neoprene keeps you warm.
You should never dive alone.
Divers have to come up slowly, otherwise they can become ill.
Underwater, divers communicate with hand signals.

abschnitte.text: In **freediving**, you simply hold your breath, as when snorkelling or diving in the swimming pool. In **scuba diving**, you carry a cylinder of compressed air on your back. Through a hose and a mouthpiece, the regulator, you get the air to breathe. Depending on the depth, you can stay underwater for half an hour or longer.

A **mask** over your eyes and nose makes sure you can see clearly, because without air in front of your eyes everything looks blurred underwater. **Fins** on your feet make swimming much easier. A suit made of **neoprene** keeps you warm, because water draws heat away from the body quickly. There is also a jacket for floating in the water, weights and a depth gauge or dive computer.

The deeper you dive, the harder the water presses; every 10 metres adds about as much **pressure** as the whole air above us. That is why you have to equalise the pressure in your ears. Under pressure, more nitrogen from the air you breathe dissolves in the blood. If you come up too fast, gas bubbles form in the body, like in an opened bottle of sparkling water; this is called **decompression sickness**.

The most important rule is: never dive alone, but always with a **dive partner**, your buddy. You cannot speak underwater, so you communicate with **hand signals**. For example, thumb and index finger forming a ring means “everything is OK”. Before you dive with a cylinder, you have to take a diving course with a test.

In 1943 the Frenchman **Jacques-Yves Cousteau**, together with Émile Gagnan, developed a practical breathing device for divers. He became world-famous with his films about the underwater world. In 1960 the Swiss **Jacques Piccard** dived into the Mariana Trench in the submersible Trieste, which his father Auguste Piccard had developed. There, almost 11,000 metres down, is the deepest point of the world's oceans.

There is a lot of diving in Switzerland too, for example in Lake Zurich, Lake Thun or Lake Maggiore. Underwater you find fish such as pike and perch, but also old shipwrecks. Because the lakes are cold, many divers wear thick **drysuits**. In mountain lakes you also have to take the altitude into account, because the air pressure is lower there.

begriffe.erklaerung: Diving with a cylinder of breathing air on your back.
Diving while holding your breath, without any breathing apparatus.
The device that delivers the air from the cylinder in a way that you can breathe it in.
A soft, insulating rubber material for diving suits.
An illness caused by gas bubbles in the body after coming up too fast.

gewusst: Underwater, colours disappear little by little; just a few metres down, red already looks almost grey.
On his dive into the Mariana Trench, Jacques Piccard went deeper than anyone before him.
Sound travels about four times faster underwater than in air, which is why you can hardly tell where a noise is coming from.

teile.einleitung: A science slam is a competition in which researchers present their work in a few minutes in as exciting and funny a way as possible. At the end the audience decides who wins. In this way science becomes an entertaining evening for everyone.
wichtigste: At a science slam researchers give short talks that the audience rates.
The model was the poetry slam, a competition for poets.
A talk typically lasts at most about ten minutes.
The first science slams took place in Germany.
The aim is to bring research closer to a wide audience.
In the related format “Three Minute Thesis” you present your doctoral project in three minutes with one slide.
FameLab is an international science communication competition supported by the British Council.

abschnitte.text: At a **science slam** several researchers perform on a stage one after another. Each has only about **ten minutes** to explain their own research topic. Almost anything is allowed: pictures, experiments, props, jokes or even singing. What matters is that people without specialist knowledge understand everything. At the end the **audience** votes, often with applause, score cards or by measuring the noise.

The model is the **poetry slam**, in which people perform texts they have written themselves and the audience decides the winner. The idea of doing the same with research came up in **Germany**. The first science slams took place there around 2006. After that the format spread quickly to many countries, including Switzerland and Austria.

Many people find science complicated or boring. A science slam shows that research can be exciting and funny. The researchers practise explaining difficult things simply, which is called **science communication**. The audience learns new things first-hand and can often ask questions afterwards.

In the **Three Minute Thesis** competition, doctoral students have to explain their whole research project in just three minutes. They may show only a single, static slide. It began at a university in Australia and is now held worldwide. At **FameLab**, supported by the British Council, young researchers also have only three minutes to speak. Whoever wins can take part in an international final.

In Swiss cities such as Zurich, Bern, Basel or Lucerne there are also regular science slams. They take place in theatres, bars, cinemas or at science festivals. Often doctoral students from universities and universities of applied sciences perform. Some events are aimed especially at school classes and young people.

begriffe.erklaerung: A stage competition in which the audience chooses the winner.
Explaining research to people outside science.
A research project lasting several years at a university, after which you receive the title of doctor.
An object that you use on stage to show something.

gewusst: At science slams complicated topics such as quantum physics have been explained with toys and jelly bears.
In Three Minute Thesis exactly one slide is allowed per talk, and it must not move.
At a science slam the loudness of the applause often decides who wins.

teile.einleitung: The penny bun, also called the cep or porcini, is one of the best-known and most popular edible mushrooms in Europe. It has a brown cap, a thick stem and fine tubes under the cap instead of gills. Mushroom pickers in Switzerland are delighted every late summer and autumn when they find a penny bun.
wichtigste: The penny bun has fine tubes under its cap instead of gills.
Its cap is brown.
The stem of a young penny bun is thick and bulging.
In German it is called “Steinpilz” (stone mushroom) because its flesh is very firm.
The penny bun grows in woods and is a very popular edible mushroom.
In Italian it is called porcino.
So that it can be kept for a long time, it is often dried.

abschnitte.text: The cap of the penny bun is **brown**, often like a freshly baked bread roll, and can grow more than 20 centimetres wide. Under the cap there are fine **tubes**, which are white in young mushrooms and later yellowish to olive green. The **stem** of young mushrooms is thick and bulging and has a fine, pale net pattern. Its flesh is white and very firm, which is where the German name “Steinpilz” (stone mushroom) comes from.

The penny bun grows in **woods**, especially under spruces, beeches, oaks and pines. It lives in a partnership with the roots of these trees, which is called **mycorrhiza**. The mushroom supplies the tree with water and mineral salts, and in return the tree gives it sugar. That is why you never find penny buns in an open meadow without trees.

In Switzerland you find penny buns mainly from summer into autumn, especially after warm rain. They grow in the Central Plateau as well as in mountain forests up to the tree line. Many cantons have **mushroom protection rules**, for example a maximum amount per person per day or days when picking is not allowed. The rules differ from canton to canton.

The penny bun can be confused with the **bitter bolete**, which tastes very bitter. Its tubes turn pink with age, and its stem has a dark net. Just one bitter bolete can make a whole mushroom dish inedible. That is why you should always have mushrooms you have picked checked at an official **mushroom inspection**, which exists in many Swiss municipalities.

Because of its nutty flavour, the penny bun is a very popular **edible mushroom**. You can fry it, use it in risotto or pasta, or cook it as a soup. Penny buns are often dried, because dried they keep for a long time and taste especially strong. In Italy it is called **porcino**, and risotto ai porcini is also a well-known dish in Ticino.

abschnitte.titel: A mushroom that cannot be farmed
abschnitte.text: Button mushrooms can be grown on compost in large sheds, but so far this has not really worked with the penny bun. The reason is its close partnership with living trees. So almost all penny buns sold in shops come from mushrooms picked in the wild. Dried penny buns often come from Eastern Europe or China.

begriffe.erklaerung: A mushroom that has fine tubes under its cap instead of gills.
A partnership between fungi and plant roots from which both benefit.
A mushroom that you can eat.
A place where experts check picked mushrooms for poisonous ones.

gewusst: The scientific name Boletus edulis means something like “edible bolete”.
A large penny bun can weigh more than one kilogram.
Porcino means “little pig” in Italian.

teile.einleitung: Survivorship bias is a mistake in thinking: you look only at the cases that have made it through a selection and forget all the others. As a result, many things seem better, more solid or more successful than they really are. If you know about this mistake, you are less likely to fall for wrong conclusions.
wichtigste: With survivorship bias, you look only at cases that have made it through a selection.
A survey of only the current members of a gym is biased, because unhappy members have already left.
Investment funds look more successful in hindsight, because bad funds are closed and drop out of the statistics.
Old houses seem more solid, because the badly built ones disappeared long ago.
Successful university dropouts do not prove that dropping out leads to success, because the many unsuccessful dropouts are missing.
Old music often seems better, because only the best songs are remembered.
You avoid the mistake by also including failed or eliminated cases.

abschnitte.text: **Survivorship bias** is a distortion that arises when you only look at the “survivors” of a selection. The cases that dropped out, failed or disappeared are missing from the picture. Because they are invisible, they are easily forgotten. This leads to wrong conclusions about causes and chances of success.

A famous example comes from the Second World War. Bombers that had returned were examined, and people wanted to add more armour to the places with lots of bullet holes. The statistician **Abraham Wald** pointed out that they were only seeing the aircraft that had come back despite being hit. So it was precisely the places without holes that should be armoured, because aircraft hit there had crashed.

Someone says: “Houses used to be built much more solidly; after all, the old ones are still standing today.” But you no longer see the badly built houses, because they were demolished or collapsed long ago. In a similar way, the music of past decades often seems better, because only the best songs have stayed in our **memory**. A survey of the current members of a gym is also biased, because unhappy members have already left.

Self-help books like to show successful entrepreneurs who dropped out of university. But the conclusion “dropping out leads to success” is questionable, because the many unsuccessful dropouts are missing from these books. It is similar with **investment funds**: bad funds are closed and drop out of the statistics. The remaining ones look more successful in hindsight than the average of all funds was.

abschnitte.titel: The cats from the tower block
abschnitte.text: Vets in New York found that cats seemed to survive falls from very high floors better than from medium ones. One possible explanation takes survivorship bias into account. Cats that died in a fall hardly ever came to the **vet's surgery** and were therefore missing from the statistics. The example shows that you always have to ask which cases do not appear in the data at all.

The best way to avoid the mistake is to also include **failed** or eliminated cases. That is why researchers ask: who dropped out of the group, and why? In studies, for example, participants who left early are counted too. In everyday life, a simple question helps: what am I actually not seeing here?

begriffe.erklaerung: A distortion or prejudice; in German it is called “Verzerrung”.
A typical error when reasoning that leads to wrong conclusions.
A selection of cases that is studied.
A pot into which many people pay money, which is invested in shares or other assets.

gewusst: Abraham Wald came from Klausenburg, today's Cluj in Romania, and fled to the USA before the Second World War.
With lottery winners, too, you almost only hear about those who won, never about the millions who lost.
The picture of an aircraft with red dots for bullet holes has become a well-known symbol of this mistake in thinking on the internet.

teile.einleitung: Spores are tiny cells with which fungi, ferns, mosses and some bacteria reproduce or survive. They are so small that you cannot see a single spore with the naked eye. Instead they are produced in huge numbers and travel far and wide on the wind.
wichtigste: Fungi reproduce with spores.
In many cap mushrooms the spores form under the cap.
A single fungal spore is so small that you cannot see it.
The wind carries the spores far away.
A single large mushroom forms many millions of spores.
Ferns and mosses also reproduce with spores.
Some bacteria form spores that survive heat and drought.

abschnitte.text: A spore is usually a single cell from which a new living thing can grow. Unlike a seed, it contains no ready-made seedling and no food supply. Many spores are only a few thousandths of a millimetre in size. The word comes from Greek and means **seed**.

The mushroom we see in the woods is only the **fruiting body**; the actual fungus lives as a network in the soil. In many cap mushrooms the spores form under the cap, on **gills** or in fine tubes. From there they trickle down and are carried away by the wind. Because only a few spores reach a good place, a large mushroom forms many millions of them.

For a **spore print** you lay a ripe mushroom cap with its underside on a piece of paper and cover it. After a few hours there is a fine powder pattern on the paper. The colour of this spore powder can be white, pink, brown or black. Mushroom experts use it to identify kinds of mushroom.

If you press a ripe **puffball**, a cloud of dust rises that consists of countless spores. Moulds on old bread also form spores, which can be seen as green or black fluff. These spores float in the air almost everywhere. In some people mould spores trigger allergies.

**Ferns** also reproduce with spores instead of seeds. On the underside of their leaves you can often see small brown clusters in which the spores ripen. Mosses form their spores in small capsules on thin stalks. Ferns and mosses are very old plant groups that existed long before the flowering plants.

Some bacteria form **resting spores** when it gets too hot, too cold or too dry for them. These spores can survive boiling and rest for years. That is why tinned food and medical instruments are sterilised at especially high temperatures and under pressure. When conditions are good again, a new bacterium grows from the spore.

begriffe.erklaerung: A tiny cell from which a new fungus, fern or bacterium can grow.
The visible part of a fungus, which forms the spores.
Thin plates under the cap of many mushrooms.
A powder picture of the spores on paper that helps to identify mushrooms.

gewusst: A giant puffball can form several trillion spores, far more than there are people on Earth.
The spores of clubmoss were once used as “witches' flour” for fire effects in the theatre.
Fungal spores have been found high up in the atmosphere.

teile.einleitung: A kick scooter, in Switzerland usually called a “Trottinett”, is a simple vehicle with a deck, two small wheels and a handlebar. You put one foot on the deck and push off from the ground with the other. The folding Micro scooter from Küsnacht on Lake Zurich became world-famous.
wichtigste: On a scooter you move forwards by pushing off with one foot.
The Micro scooter was invented by the Swiss Wim Ouboter.
The way to a snack bar in Zurich was too far for him to walk and too short to cycle.
The Micro scooter can be folded up.
Its frame is usually made of aluminium.
The company Micro is based in Küsnacht on Lake Zurich.
In the USA the scooter used to be sold under the name Razor.

abschnitte.text: A **kick scooter** consists of a flat **deck**, two or three wheels and a handlebar with grips. You put one foot on the deck and push off from the ground with the other foot. In this way you roll forwards almost without effort. You usually brake with a foot brake over the back wheel, which you press down. In Switzerland it is called a **Trottinett**, a word that comes from French.

Simple wooden scooters already existed at the beginning of the 20th century. Children often built them themselves from planks and old wheels. For a long time the scooter was seen mainly as a children's toy. That changed at the end of the 1990s, when light metal scooters with small wheels appeared. Suddenly teenagers and adults were riding them through the cities too.

The Swiss **Wim Ouboter** says that the way to his favourite snack bar in **Zurich** was too far to walk and too short to cycle. So he built himself a small, light scooter. At first he was embarrassed to ride it, so he often used it in the evening. When the neighbours' children wanted to try it, he realised that his idea excited a lot of people. This led to the company **Micro**, based in Küsnacht on Lake Zurich.

The Micro scooter has a frame made of **aluminium** and small plastic wheels, like those of inline skates. It can be **folded up**, so it fits into the train, the tram or under a desk. Around the year 2000 it became a huge sales success around the world. In the USA it was sold under the name **Razor** at the time. Later Micro also developed three-wheeled kickboards for small children, which you steer by leaning.

When riding a scooter you should wear a **bike helmet**, because falls happen quickly. Small wheels easily get caught on stones, grooves or tram rails. On pavements you have to be considerate towards pedestrians. In Switzerland, separate rules apply to **e-scooters** with an electric motor, for example a minimum age. In the wet you should ride more slowly, because braking distances get longer.

begriffe.erklaerung: The Swiss word for a kick scooter.
The flat board that you stand on when riding a scooter.
A light, silvery metal that does not rust.
A scooter with three wheels that you steer by leaning.

gewusst: With his company, Wim Ouboter also invented a small electric car called the Microlino.
The word Trottinett comes from the French “trotter”, which means something like to scurry or trot.
Around the year 2000, millions of these aluminium scooters were sold around the world.

teile.einleitung: A trophic level is a step in a food chain, that is, the question of who eats whom. At the very bottom are the plants, above them the plant-eaters and then the meat-eaters. With this model you can understand how energy and food flow through an ecosystem.
wichtigste: The first trophic level is formed by the producers, mainly green plants.
Plant-eaters on the second level are called primary consumers.
In the chain grass, grasshopper, frog, grass snake, goshawk, the frog is on the third level.
Decomposers use dead biomass from all levels.
Humans are omnivores and cannot be assigned exactly to one level; on average they are at about 2.2.
When a top predator has an effect over several levels right down to the plants, it is called a trophic cascade.
The pyramid of numbers of trophic levels is named after the British ecologist Charles Elton.

abschnitte.text: The word comes from the Greek trophe, which means **nourishment**. Every living thing in an ecosystem is given a level, depending on how far away it is from the plants. On the first level are the **producers**, which make their own food with the help of sunlight. Above them come the **consumers**, which eat other living things.

Let us take the food chain grass, grasshopper, frog, grass snake, goshawk. The grass is on the first level, and the grasshopper, as a **primary consumer**, is on the second. The frog eats the grasshopper and so is on the third level; it is a secondary consumer. The grass snake follows on the fourth level and the goshawk, as the **top predator**, on the fifth. In nature, though, such chains are usually woven together into a large food web.

From one level to the next a lot of energy is lost, because animals use it to live, move and keep warm. As a rule of thumb, only about ten per cent of the energy reaches the next level. That is why there are many more plants than plant-eaters and many more plant-eaters than predators. If you show this as a stack, you get an **ecological pyramid**. The pyramid of numbers is named after the British ecologist **Charles Elton**, who described it in 1927.

**Decomposers** such as fungi, bacteria and earthworms break down dead plants and animals from all levels. They turn them back into nutrients for the plants and so close the cycle. Omnivores such as humans, foxes or bears eat on several levels. In 2013 researchers led by Sylvain Bonhommeau calculated an average trophic level of about 2.2 for humanity, because we mainly eat plants.

A **top predator** can change a whole ecosystem. In Yellowstone National Park in the USA, wolves were reintroduced in 1995. After that the deer behaved differently and in some places ate fewer young trees, which were then able to recover. Such an effect across several levels is called a **trophic cascade**. In Switzerland too, there is discussion about how the wolf and the lynx affect the forest and wild animals.

In 1998 the marine researcher **Daniel Pauly** showed that the average trophic level of fish catches around the world is falling. This means that the large predatory fish were fished out first, and then people switched to smaller species. He called this “fishing down marine food webs”. This discovery shows how strongly humans are changing the seas.

begriffe.erklaerung: A living thing that makes its own food with sunlight, for example a plant.
A living thing that eats other living things.
A living thing such as a fungus or bacterium that breaks down dead material.
A series of living things in which each is eaten by the next.
A chain reaction in which a predator has an effect over several levels down to the plants.

gewusst: Food chains rarely have more than five links, because too little energy is left at the top.
With a trophic level of over five, a polar bear is far higher than humans.
Some plants, such as the sundew, catch insects and so mix up the trophic levels.

teile.einleitung: A trace fossil is a fossilised trace that a living thing has left behind, for example a footprint, a burrow or feeding marks. Unlike bones, it shows how an animal moved and behaved.
wichtigste: A fossilised footprint of a dinosaur is a trace fossil.
It formed when the animal stepped into soft mud that later became hard.
A whole row of footprints from one animal is called a trackway.
From trackways you can read how fast an animal walked.
In the quarry at Lommiswil in the canton of Solothurn there are dinosaur tracks on a steep wall.
The large round prints come from huge plant-eaters with long necks.
When the A16 motorway was built in the canton of Jura, thousands of dinosaur tracks were found.

abschnitte.text: A **trace fossil** is not part of a body but a sign that a living thing has left behind. These include footprints, crawling tracks of worms, burrows in the ground, bite marks and fossilised droppings. The science that studies such traces is called **ichnology**. Trace fossils show how animals lived, ate and moved.

abschnitte.titel: How does a footprint get into stone?
abschnitte.text: A dinosaur stepped, for example, into soft **mud** on the shore of a sea. Then the print dried in the sun and was covered by new sand or mud. Over millions of years the layers were pressed into solid rock. Today the print can come to light again when the upper layers are worn away.

A row of footprints from the same animal is called a **trackway**. From the size of the prints and the distance between the steps researchers can work out how big and how fast an animal was. Many trackways side by side in the same direction suggest that animals may have lived in a **group**. In this way tracks tell stories that bones alone do not reveal.

abschnitte.titel: Lommiswil in the canton of Solothurn
abschnitte.text: In the quarry at **Lommiswil** at the foot of the Weissenstein you can see dinosaur tracks on an almost vertical rock face. Originally the tracks lay on a flat beach from the Jurassic period. When the **Jura Mountains** formed, the rock layer was tilted up at an angle. The large round prints come from huge plant-eaters with long necks, the sauropods.

During the building of the A16 motorway, the Transjurane, experts in the canton of **Jura** found thousands of dinosaur tracks around Porrentruy. The sites were carefully studied, measured and photographed over many years. Some tracks were recovered and can be seen today in the **Jurassica** museum in Porrentruy. The finds are among the most important dinosaur trackways in Europe.

begriffe.erklaerung: A row of footprints that an animal left behind while walking.
The science that studies trace fossils.
Huge plant-eating dinosaurs with a long neck and a long tail.
A period of Earth's history about 200 to 145 million years ago, named after the Jura Mountains.

gewusst: Fossilised droppings also count as trace fossils and are called coprolites.
The Jurassic period is named after the Jura Mountains on the border between Switzerland and France.

teile.einleitung: A thermometer is a measuring instrument that shows the temperature. With it you find out how warm or cold the air, the water or your body is. In Switzerland, temperature is measured in degrees Celsius.
wichtigste: A thermometer shows the temperature.
In Switzerland, temperature is measured in degrees Celsius.
Water freezes at 0 degrees and boils at sea level at 100 degrees Celsius.
There are liquid thermometers, bimetallic thermometers and digital thermometers.
With a clinical thermometer you measure body temperature.
Anders Celsius proposed his temperature scale in 1742.

abschnitte.text: The name comes from Greek: thermos means warm and metron means measure. A thermometer makes use of the fact that many substances change when they get warm, for example by expanding. You read off how warm it is on a **scale**. The unit used in Switzerland is **degrees Celsius**, abbreviated °C.

In a **liquid thermometer**, a coloured liquid, often alcohol, is held in a thin glass tube. When it gets warmer, the liquid expands and rises in the tube. A **bimetallic thermometer** consists of two metal strips joined together, which expand by different amounts when warm and therefore bend. Digital thermometers use an electronic sensor to measure how electric current behaves at different temperatures.

Around 1592 Galileo Galilei built a simple device that showed changes in temperature, a so-called thermoscope. Around 1714 the physicist Daniel Gabriel **Fahrenheit** built an accurate mercury thermometer and invented the Fahrenheit scale, which is still used in the USA today. In 1742 the Swede **Anders Celsius** proposed a scale with 100 steps between the freezing and boiling points of water. Originally, on his scale, the boiling point was at 0 and the freezing point at 100; only later was the scale turned round.

The normal body temperature of a person is about 36.5 to 37.5 degrees Celsius. From about 38 degrees, it is called a **fever**. Clinical thermometers used to contain poisonous mercury, but today digital devices are mostly used. Some measure in the ear or on the forehead using invisible infrared radiation.

The lowest officially measured temperature in Switzerland was recorded on 12 January 1987 in **La Brévine** in the Neuchâtel Jura: minus 41.8 degrees. That is why the valley is also called the “Siberia of Switzerland”. MeteoSwiss weather stations constantly measure the air temperature throughout the country. So that they measure correctly, the thermometers are in the shade and about two metres above the ground.

You can find thermometers in many places: at the window, in the fridge, in the oven and in the car. Cooks use meat thermometers to check whether meat is cooked. In science, the **kelvin** scale is also used, which starts at absolute zero. A heating system with a **thermostat** switches on automatically when the thermometer reports values that are too low.

begriffe.erklaerung: A measure of how warm or cold something is.
The unit of temperature used in Switzerland.
A raised body temperature with which the body fights pathogens.
A scientific unit of temperature in which 0 kelvin is the lowest possible temperature.
A control that automatically keeps to a set temperature.

gewusst: Absolute zero is minus 273.15 degrees Celsius; it cannot get any colder.
In the USA temperature is measured in Fahrenheit, and there 100 degrees Fahrenheit is about 38 degrees Celsius.
Early thermometers were sometimes filled with wine or spirits of wine.

teile.einleitung: Tropical rainforests are dense, evergreen forests around the equator, where it rains almost every day and it is warm all year round. They are the habitats on land with the most species. Even famous explorers such as Alexander von Humboldt ventured on adventurous expeditions into the rainforest.
wichtigste: Tropical rainforests grow near the equator, where it is warm and wet all year round.
More than half of all known animal and plant species in the world live in rainforests.
The largest rainforest is the Amazon rainforest in South America.
Around 1800 Alexander von Humboldt travelled by canoe on the Orinoco and was plagued by mosquitoes there.
Certain trees from the rainforest supply natural rubber.
Researchers still keep discovering new animal species in the rainforest.
Large areas of rainforest are lost every year through deforestation.

abschnitte.text: Tropical rainforests lie in a belt around the **equator**. The largest areas are the Amazon basin in South America, the Congo basin in Africa and the islands of South-East Asia such as Borneo. The temperature is about 25 to 28 degrees all year round, and there are no seasons as we have them. Usually more than 2000 millimetres of rain falls a year, often as a heavy afternoon shower. The air is therefore very damp and muggy.

A rainforest is built up in **storeys** like a tower block. At the very top, individual giant trees rise more than 50 metres high. Below them the **canopy** forms an almost closed green ceiling, in which most of the animals live. It is dark on the ground, because only a little sunlight gets right down. That is why many plants such as lianas and orchids climb up trees to reach the light.

Although rainforests cover only a small part of the land area, more than half of all known species live there. Hundreds of species of beetle can live on a single tree. Typical animals are monkeys, sloths, parrots, poison dart frogs, jaguars and orangutans. Many crops originally come from the rainforest, for example **cocoa**, vanilla and bananas. Certain trees supply **natural rubber**, from which rubber goods are made.

The German naturalist **Alexander von Humboldt** travelled through South America from 1799 to 1804 with the Frenchman Aimé Bonpland. In 1800 they paddled by canoe on the **Orinoco** through the rainforest and were driven almost to despair by mosquitoes. Because there were hardly any roads, explorers in the Amazon region usually travelled by boat. With machetes and compasses they cut their way through the dense forest. Today researchers get high up into the treetops with ropes and cranes and keep discovering new species on **expeditions**.

Every year large areas of rainforest are cut down or burnt. In their place come pastures for cattle, fields for soya and **oil palm plantations**, or timber is felled. This destroys habitats for animals and plants and for indigenous peoples who have always lived in the forest. Because trees store a lot of **carbon**, deforestation is also bad for the climate. Labels for wood and paper such as FSC are meant to help people recognise products from sustainable forestry.

In Switzerland, too, we use many products from the tropics, for example cocoa for chocolate, coffee or palm oil. In the 1980s the Swiss Bruno Manser lived for several years with the Penan people on Borneo and campaigned to protect their rainforest. He has been missing since 2000. The Bruno Manser Fund in Basel still carries on his work today.

begriffe.erklaerung: The imaginary line that divides the Earth into a northern and a southern half.
The dense layer of treetops high above the forest floor.
The large number of different animal and plant species in one place.
The milky sap of certain trees, from which rubber is made.
A research journey into an unknown area.

gewusst: Often only about one to two per cent of the sunlight reaches the floor of a rainforest.
In the rainforest, a raindrop can drip through the leaves for minutes before it reaches the ground.
On his journey Humboldt collected thousands of plant species, many of which were still unknown in Europe.

teile.einleitung: The Swiss Army knife is a small red knife with many fold-out tools. It was originally made for the soldiers of the Swiss Army and is now a symbol of Switzerland all over the world.
wichtigste: The Swiss Army knife usually has a red handle with the Swiss cross.
It was first made as a soldier's knife for the army.
Even the first soldier's knife of 1890 had a tin opener.
In 1891 Karl Elsener in Ibach took over its production.
Ibach is in the canton of Schwyz.
The company Victorinox is named after Victoria, the founder's mother.
“Inox” stands for stainless steel.

abschnitte.text: A Swiss Army knife is a **folding knife** with several tools in the handle. As well as blades there are screwdrivers, tin openers, corkscrews, scissors, saws or tweezers. The handle is usually **red** and has the Swiss cross on it. There are models with only a few tools and huge collectors' models with dozens of functions.

At the end of the 19th century the Swiss Army wanted a practical knife for all its **soldiers**. The first soldier's knife of 1890 had a blade, a tin opener, a screwdriver and an awl. The soldiers opened their tins with the tin opener and took their rifles apart with the screwdriver. The first knives were still made in Germany.

In 1891 the cutler **Karl Elsener** in Ibach in the canton of Schwyz took over the production of the soldiers' knives. A few years later he developed a lighter officer's knife with an extra corkscrew. After the death of his mother Victoria, he named the company after her. When stainless steel came in, “inox” was added, an abbreviation from the French for **stainless**, and so the name Victorinox was created.

After the Second World War American soldiers took many knives home with them. They called it the **Swiss Army Knife**. Since then the pocket knife has been a popular souvenir and a symbol of Swiss quality. For a long time there were two manufacturers, Victorinox in Ibach and Wenger in the Jura, until Victorinox took over the Wenger company.

A pocket knife is very useful for hiking, camping and making things. You should always move the blade away from your body and fold it away carefully after use. With the **corkscrew** you pull the cork out of a bottle. You are not allowed to take a pocket knife in your hand luggage on planes or into many buildings.

begriffe.erklaerung: A knife whose blade can be folded into the handle.
Steel that does not rust because metals such as chromium have been mixed into it.
A pointed tool for making holes in leather or cloth.
A company in Ibach in the canton of Schwyz that makes Swiss Army knives.

gewusst: Swiss Army knives have even been on board NASA space missions.
In the past officers did not get the officer's knife from the army; they had to buy it themselves.

teile.einleitung: Thomas Stocker is a Swiss climate physicist who did research at the University of Bern for many years. He studies how the Earth's climate has changed in the past and what could happen in the future. Ancient ice from Greenland and Antarctica, as well as computer models, help him in this.
wichtigste: Thomas Stocker studied at ETH Zurich.
From 1993 he headed the Division of Climate and Environmental Physics at the University of Bern.
He was a professor in Bern until his retirement in 2024.
Ice cores from Greenland and Antarctica are central climate archives in his research.
His group uses the Bern climate model Bern3D for very long periods of time.
He worked on the bipolar seesaw between the northern and southern hemispheres.
In 2015 he stood as a candidate for chair of the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change.

abschnitte.text: Thomas Stocker was born in Zurich in 1959. He studied at **ETH Zurich** and also wrote his doctoral thesis there. After that he did research abroad for some years, among other places in Canada and the USA. In 1993 he came to the **University of Bern**, where he took over the Division of Climate and Environmental Physics at the Physics Institute. He stayed there until his retirement in 2024.

In Greenland and Antarctica there is ice that has built up layer by layer over hundreds of thousands of years. Researchers drill it out and get long **ice cores**. Tiny air bubbles in the ice contain air from earlier times. From this you can read how much carbon dioxide used to be in the air. Bern researchers took part in big drilling projects and were able to reconstruct the climate of about 800,000 years.

The Bern institute was strongly shaped by the physicist **Hans Oeschger**, a pioneer of ice core research. Oeschger showed early on that the history of the atmosphere can be read from ice. Stocker continued this tradition and combined the measurements with computer models. That is why Bern is still regarded as one of the most important places for climate research in the world.

Stocker's group developed the climate model **Bern3D**. It is simplified and therefore calculates quickly enough to simulate tens of thousands of years. An important topic was the **bipolar seesaw**. It describes how, during sudden climate changes, the north can warm up while the south cools down, and the other way round. The reason is changes in the ocean currents in the Atlantic, which distribute heat between the hemispheres.

The **Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change** (IPCC) summarises knowledge about climate change every few years. From 2008 to 2015 Thomas Stocker, together with a Chinese colleague, led the working group on the physical science basis. This group published a large report in 2013, to which hundreds of experts contributed. In 2015 Stocker stood as a candidate for chair of the whole IPCC, but another candidate was elected.

Stocker often explains his research in talks and interviews for a wide audience. He points out that Switzerland, as an Alpine country, is particularly strongly affected by warming. Glaciers are melting, and very hot summers are becoming more frequent. His work shows how closely basic research and questions about the future are connected.

begriffe.erklaerung: A long column of ice that is drilled out of a glacier or ice sheet.
A computer program that recalculates the Earth's climate.
An international body that summarises knowledge about climate change.
When it gets warmer in one hemisphere and colder in the other.
When a professor retires from their post.

gewusst: The air in the bubbles of Antarctic ice can be several hundred thousand years old.
Bern researchers are among the experts in the world who can measure gases from such air bubbles most precisely.
A simplified climate model like Bern3D can calculate much longer periods of time than a very detailed model.

teile.einleitung: Troy was an ancient city in the north-west of today's Turkey, near the Dardanelles strait. It is famous for the legends of the Trojan War, which the poet Homer tells in the “Iliad”. Archaeologists have dug up the ruins on a hill called Hisarlık and discovered there a fascinating history of more than 3000 years.
wichtigste: Troy lies on the settlement mound of Hisarlık in today's Turkey.
The legend of the Trojan War and the wooden horse made Troy world-famous.
Heinrich Schliemann dug at Troy from 1871 and found a gold treasure, which he called “Priam's Treasure”.
With a large trench, Schliemann destroyed many layers, for which he is criticised today.
Archaeologists divide the mound into nine main layers.
Most of Priam's Treasure is today in the Pushkin Museum in Moscow.
Since 1998 Troy has been a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

abschnitte.text: The ruins of Troy lie on the hill of **Hisarlık** in the Troad region in the north-west of Turkey. Nearby runs the **Dardanelles** strait, which connects the Mediterranean with the Black Sea. Whoever controlled this sea route could earn a lot from trade. At that time the city was closer to the sea than today, because rivers have filled the bay with earth over time.

According to Greek legend, the Trojan prince Paris carried off the beautiful Helen from Sparta. After that the Greeks besieged Troy for ten years, with heroes such as Achilles and Odysseus. In the end, Greek warriors hid in a huge wooden horse, the **Trojan Horse**. The Trojans pulled it into the city; at night the warriors climbed out and opened the gates. The poet **Homer** tells part of this story in the “Iliad”.

The German merchant **Heinrich Schliemann** was convinced that Homer's Troy really existed. From 1871 he dug on the hill of Hisarlık and had a huge trench cut right through the mound. In doing so he destroyed many walls and layers of finds that would be valuable today. In 1873 he found a treasure of gold, silver and bronze and called it **Priam's Treasure**, after the king in the legend. Later it turned out that the treasure is about a thousand years older than the Trojan War.

Troy was destroyed and rebuilt again and again, so the mound grew higher layer by layer. Archaeologists divide it into **nine main layers**, from Troy I to Troy IX. The oldest settlement was founded about 5000 years ago, and the youngest layer dates from the time of the Greeks and Romans. After Schliemann, researchers such as Wilhelm Dörpfeld, Carl Blegen and, from 1988, Manfred Korfmann from Tübingen dug there. Whether one of the layers really is the Troy of Homer's story is still debated among experts today.

Schliemann secretly took the treasure out of the Ottoman Empire and later gave it to the city of Berlin. At the end of the Second World War in 1945, Soviet troops took the treasure to Moscow. For a long time it was unclear where it had ended up. Only in the 1990s did it become known that most of it is in the **Pushkin Museum** in Moscow. Germany, Russia and Turkey still do not agree today on who the treasure should belong to.

In 1998 UNESCO declared Troy a **World Heritage Site**. Today visitors can walk along paths through the ruins and see walls from different periods. At the entrance there is a large replica wooden horse that you can climb. A modern Troy museum was opened nearby in 2018. The expression “Trojan horse” is also used today for computer programs that disguise themselves as harmless.

begriffe.erklaerung: The science that studies the past through excavations.
A hill that forms when people build again and again on the remains of old houses.
An ancient Greek epic poem by Homer about the Trojan War.
A deposit from a particular period that becomes visible during an excavation.

gewusst: Priam's Treasure probably has nothing to do with King Priam, because it is much older.
Schliemann had his wife Sophia wear jewellery from the treasure for a famous photo.
Many researchers think the layer Troy VI or VIIa is the city that best fits the legend.

teile.einleitung: A sample is a small selection from a larger group that is examined more closely. From the result you then draw conclusions about the whole group, just as when cooking you taste a spoonful of soup to find out how the whole pot tastes.
wichtigste: A sample is a selection from a larger group.
The whole group in question is called the population.
Samples save time and money.
A representative sample reflects the population well.
In a random sample, every element has the same chance of being chosen.
Larger samples usually give more reliable results.
If only one particular group is asked, the sample is biased.

abschnitte.text: In statistics you often want to know something about a large group, the **population**. This could be all the children at a school, all the voters in Switzerland or all the apples in a harvest. Instead of examining all of them, you choose a part, the **sample**. This is quicker, costs less and is sometimes the only possibility, for example when products have to be destroyed during testing.

A good sample is **representative**, which means that it reflects the population well. If you want to know which sport young people in Switzerland like best, you must not only ask members of a football club. Otherwise the sample is **biased**, and the result is not true for everyone. So you have to ask young people from different regions, age groups and interests.

A safe way is the **random sample**. In it, every element of the population has the same chance of being chosen, as in a draw from a lottery drum. In this way nobody is favoured and nobody is forgotten. The larger the sample, the more reliable the result usually is, because chance effects even out better.

If 50 out of 200 people answer yes in a survey, that is 25 per cent. If, in a sample of 100 pupils, 30 come by bike, that is 30 per cent. For a whole school with 600 children you would then estimate that about 180 come by bike. Such an estimate is called a **projection**, and it is never completely accurate.

When there are votes in Switzerland, research institutes publish **projections** as early as Sunday afternoon, based on the municipalities that have already been counted. Surveys before elections usually ask a few thousand people instead of all voters. Food inspectors test samples of goods in the laboratory. In medicine, too, new medicines are first tested on a sample of volunteers.

begriffe.erklaerung: The whole group that you want to find something out about.
Standing well for the whole.
A selection in which every element has the same chance of being drawn.
An error that occurs when a sample does not reflect the population correctly.

gewusst: The German word for sample, “Stichprobe”, comes from metal smelting, where molten metal from a tapped furnace was tested.
Even a well-chosen sample of about a thousand people can allow fairly accurate statements about a whole country.

teile.einleitung: Camouflage means that an animal looks like its surroundings so that it is not discovered. Some animals are adapted in colour, others look like twigs or leaves. Camouflage helps animals hide from enemies, but also to creep up on prey.
wichtigste: Camouflage helps animals not to be discovered so easily.
The mountain hare and the rock ptarmigan get a white coat in winter.
The stoat turns white in winter, and only the tip of its tail stays black.
Young roe deer have white spots in their fur for camouflage.
The chameleon can change the colour of its skin.
The stick insect looks like a thin twig.
The leaf insect looks like a green leaf.

abschnitte.text: With **camouflage**, an animal matches its surroundings in colour, pattern or shape. An enemy or a prey animal then easily overlooks it. For prey animals this means protection from predators. Hunters such as tigers or owls, on the other hand, use camouflage to creep up unnoticed.

abschnitte.titel: White winter coats in the Alps
abschnitte.text: In the Swiss Alps, some animals change their coat in autumn. The **mountain hare** gets a white winter coat, and the **rock ptarmigan** wears white feathers in winter. The **stoat**, a small member of the weasel family, also turns white, and only the tip of its tail stays black. In spring all three become brown or grey-spotted again, to match rocks and earth.

Young roe deer, the fawns, have white spots in their brown fur. When they lie in the grass, the pattern looks like spots of sunlight falling through leaves. Zebra stripes or leopard spots break up the outline of the body; this is called **disruptive colouration**. Many fish are dark on top and pale underneath, so they are hard to see from above and from below.

Some animals imitate objects from their surroundings; this is called **mimesis**. The **stick insect** looks like a thin twig and even moves with a rocking motion like a twig in the wind. The **leaf insect** is green and flat and has veins like a real leaf. Some caterpillars look like bird droppings, so that nobody wants to eat them.

The **chameleon** can change the colour of its skin; for this it has special cells with tiny crystals in its skin. But it does not change colour only for camouflage, but also depending on its mood and the temperature. The real masters are cuttlefish and octopuses, which change colour and pattern in fractions of a second. Flatfish such as the plaice even adapt to the pattern of the seabed.

Humans use camouflage too, for example soldiers with **camouflage suits** in mottled patterns. Hunters and wildlife photographers hide behind camouflage nets to watch wild animals. The models for this come from nature. Researchers are even developing fabrics that can change their colour like a chameleon.

begriffe.erklaerung: The way an animal matches its surroundings so that it is not discovered.
An animal imitates an object, for example a twig or a leaf.
Patterns such as stripes or spots visually break up the outline of the body.
The fur or feathers that an animal wears in winter.

gewusst: The polar bear actually has black skin; its fur only looks white.
Because of climate change there is often less snow in the Alps, and then white mountain hares stand out especially on brown ground.
Some octopuses can change not only their colour but also the surface of their skin, so that it looks rough like a stone.

teile.einleitung: Trilobites were prehistoric sea animals with a hard shell that lived hundreds of millions of years ago. They belong to the arthropods and are therefore distant relatives of crabs, spiders and insects. Today they are only known as fossils, which are among the best-known fossils of all.
wichtigste: The name “trilobite” means three-lobed.
Trilobites lived in the sea.
Most were about 3 to 10 centimetres long.
A hard shell protected their body.
Their compound eyes can often still be seen in fossils.
When they grew bigger, they moulted.
They lived long before the dinosaurs.

abschnitte.text: Trilobites had a flat, oval body with a hard **shell** made of chitin and calcite. Lengthwise, the body was divided into three parts, a raised middle and two side lobes, hence the name **three-lobed**. From front to back they consisted of a head shield, a body made of movable segments and a tail shield. Under the shell there were many jointed little legs.

Many trilobites had **compound eyes** like today's insects. Their lenses were made of the mineral calcite and are therefore often still well preserved in fossils. They are the oldest complex eyes in the history of the Earth that are known in detail. Some species had eyes on stalks, while others were completely blind.

Trilobites lived only in the **sea**, from shallow coastal water to great depths. Most crawled over the seabed and ate small particles or tiny animals. Some also swam freely in the water. When in danger, many species could roll up into a ball, similar to today's pill bugs.

The first trilobites appeared about 520 million years ago in the **Cambrian**. They lived on Earth for almost 270 million years, much longer than the dinosaurs. In the great mass extinction at the end of the Permian, about 252 million years ago, the last trilobites disappeared. The first dinosaurs only appeared after that.

Today more than 20,000 species of trilobite are known. Because they **moulted** as they grew, each animal left behind several shells that could become fossils. Famous sites are in Morocco, the Czech Republic, the USA and Canada. Most species were a few centimetres long, but the largest reached up to about 70 centimetres.

begriffe.erklaerung: A petrified remain or imprint of a living thing from prehistoric times.
A group of animals with an outer skeleton and jointed legs, for example insects and crabs.
Shedding the old shell so that the animal can grow.
A geological period from about 540 to 485 million years ago, in which many groups of animals arose.

gewusst: Trilobite fossils are among the most popular collectors' items at mineral fairs.
Some trilobites had long spines that protected them from enemies.
The first robot vacuum cleaner from Electrolux was named after the trilobites.

teile.einleitung: Taphonomy is the science of what happens to a living thing after its death, until perhaps it becomes a fossil. It explains why some animals and plants are preserved for millions of years while others vanish without a trace. In this way it helps researchers to interpret fossils correctly.
wichtigste: Taphonomy studies the processes from the death of a living thing to its fossilisation.
The term was introduced by the Soviet researcher Ivan Yefremov in 1940.
Biostratinomy studies the time between death and burial in sediment.
Living things with hard shells are heavily overrepresented in the fossil record.
Soft parts are most likely to be preserved if they are buried quickly without oxygen.
Petrified wood forms through permineralisation, for example with silica.
A steinkern, or internal mould, is the hardened filling of a shell.

abschnitte.text: The word **taphonomy** comes from Greek and means something like “the study of burial”. It was introduced in 1940 by the Soviet palaeontologist **Ivan Yefremov**, who also wrote science fiction novels. Taphonomy studies all the processes from the death of a living thing to its **fossilisation**. It is part of palaeontology, the science of the living things of prehistoric times.

The branch called **biostratinomy** studies the time between death and burial in sediment. During this time, scavengers feed on the body, bacteria break it down, and water can wash parts away. For something to be preserved, the body must be covered quickly by **sediment** such as mud, sand or volcanic ash. This works best in calm water with little oxygen.

**Hard parts** such as shells, bones and teeth break down much more slowly than skin, muscles or organs. That is why mussels, snails and ammonites are heavily overrepresented in the fossil record. Jellyfish or worms, on the other hand, only rarely become fossils. Soft parts are preserved mainly when they are buried quickly in a **low-oxygen** environment.

In **permineralisation**, dissolved minerals such as silica get into cavities and turn them to stone; this is how petrified wood forms. If the inside of a shell fills with sediment that hardens, a **steinkern** (internal mould) is formed. In **carbonisation**, plant remains sealed off from the air turn into a thin film of carbon. Small insects can also be completely enclosed in amber.

Places with especially well-preserved fossils are called **fossil Lagerstätten**. In Switzerland, these include **Monte San Giorgio** in Ticino, where marine reptiles and fish from the Triassic period have been found. It has been a UNESCO World Natural Heritage Site since 2003. In Germany the Messel Pit is well known, where even feathers and stomach contents of prehistoric animals have been preserved.

begriffe.erklaerung: A petrified remain or a trace of a living thing from earlier ages of the Earth.
Deposited material such as mud, sand or limestone that turns into rock over time.
Minerals fill the cavities of a remain and turn it into stone.
A fossil made of hardened sediment that has filled the inside of a shell.
The science of the living things of past ages of the Earth.

gewusst: Only a tiny fraction of all the living things that have ever lived have been preserved as fossils.
Ivan Yefremov was not only a researcher but also a well-known science fiction author.
Footprints, feeding marks and nests can also become fossils; they are called trace fossils.

teile.einleitung: Stress is the reaction of body and mind to demands or threats. Before an exam, during an argument or when a dog suddenly barks, the body switches into a state of alarm. A little stress can spur you on, but too much stress over a long time makes you ill.
wichtigste: Positive stress that spurs you on is called eustress.
During acute stress, the heartbeat speeds up.
The adrenal glands release stress hormones such as adrenaline and cortisol.
During stress, the sympathetic nervous system, part of the nervous system, is activated.
The quick emergency reaction to a threat is called the fight-or-flight response.
According to the Yerkes-Dodson law, performance is usually best at a medium level of arousal.
If stress lasts a long time, according to Selye the final phase is exhaustion.
Regular exercise has been shown to help reduce stress.

abschnitte.text: Stress is a reaction to **stressors**, that is, to things that challenge or threaten us. This can be an exam, noise, time pressure, an argument or a dangerous situation. Positive stress that spurs you on is called **eustress**, and stress that weighs you down is called **distress**. Whether something feels like stress also depends on whether you feel up to the task.

When there is danger, the brain activates the **sympathetic nervous system**, part of the nervous system. The **adrenal glands** release stress hormones, first adrenaline and a little later cortisol. The heartbeat speeds up, you breathe faster, and the muscles get a better blood supply. This emergency reaction is called the **fight-or-flight response**, because it made our ancestors ready to fight or to run away.

The American physiologist Walter Cannon described the fight-or-flight response at the beginning of the 20th century. The Vienna-born researcher **Hans Selye** made the term stress well known from the 1930s onwards. He described the **general adaptation syndrome** with three phases: alarm reaction, resistance and exhaustion. If the stress lasts a long time, your strength is used up in the end.

According to the **Yerkes-Dodson law**, performance is usually best at a medium level of arousal. People who are not tense at all are often unfocused, while those who are too nervous make mistakes or have a blackout. A little stage fright before a talk can therefore even help. The law was described in 1908 by two American psychologists.

Short-term stress is normal and usually harmless. But if it lasts for weeks or months, it can lead to sleep problems, headaches or tummy aches and frequent colds. Lack of motivation, irritability and problems concentrating can also be warning signs. With very strong long-term stress, people sometimes speak of **burnout**, a state of complete exhaustion.

**Regular exercise** has been shown to help break down stress hormones. Enough sleep, breaks without screens, calm breathing and time with friends also do you good. Big tasks are easier to manage if you split them into small steps. If you are worried or do not know what to do, in Switzerland you can call Pro Juventute free of charge on 147, day and night.

begriffe.erklaerung: Something that causes stress, for example noise or time pressure.
Positive stress that spurs you on.
Negative stress that weighs you down.
A hormone that gets the body ready for an emergency within seconds.
The part of the nervous system that activates the body during stress.

gewusst: The word stress originally comes from engineering, where it meant load or strain on a material.
The adrenal glands sit like little caps on top of the kidneys.
Animals have stress too, for example zebras fleeing from a lion, but their bodies usually calm down again quickly afterwards.

teile.einleitung: The golden eagle is one of the largest birds of prey in Europe and a king of the skies in the Alps. With its broad wings it circles for hours over mountains and valleys. Its eyes are so sharp that it can spot a marmot from a great height.
wichtigste: In Switzerland the golden eagle lives in the Alps.
Its outspread wings are about 2 metres wide.
The plumage of an adult golden eagle is mainly dark brown.
In summer it often hunts marmots.
It seizes its prey with its talons.
The large nest of an eagle is called an eyrie.
Its English name “golden eagle” comes from its golden nape; in German it is called “Steinadler”, stone eagle.

abschnitte.text: The golden eagle has a **wingspan** of about 2 metres. Its plumage is mainly dark brown, and on the back of the head and the nape it shimmers golden yellow. Young eagles can be recognised by white patches on the wings and tail. The females are clearly larger and heavier than the males and weigh up to over 6 kilograms.

Golden eagles live in mountains and wide, open landscapes in the Northern Hemisphere, from Europe across Asia to North America. In Switzerland they live in the **Alps**, mainly above the tree line, where they have a clear view. A pair occupies a large **territory**, which can cover many square kilometres. Golden eagles usually stay in the same area all their lives.

In summer the golden eagle often hunts **marmots**, as well as mountain hares, foxes, grouse or young chamois. With its sharp eyes it spots prey from a great height. It swoops down at lightning speed and seizes it with its strong **talons**. In winter it also eats carrion, for example from animals that have died in avalanches.

The golden eagle builds its large nest, the **eyrie**, from branches, usually on a rock face. A pair often has several eyries, which it uses in turn and builds up further every year. The female usually lays one or two eggs, and often only one chick survives. The young eagles leave the eyrie after about two and a half months.

In the past the golden eagle was heavily persecuted as a supposed pest and had almost disappeared from many areas. In Switzerland it is protected today, and numbers have recovered well. Several hundred pairs now breed again in the Swiss Alps. Dangers today include, for example, lead poisoning from remains of ammunition in carrion and disturbance at the eyrie.

Eagles have always been regarded as a sign of strength and power and appear on many **coats of arms**. In Central Asia falconers hunt foxes with trained golden eagles.
