In Switzerland, with a bit of luck, you can watch golden eagles, for example in the Swiss National Park. The coat of arms of Mexico shows a golden eagle holding a snake.

begriffe.erklaerung: A bird that seizes prey with its claws, such as an eagle or a falcon.
The large nest of an eagle or another bird of prey.
The feet of a bird of prey with their sharp claws.
An area that an animal or a pair claims for itself.
The distance from one wingtip to the other.

gewusst: A golden eagle sees many times more sharply than a person.
In a dive a golden eagle can reach very high speeds of well over 100 kilometres per hour.
In the wild golden eagles can live to over 20 years of age.

teile.einleitung: The Sun is the star at the centre of our solar system and gives us light and warmth. Without it there would be no life on Earth. It is a huge, glowing ball of gas in whose interior energy is constantly produced.
wichtigste: The Sun is a star that gives us light and warmth.
It is about 150 million kilometres away from the Earth.
Its diameter is around 109 times that of the Earth.
The Sun consists mainly of hydrogen and helium.
Its energy comes from nuclear fusion in its interior.
The Sun is about 4.6 billion years old.
You must never look straight at the Sun with your bare eyes.

abschnitte.text: The Sun is a quite ordinary **star**, like the many stars in the night sky. It only seems so large and bright because it is much closer to us than all the other stars. Its light takes about eight minutes to reach the Earth. Experts call it a **yellow dwarf**, although it is huge for us.

The diameter of the Sun is around 1.4 million kilometres. About 1.3 million Earths would fit inside it. The Sun contains over 99 per cent of the total mass of the solar system. Its visible surface, the **photosphere**, is about 5,500 degrees Celsius hot, and the core is even around 15 million degrees.

abschnitte.titel: Where does the energy come from?
abschnitte.text: In the core of the Sun it is so hot and the pressure is so great that hydrogen particles fuse together. This produces **helium**, and an enormous amount of energy is released. This process is called **nuclear fusion**. The energy travels outwards and radiates into space as light and heat.

On the Sun there are darker, somewhat cooler places, the **sunspots**. Their number rises and falls again in a cycle of about eleven years. The Sun also constantly hurls charged particles into space, the **solar wind**. When these hit the Earth, they can produce the northern and southern lights.

Plants use sunlight for **photosynthesis** and so produce food and oxygen. The Sun drives the weather and the water cycle. With solar cells we get electricity from sunlight, including on many Swiss roofs. In Davos the Physikalisch-Meteorologisches Observatorium has been measuring the Sun's radiation for over a hundred years.

The Sun formed about 4.6 billion years ago from a cloud of gas and dust. It has about half of its life behind it. In around five billion years it will swell into a **red giant**. In the end a small, slowly cooling white dwarf will remain.

begriffe.erklaerung: A huge ball of hot gas that shines by itself.
The joining of small atomic nuclei, which releases a lot of energy.
A darker, somewhat cooler place on the surface of the Sun.
The distance that light travels in one year.

gewusst: The light you are seeing right now left the Sun about eight minutes ago.
The Sun also turns on its own axis, at the equator about once every 25 days.
In a total solar eclipse the Moon moves exactly in front of the Sun, and it becomes dark in the middle of the day.

teile.einleitung: Swissuniversities is the rectors' conference of Swiss higher education institutions. Here the heads of universities, universities of applied sciences and universities of teacher education work together. The organisation represents the institutions to politicians and the public.
wichtigste: Swissuniversities is the rectors' conference of Swiss higher education institutions.
It has existed in its current form since 2015.
It is based on the Higher Education Act, HEdA for short.
Its chambers represent universities, universities of applied sciences and universities of teacher education.
Swissuniversities is based in Bern.
Among other things, it provides information about admission with foreign qualifications.
The highest political body in higher education is the Swiss Conference of Higher Education.

abschnitte.text: Swissuniversities is the joint **rectors' conference** of Swiss higher education institutions. A rector heads a university, in a similar way to how a head teacher runs a school. In Swissuniversities the rectors discuss common questions and speak with one voice. The organisation is based in **Bern**.

Swissuniversities has existed in its current form since **2015**. Before that, each type of institution had its own rectors' conference. The basis for the merger is the **Higher Education Act** (in German HFKG). This law sets out how the Confederation and the cantons jointly steer and fund higher education.

Swissuniversities is divided into three **chambers**. The first represents the universities, that is, the cantonal universities and the two Federal Institutes of Technology in Zurich and Lausanne. The second represents the **universities of applied sciences**, which offer practical training, for example in engineering, business or design. The third represents the **universities of teacher education**, where teachers are trained.

Swissuniversities coordinates questions about studies, teaching and research between the institutions. For example, it informs people from abroad who want to study about **admission** with foreign qualifications. It also represents Swiss higher education institutions in international networks. It works closely with the **Swiss Conference of Higher Education**, the highest political body of the Confederation and cantons in the field of higher education.

abschnitte.titel: Universities in all parts of the country
abschnitte.text: Switzerland has higher education institutions in all its language regions. The **Università della Svizzera italiana** in Lugano is the country's only Italian-speaking university. In Fribourg, students study bilingually in German and French. This diversity is typical of Switzerland and is represented jointly in Swissuniversities.

begriffe.erklaerung: A place of study after the Matura or vocational Matura, where people study and do research.
The person who heads a university.
A higher education institution with practical training, for example in engineering, business or health.
A higher education institution where future teachers are trained.

gewusst: The name Swissuniversities is usually written in lower case, that is, “swissuniversities”.
The University of Fribourg is one of the few universities in Europe where you can complete a whole degree bilingually.

teile.einleitung: The Terracotta Army is an army of thousands of life-size warriors made of fired clay. It was created more than 2200 years ago for the first emperor of China, Qin Shi Huangdi, and buried near his tomb. It was only discovered by chance by farmers in 1974 and is regarded today as one of the greatest archaeological finds in the world.
wichtigste: The Terracotta Army was created for the first Chinese emperor, Qin Shi Huangdi.
It lies near the city of Xi'an in China.
In 1974 farmers came across it by chance while digging a well.
According to estimates it consists of about 8000 figures.
Almost all the clay warriors have different faces.
The figures were brightly painted, but the paint quickly flakes off in the air.
Since 1987 the mausoleum with the army has been a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

abschnitte.text: In 221 BC, **Qin Shi Huangdi** united several Chinese kingdoms into one empire. He introduced standard measures, weights, coins and a standard script. Under him, work was also done on forerunners of the Great Wall of China. Even during his lifetime he had a huge tomb complex built, on which hundreds of thousands of people are said to have worked. He died in 210 BC.

In March 1974, farmers near the city of **Xi'an** were digging a well. They found fragments of clay figures. Archaeologists soon realised that they had come across a huge underground army. Several large **pits** are known today, but only some of the figures have been dug up.

The warriors are roughly life-size and made of **terracotta**, that is, fired clay. There are archers, foot soldiers, officers, charioteers and horses. The figures were assembled from separate parts, but faces, hairstyles and clothing were shaped individually. That is why almost all the warriors look different. Originally they were **brightly painted**, but the paint flakes off within minutes in the air.

The warriors carried real weapons made of **bronze**, such as swords, spears, crossbows and arrowheads. Some blades were so well preserved that they were still sharp after more than 2000 years. However, many weapons were looted during uprisings shortly after the emperor's death. At that time parts of the pits were also set on fire.

The emperor's actual **burial mound** lies about one kilometre away from the warriors. It has not been opened to this day, because people do not want to damage the finds by excavating. An ancient Chinese historian reported rivers of mercury in the tomb, and indeed raised levels of mercury have been measured in the ground. Since 1987 the site has been a **UNESCO World Heritage Site**, and it attracts millions of visitors every year.

begriffe.erklaerung: Fired clay, from which figures, pots or tiles are made.
A large, splendid tomb.
The science that digs up and studies old traces of people.
A mixture of copper and tin from which weapons and tools used to be made.

gewusst: The army was meant to protect the emperor in the afterlife.
One of the farmers who discovered the army later signed autographs in a museum shop.
Individual clay warriors have travelled around the world for exhibitions, including to Bern in Switzerland.

teile.einleitung: A termite mound is the nest of a termite colony, often a huge hill of earth. Inside, thousands to millions of termites live in a clever system of tunnels and chambers. The mounds are so cleverly ventilated that architects use them as a model for buildings.
wichtigste: Many termites build large mounds.
They build their mounds from earth and saliva.
Termite mounds can grow several metres high.
Many tunnels and channels provide fresh air.
Most termites live in warm countries.
Many termites eat wood.
In Africa there is an office building that is ventilated like a termite mound and so saves electricity for cooling.

abschnitte.text: **Termites** are small, usually pale insects that live together in large colonies. Although they are often called “white ants”, they are more closely related to cockroaches. A colony has workers, soldiers and a royal couple. Most termite species live in **warm countries** in Africa, Australia, Asia and South America.

Termites build their mounds from **earth**, which they mix with **saliva** and droppings. Once it dries, the mixture becomes as hard as concrete. The mounds can grow several metres high, which for these tiny animals is like a skyscraper. But many species also build nests underground or in dead wood.

Inside a mound there is a network of many **tunnels** and channels. Warm, stale air rises and escapes through the thin walls, and fresh air flows in. In this way the temperature and humidity in the nest stay almost the same, even when it is very hot or cool outside. This is called natural **ventilation**.

Many termites eat **wood**, but also grass and leaves. They can only digest the hard wood with the help of tiny microorganisms in their gut. Some African species even grow **fungus gardens** in their mounds, which break down the plant material for them. In nature, termites are an important rubbish collection service, because they break down dead plant material.

In Harare in **Zimbabwe** there is an office building, the Eastgate Centre, that is ventilated like a termite mound. The architect Mick Pearce was inspired by termite mounds when designing it. The building hardly needs any air conditioning and so saves a lot of **electricity** for cooling. When people take ideas from nature, it is called **biomimetics**.

begriffe.erklaerung: A large nest of earth that termites build above the ground.
A large community of insects that lives together in one nest.
The exchange of stale air for fresh air.
A technology that uses ideas from nature for inventions.

gewusst: In Australia there are compass termites, whose flat mounds all point in a north-south direction.
Some termite mounds in Africa are more than a hundred years old and are lived in from generation to generation.
Compared with their body size, termites build higher than humans do with their tallest skyscrapers.

teile.einleitung: The bee dance is the way honeybees show each other where there is food. To do this they perform special dances on the honeycombs in the dark hive. This amazing language was decoded by the researcher Karl von Frisch.
wichtigste: Honeybees dance to show other bees where there is food.
They dance on the honeycombs in the hive.
If the food is very close, they perform the round dance.
If the food is far away, they perform the waggle dance.
In the waggle dance, the bees use the sun to orient themselves.
From the scent that is brought back, the other bees recognise the type of flower.
Karl von Frisch decoded the bee dance and was awarded the Nobel Prize for it.

abschnitte.text: When a **forager bee** has found a good source of food, it flies back to the hive. There it performs a particular dance on the upright **honeycombs**. Other bees follow close behind it and feel its movements, because it is dark in the hive. In this way they learn in which direction and how far they have to fly.

If the food is very close to the hive, the bee performs the **round dance**. It runs in small circles, alternately to the left and to the right. This dance only says: “There is food very close by; search the surrounding area.” The round dance does not give an exact direction.

If the food is further away, the bee performs the **waggle dance**, which looks like a figure of eight. In the middle it runs straight ahead, waggling its abdomen strongly. The direction of this run shows the angle between the **sun** and the source of food: if it runs straight upwards, the food is exactly in the direction of the sun. The longer the bee waggles, the further away the destination is.

From the **scent** that the dancer brings back from the flowers, the other bees can smell which flowers they have to look for. The dancer often hands out samples of nectar too. The better the source of food, the more lively and longer it dances. In this way the most bees fly to the best flowers.

The Austrian researcher **Karl von Frisch** studied bees for decades using little food dishes and marked bees. He worked in Munich and Graz, among other places. For his discoveries he received the **Nobel Prize** in Physiology or Medicine in 1973, together with Konrad Lorenz and Nikolaas Tinbergen. His work showed that even insects communicate with each other with amazing precision.

begriffe.erklaerung: The movements with which honeybees tell other bees about sources of food.
A wall of six-sided wax cells in the beehive.
A dance in small circles that shows food nearby.
A figure-of-eight dance with waggling that shows the direction and distance of food.

gewusst: Bees can locate the sun even behind clouds, because they can see polarised light.
A waggle dance can show feeding places that are several kilometres away from the hive.
When dancing, bees even take into account that the sun moves on over the course of the day.

teile.einleitung: An observatory is a building from which people use telescopes to observe stars, planets and other celestial bodies. Some are used for research, others are public observatories that anyone who is interested can visit.
wichtigste: In an observatory you observe stars and planets.
The most important instrument is the telescope.
At the top of the dome, a slit opens for the telescope.
The best time to visit an observatory is on a clear night.
Many observatories are far away from towns, because it is darker there.
The Urania observatory stands right in the middle of the city of Zurich.
With a telescope you can see the craters on the Moon and the rings of Saturn.

abschnitte.text: An observatory, called **“Sternwarte”** or “Observatorium” in German, is a place for observing the sky. Its heart is a large **telescope**, which collects much more light than our eyes. With it you can see faint stars, planets, star clusters and distant galaxies. Research observatories mainly take measurements and photos, while public observatories show the sky to all visitors.

Many observatories have a round **dome** that can be turned. At the top, a slit opens through which the telescope looks at the sky. Because the Earth rotates, the stars move across the sky, so the telescope has to follow them. The dome protects the delicate instrument from rain, wind and dust.

The best time to observe is on a clear night without a moon. The light from street lamps and houses brightens the sky; this is called **light pollution**. That is why large observatories are usually far away from towns, often on high mountains where the air is dry and calm. Famous examples are the observatories in the Atacama Desert in Chile and on Mauna Kea in Hawaii.

Even with a small telescope you can make out the **craters** on the Moon. With the planet **Saturn** you can see its rings, and with Jupiter four bright moons. The star closest to the Earth is the Sun, and you must never look at it through a telescope without a special filter. Otherwise you could go blind immediately.

The **Urania** in Zurich is an observatory right in the middle of the city and was opened in 1907. Many places in Switzerland have public observatories, which are run by clubs and regularly offer public evenings. On the Jungfraujoch and the Gornergrat, research is carried out at high altitude. The University of Geneva runs an observatory whose researchers discovered the first planet orbiting a Sun-like star in 1995.

begriffe.erklaerung: An instrument that collects light and shows distant things enlarged.
A building or place for observing the sky; in German also “Sternwarte”.
Artificial light that brightens the night sky and makes stars invisible.
An observatory that is meant for the general public.

gewusst: Large telescopes are so sensitive that they could detect the light of a candle on the Moon.
Some observatories do not observe with light but with radio waves; they are called radio telescopes.

teile.einleitung: A symbiosis is when two different species live together and both benefit. The term comes from Greek and means “living together”. Symbioses exist everywhere in nature, in the forest, in the sea and even in our own tummies.
wichtigste: In a symbiosis, two species live together for their mutual benefit.
Mycorrhiza is a symbiosis between fungi and the roots of many trees.
Nodule bacteria supply legumes such as peas with nitrogen from the air.
Clownfish and sea anemones protect each other.
Cleaner fish free large fish from skin parasites.
Bacteria in the gut of cows break down hard-to-digest cellulose.
If only one species benefits without harming the other, it is called commensalism.

abschnitte.text: In a **symbiosis**, two different species live closely together and help each other. Each partner gives something and gets something back, for example food, protection or a home. The term was used by the German researcher Heinrich Anton de Bary in 1879. Some partners can no longer survive without each other at all.

Not every way of living together benefits both sides. In **commensalism**, one species benefits and the other has neither an advantage nor a disadvantage, like birds that nest in a tree. In **parasitism**, one has an advantage and the other is harmed, for example by a tick bite. So symbiosis is the friendliest form of living together.

Many trees such as spruces, beeches or larches live together with fungi; this is called **mycorrhiza**. The fungal threads wrap around the roots and supply the tree with water and mineral salts. In return the fungus gets sugar, which the tree makes using sunlight. Legumes such as peas, beans and clover house **nodule bacteria**, which supply them with nitrogen from the air.

The **clownfish** lives among the poisonous tentacles of a sea anemone, which protects it from enemies. In return it chases away fish that want to nibble the anemone. Small **cleaner fish** free large fish from skin parasites and get their food that way. Bees and flowers are partners too: the bee gets nectar, and the flower is pollinated so that fruit can form.

Cows eat a lot of grass, but they cannot digest the tough **cellulose** in it themselves. This work is done by tiny bacteria in their rumen, part of the stomach. Trillions of useful bacteria also live in the human gut; they are called the **gut flora**. They help with digestion and protect against pathogens.

A special symbiosis is found in **lichens**, which consist of a fungus and an alga. The fungus provides support and stores water, while the alga makes food using sunlight. Together, lichens can grow on bare rocks, tree bark or walls. In the Swiss Alps they often cover whole stones with yellow, grey or orange patches.

begriffe.erklaerung: Two species living together in a way that benefits both.
One species benefits, the other has neither an advantage nor a disadvantage.
One species lives at the expense of another and harms it.
The partnership between fungi and the roots of plants.
A tough substance in the walls of plant cells that is hard to digest.

gewusst: Many edible mushrooms such as the penny bun only grow where their partner tree stands.
Lichens often grow only a few millimetres a year and can become very old.
Corals live together with tiny algae that give them their bright colours and part of their food.

teile.einleitung: Sigmund Freud was an Austrian doctor who founded psychoanalysis. He was convinced that much of what we think and feel comes from a hidden part of our mind, the unconscious. His ideas changed psychology, art and the way people think about themselves.
wichtigste: Sigmund Freud founded psychoanalysis, a theory and a method of treatment.
He lived and worked for most of his life in Vienna.
His structural model of the mind distinguishes between the id, the ego and the superego.
His work “The Interpretation of Dreams” appeared around 1900 and saw dreams as a path to the unconscious.
In free association, patients say everything that comes into their minds.
Freud called keeping unpleasant thoughts away from consciousness repression.
His daughter Anna Freud developed the theory of defence mechanisms further and shaped child analysis.
A slip of the tongue that supposedly gives away a hidden thought is called a Freudian slip.

abschnitte.text: **Sigmund Freud** was born in 1856 in Freiberg in Moravia, which is now called Příbor and lies in the Czech Republic. As a small child he moved with his family to **Vienna**, where he spent almost his whole life. He studied medicine and at first worked as a doctor for nervous illnesses. In this work he treated people with mental suffering for which there was no explanation at the time. From this work he gradually developed **psychoanalysis**.

Freud divided the human mind into three parts. The **id** stands for drives and wishes that want to be fulfilled at once. The **superego** is like an inner judge with rules and a conscience. The ego mediates between the two and reality. According to Freud, problems arise when these parts come into conflict.

In psychoanalytic treatment, patients often lay on a **couch**. They were asked to say everything that came into their minds, the so-called **free association**. Freud listened and looked for hidden connections. He believed that unpleasant memories are kept away from consciousness through **repression**. If they become conscious again, the person could feel better.

abschnitte.titel: Dreams and slips of the tongue
abschnitte.text: In his famous book **“The Interpretation of Dreams”** (in German “Die Traumdeutung”), which appeared around 1900, Freud described dreams as a path to the unconscious. In dreams, hidden wishes often showed themselves in coded images. In his opinion, small mistakes in everyday life, such as slips of the tongue or forgetting, could also give something away. That is why people still speak of a **Freudian slip** today.

In 1938 the National Socialists took over Austria. Freud was Jewish, his books were burned, and his family was in danger. With his daughter **Anna Freud** he fled to London. He died there in September 1939 at the age of 83. His flat in Vienna at Berggasse 19 is a museum today.

Freud's ideas had a very strong influence on medicine, literature, film and art. Terms such as the unconscious, repression or the ego are part of everyday language today. For a time his companions included the Swiss psychiatrist **Carl Gustav Jung**, who later went his own way. Many researchers criticise the fact that Freud's theories can hardly be tested scientifically. Nevertheless, he is regarded as one of the most influential thinkers of the 20th century.

begriffe.erklaerung: Freud's theory of the unconscious and a talking treatment based on it.
The part of our mind whose thoughts and wishes we are not aware of.
The unconscious pushing away of unpleasant thoughts or memories.
A method in which you say everything that comes to mind without choosing.
The soul or inner life of a person, with feelings and thoughts.

gewusst: Freud's famous couch is now in the Freud Museum in London.
The book “The Interpretation of Dreams” came out at the end of 1899 but bears the date 1900.
Freud's daughter Anna herself became a well-known psychoanalyst and child researcher.

teile.einleitung: Stratigraphy is the study of layers in the ground and in rock. Archaeologists and geologists read these layers like the pages of a book to find out what happened first and what happened later.
wichtigste: Stratigraphy deals with the sequence of layers of soil and rock.
The Latin word stratum means covering or layer.
In 1669 Nicolaus Steno formulated the law of superposition.
Stratigraphy provides a relative dating.
Archaeologists show the sequence of layers in a Harris matrix.
A cultural layer contains traces of human activity.
In the Middle East, mounds made of many settlement layers are called tells.

abschnitte.text: The word comes from the Latin **stratum**, covering or layer, and the Greek graphein, to write. Stratigraphy studies how layers lie on top of one another in the ground. In geology it is about rock layers that formed over millions of years. In **archaeology** it is about layers that people left behind with rubbish, buildings and fires.

In 1669 the Danish naturalist **Nicolaus Steno** formulated the law of superposition. It states that in undisturbed layers, the lower ones are older than the upper ones. You can imagine a pile of newspapers onto which a new one is put every day. At the very bottom is the oldest newspaper, at the very top the newest. Steno is therefore regarded as one of the founders of geology.

Stratigraphy tells you what is older and what is younger, but not exactly how old. This is called **relative dating**. If you find a coin in a layer that was minted in AD 150, the layer was formed in the year 150 at the earliest. A pit that cuts through three layers is younger than these layers. For exact dates you need further methods such as radiocarbon dating or the tree rings of wood.

During an excavation, archaeologists carefully remove one layer after another and record everything. Each layer, pit or wall is given a number. They show the sequence in a diagram, the **Harris matrix**, which the archaeologist Edward Harris developed in the 1970s. This shows at a glance what came into being before and after something else.

A **cultural layer** contains traces of human activity such as shards, bones, ash or remains of wood. In Switzerland, such layers are found for example at the pile-dwelling settlements on lake shores, which are a UNESCO World Heritage Site. In the Middle East, towns grew higher and higher on their own ruins over thousands of years. This created mounds made of many settlement layers, which are called **tells**.

begriffe.erklaerung: A deposit of earth, rock or rubbish that has settled over another one.
Working out what is older and what is younger, without an exact date.
A layer of soil with traces of people, such as shards or ash.
A mound that has formed from many settlements lying on top of one another.

gewusst: In the walls of the Grand Canyon in the USA, you can read almost two billion years of Earth's history in the layers.
Nicolaus Steno was not only a naturalist; he later also became a bishop.

teile.einleitung: The solar system is our cosmic home: the Sun and everything that orbits it. It includes eight planets, their moons, dwarf planets, asteroids and comets. The Earth is the third planet from the Sun.
wichtigste: Our solar system has eight planets.
At its centre is the Sun, which holds everything together with its gravity.
The four inner planets are made of rock; the four outer ones are giant planets.
Jupiter is the largest planet, Mercury the smallest.
Since 2006 Pluto has been regarded as a dwarf planet.
The solar system formed about 4.6 billion years ago.

abschnitte.text: Seen from the Sun, the planets are called Mercury, Venus, Earth, Mars, Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus and Neptune. A memory sentence helps: “My Very Easy Method Just Speeds Up Naming”. In German children learn “Mein Vater erklärt mir jeden Sonntag unseren Nachthimmel” (My father explains our night sky to me every Sunday). Each **planet** orbits the Sun on its own path. Mercury needs only 88 days for this, but Neptune about 165 years.

Mercury, Venus, Earth and Mars are **rocky planets** with a solid surface. Jupiter and Saturn are **gas giants**, made mainly of hydrogen and helium. Uranus and Neptune are called ice giants because they contain a lot of frozen water, methane and ammonia. Over 1,300 Earths would fit inside Jupiter.

Most planets have **moons**; only Mercury and Venus do not. The Earth has one moon, Mars two small ones. Jupiter and Saturn each have well over 90 known moons, and new ones are still being discovered. Saturn is famous for its rings of ice and rock, but the other giant planets also have faint rings.

Between Mars and Jupiter lies the **asteroid belt** with countless lumps of rock. Beyond Neptune begins the Kuiper belt, where Pluto also orbits. In 2006 the International Astronomical Union declared Pluto a **dwarf planet**. Comets of ice and dust come from the outermost regions and form long glowing tails near the Sun.

About 4.6 billion years ago a huge cloud of gas and dust contracted. The Sun formed at its centre. The planets formed from the remaining material in a flat disc. That is why all the planets orbit in roughly the same plane and in the same direction.

Because the distances in the solar system are so huge, there are many **planet trails** in Switzerland. A well-known one leads from the Uetliberg to the Felsenegg near Zurich, on a scale of 1 to 1 billion. There the Sun is the size of a ball 1.4 metres across, and the Earth only the size of a marble. To reach Pluto you walk around six kilometres.

begriffe.erklaerung: A large body in space that orbits a star and does not shine by itself.
A smaller, round body that has not cleared its orbit, such as Pluto.
A small lump of rock that orbits the Sun.
A lump of ice and dust that forms a glowing tail near the Sun.

gewusst: The space probe Voyager 1 was launched in 1977 and is today the human-made object furthest from the Earth.
It is hotter on Venus than on Mercury, although Mercury is closer to the Sun.
A day on Venus lasts longer than a year on Venus.

teile.einleitung: “Schweizer Jugend forscht” (Swiss Youth in Science) is a foundation that wants to inspire young people about science and technology. Since 1967 young people have been able to present their own research projects here in a national competition.
wichtigste: “Schweizer Jugend forscht” is a research competition for young people.
The competition has existed since 1967.
The foundation is based in Bern.
The National Competition is aimed mainly at young people at upper secondary and vocational schools.
Many grammar school pupils submit their Matura project.
The best rating is “outstanding”.
As well as the competition there are week-long study weeks.

abschnitte.text: “Schweizer Jugend forscht” is a **foundation** that was set up in 1967 and is based in Bern. It supports young people who are interested in the natural sciences, technology and computing, but also in history, language or society. The aim is for young people to do research themselves and to test their ideas seriously. The foundation is supported by the federal government, companies, universities and other partners.

The **National Competition** is the heart of the foundation. It is open mainly to young people at grammar schools, specialised upper secondary schools and vocational schools. Many submit their **Matura project** or a project from their apprenticeship. A jury of experts assesses the work, and the best participants are invited to the final.

At the **final** the young people present their own project at a stand. They explain to the jury and to visitors what they have found out. The projects are rated good, very good or **outstanding**. In addition there are cash prizes and special prizes, for example a trip to an international competition abroad.

As well as the competition, the foundation offers **study weeks** that last one week. There young people work in research laboratories of universities or companies. In this way they learn how real scientists work. There are study weeks on subjects such as biology, chemistry, computing or history.

The best projects may represent Switzerland at international competitions. These include, for example, the European Union Contest for Young Scientists. There the young people meet others of their age from many countries. For some, “Schweizer Jugend forscht” is the first step towards a university course or a **career in research**.

begriffe.erklaerung: An organisation with money or assets that are used for a particular purpose.
A larger piece of independent work that grammar school pupils write before the Matura.
A group of experts who assess work and award prizes.
An assessment, for example “very good” or “outstanding”.

gewusst: Projects at “Schweizer Jugend forscht” can also come from subjects such as history, music or economics.
Some participants later founded their own company with their project.

teile.einleitung: The “Trieste” was a submersible for great depths, a so-called bathyscaphe. It was designed by the Swiss physicist Auguste Piccard. In 1960, with his son Jacques Piccard and the American Don Walsh on board, it reached the deepest point of the world's oceans.
wichtigste: The Swiss physicist Auguste Piccard designed the “Trieste”.
The word bathyscaphe means roughly “deep ship”.
The large float was filled with petrol to provide buoyancy.
To rise to the surface, the “Trieste” dropped iron balls used as ballast.
The crew sat in a small steel sphere under the float.
It was named after the Italian city of Trieste.
In 1958 the US Navy bought the submersible.
In 1960 the descent to the seabed took almost five hours.

abschnitte.text: The “Trieste” was a **bathyscaphe**, a submersible for the deep sea. The word comes from Greek and means roughly “deep ship”. Its inventor was the Swiss physicist **Auguste Piccard**, who had earlier gone up into the stratosphere in a balloon. The boat was built largely in Italy and launched in 1953. It was named after the port city of **Trieste**, which supported its construction.

The “Trieste” worked in a similar way to a balloon, only underwater. On top was a large **float** filled with petrol. Petrol is lighter than water and can hardly be compressed, so it provided buoyancy even at great depth. To dive, tonnes of **iron balls** were taken along as ballast. When the crew wanted to come up, they let the balls drop, and the boat slowly rose.

Under the float hung a small **steel sphere** in which the crew sat. Inside it was only about two metres across, and it had very thick walls to withstand the enormous pressure. Through a small window you could look outside. It was cramped and cold, and two people hardly had room to move. Strong floodlights provided light, because it is completely dark in the deep sea.

In 1958 the **US Navy** bought the “Trieste” and rebuilt it for even greater depths. On 23 January 1960 **Jacques Piccard** and Don Walsh dived into the Mariana Trench in the Pacific. The descent to the bottom of the Challenger Deep took almost five hours. At a depth of almost 11 kilometres they stayed only about 20 minutes, because a window pane had cracked. Then they rose again and were celebrated as heroes.

The dive proved that humans can reach the deepest point of the oceans. Only in 2012 did a person dive that deep again: the film director James Cameron. The “Trieste” is now on display in a US Navy museum in Washington. The Piccard family stayed true to research and adventure: Auguste Piccard's grandson **Bertrand Piccard** travelled round the Earth by balloon and by solar-powered aircraft.

begriffe.erklaerung: A submersible for great depths that works like an underwater balloon.
Heavy material that makes a vehicle sink.
The force that pushes something upwards in water.
The deepest ocean trench on Earth, in the Pacific.

gewusst: For the record dive in 1960, the “Trieste” was given a new, even thicker pressure sphere from Germany.
Auguste Piccard is said to have been a model for the absent-minded Professor Calculus in the Tintin comics.
The float of the “Trieste” held many thousands of litres of petrol.

teile.einleitung: A sonar is a device that “sees” under water with sound. It sends out sound waves and listens for their echo to locate depths, obstacles, fish or submarines. Dolphins and bats have mastered this principle for millions of years.
wichtigste: A sonar measures distances under water using sound waves and their echo.
The English abbreviation stands for “Sound Navigation and Ranging”.
Sound travels through seawater at about 1,500 metres per second.
An echo sounder measures the depth of the water under a ship.
If the echo comes back after 2 seconds, the sea is about 1,500 metres deep at 1,500 m/s.
Dolphins find their way with echoes, much like a sonar.
The sinking of the Titanic in 1912 encouraged the development of underwater detection devices.
Modern multibeam echo sounders make maps of the seabed.

abschnitte.text: A sonar sends a short **pulse of sound** into the water. If the sound hits the seabed, a fish or a wreck, it is thrown back. The device picks up this **echo** and measures the time until it arrives. Because sound in seawater travels at about **1,500 metres per second**, the distance can be calculated from this. Important: the sound covers the distance twice, there and back.

An **echo sounder** receives the echo after 2 seconds. In this time the sound travels 2 times 1,500, that is 3,000 metres. Since this is the way there and back, you divide by two. So at this spot the sea is about 1,500 metres deep. Light only reaches a few hundred metres in the sea, but sound reaches many kilometres, which is why it is used under water.

After the sinking of the **Titanic** in 1912, inventors looked for ways to locate icebergs and obstacles with sound. Shortly afterwards the German **Alexander Behm** developed the echo sounder. In the First World War there was intensive research on devices to track down enemy submarines. The name **sonar** comes from English and stands for “Sound Navigation and Ranging”, that is, navigation and measuring distance with sound.

An **active sonar** sends out sound itself and analyses the echoes. A **passive sonar** sends out nothing but only listens for noises, for example from ships' propellers. Submarines often use passive sonar so that they are not discovered themselves. Fishermen use small sonar devices, called fish finders, to find shoals of fish.

Modern **multibeam echo sounders** send out many beams of sound at the same time in a wide fan. In this way research ships survey a whole strip of the seabed at once. This produces exact maps of underwater mountains, trenches and wrecks. Even so, only part of the seabed has been surveyed precisely to this day. The depths of Swiss lakes such as Lake Geneva or Lake Constance have also been measured with echo sounders.

**Dolphins** and toothed whales make clicking sounds and listen for the echoes. In this way they find prey even in murky water. **Bats** use the same principle in the air with ultrasound. This ability is called **echolocation**. However, noise from ships and powerful sonar devices can disturb and confuse marine mammals.

begriffe.erklaerung: Sound that is thrown back by an obstacle.
A device that measures the depth of water with sound.
The way animals find their way using sounds and their echoes.
Sound so high that people cannot hear it.

gewusst: Sound travels about four times as fast in water as in air.
With their clicks, dolphins can tell apart objects they cannot even see.
The word sonar is an abbreviation from English.

teile.einleitung: The Rosetta Stone is an old stone slab from Egypt on which the same text is written in three different scripts. With its help it became possible to decipher the mysterious Egyptian hieroglyphs. Today it is one of the most famous exhibits in the British Museum in London.
wichtigste: The stone was found in 1799 by French soldiers.
It gets its name from the place where it was found, Rosetta in the Nile Delta.
It is made of granodiorite, a hard, dark rock.
On it is a decree by priests in honour of King Ptolemy V.
Scholars could already read the ancient Greek writing on it.
In 1822 Jean-François Champollion deciphered the hieroglyphs with its help.
After the defeat of the French in Egypt, the stone came into British hands as spoils of war.

abschnitte.text: The Rosetta Stone is a fragment of a larger stone slab made of **granodiorite**. It is a little over a metre high and weighs about 760 kilograms. On it is a decree by priests from the year 196 BC in honour of King **Ptolemy V**. Such decrees were set up in temples throughout the land so that everyone could read them.

The same text appears on the stone in three scripts: at the top in **hieroglyphs**, in the middle in **Demotic** and at the bottom in **ancient Greek**. Hieroglyphs were the sacred picture writing for temples and tombs. Demotic was the everyday script of the Egyptians. Greek was the language of the ruling Ptolemaic family, which came from Macedonia.

In July 1799 **French soldiers** came across the stone during building work on a fort near Rosetta in the Nile Delta. They had come to Egypt with Napoleon Bonaparte, together with many scholars. After the defeat of the French in Egypt, they had to hand the stone over to the British in 1801. Since 1802 it has been in the **British Museum** in London.

Because the scholars could read ancient Greek, they knew what the text meant. The Briton **Thomas Young** recognised that the oval frames, the **cartouches**, contain the names of rulers. The Frenchman **Jean-François Champollion** compared the names Ptolemy and Cleopatra and found out that hieroglyphs stand for both sounds and ideas. In 1822 he presented his deciphering, and so after around 1,400 years Egyptian texts could be read again.

Thanks to the Rosetta Stone, thousands of Egyptian inscriptions, papyri and tomb texts can be read today. This made **Egyptology** possible as a science. The expression “Rosetta Stone” now stands in general for a key that makes a puzzle solvable. Egypt has long demanded that the stone be returned.

begriffe.erklaerung: The picture writing of the ancient Egyptians.
A simplified everyday script in ancient Egypt.
An oval around a group of hieroglyphs that contains a ruler's name.
The science of ancient Egypt.
A hard rock similar to granite.

gewusst: The Rosetta Stone is one of the most visited exhibits in the British Museum.
For a long time the carved signs were filled in with white chalk so that visitors could read them better.
The town where it was found is now called Rashid.

teile.einleitung: A dice is a small cube with six sides on which there are dots from one to six. It is used in many games to let chance decide. Dice are among the oldest gaming tools of humankind.
wichtigste: A dice has 6 faces, 8 corners and 12 edges.
The dots on a dice are called pips.
The pips on two opposite sides always add up to 7.
That is why the 6 lies opposite the 1.
All six sides together have 21 pips.
With two dice the smallest total is 2 and the largest 12.
With a fair dice every number has the same chance.

abschnitte.text: An ordinary dice is a **cube** in the geometrical sense: it has 6 square faces of equal size, 8 corners and 12 edges. On the faces 1 to 6 dots, the **pips**, are arranged. Opposite sides always add up to 7, that is 1 and 6, 2 and 5, and 3 and 4. If you add up all the pips, you get 21.

With a fair dice every number is equally likely; the chance of a particular number is 1 in 6. That is why a dice is good for understanding **probability**. If you throw two dice, there are 36 possible combinations. The total 7 comes up most often, because there are six ways to throw it, whereas 2 and 12 have only one way each.

Dice have existed for several thousand years. In ancient cultures in Asia and the Middle East people already played with dice made of bone, stone or clay. The Greeks and Romans often threw small ankle bones of sheep, the **astragali**. The Roman general Julius Caesar is said to have said “The die is cast” when a decision could no longer be undone.

Besides the six-sided dice there are also dice with 4, 8, 10, 12 or 20 sides. Many of them are so-called **Platonic solids**, in which all the faces look the same. They are used above all in role-playing games. There are also dice with colours, letters or pictures instead of pips.

In Switzerland **“Eile mit Weile”** (roughly “more haste, less speed”), a game similar to Ludo, is a popular dice game for the whole family. In snakes and ladders, Monopoly or backgammon, too, the dice decides how far you may move. In the game Yahtzee you try to get certain combinations with five dice. Dice make games exciting, because luck is part of it and not just skill.

begriffe.erklaerung: The dots on the sides of a dice.
A measure of how great the chance is that something will happen.
A solid whose faces are all identical regular polygons of the same size.
A small ankle bone that was used as a dice in the past.

gewusst: Dice in casinos have sharp edges and are transparent so that nobody can cheat.
On Western dice the pips 1 to 3 meet at one corner, and the same is true of 4 to 6.
On many Asian dice the pip of the 1 is red and especially large.

teile.einleitung: In biology, translation is the process in which the cell makes a protein from instructions written in RNA. It takes place at tiny protein factories, the ribosomes. In it, the language of the bases is translated into the language of the amino acids, hence the name translation.
wichtigste: Translation takes place at the ribosomes.
In it, the information of the mRNA is translated into a chain of amino acids.
The tRNA with the growing peptide chain binds at the P site of the ribosome.
The peptide bond is made by the ribosomal RNA.
When a stop codon reaches the A site, a release factor frees the finished chain.
Several ribosomes reading the same mRNA at the same time are called a polysome.
The antibiotic tetracycline blocks the binding of tRNA to the ribosome in bacteria.

abschnitte.text: **Proteins** consist of long chains of **amino acids**. The order of these amino acids is stored in the mRNA. Every three bases of the mRNA, a **codon**, stand for a particular amino acid. This assignment is called the genetic code and is the same in almost all living things. Translation follows transcription.

Ribosomes are tiny structures made of RNA and proteins. They consist of a small and a large subunit. Based on how they behave in a centrifuge, ribosomes in the cytoplasm of eukaryotes are called **80S ribosomes**; in bacteria they are 70S ribosomes. The ribosome has three binding sites for tRNA: the A site, the **P site** and the E site. Its heart is the **ribosomal RNA**, which makes the connection between the amino acids.

**Transfer RNA**, tRNA for short, brings the right amino acids to the ribosome. Each tRNA has three bases at one end, the anticodon, which exactly match a codon on the mRNA. At the other end it carries the matching amino acid. In this way the right amino acid always ends up in the right place.

Translation begins at a **start codon**, usually AUG, which stands for the amino acid methionine. In bacteria, the Shine-Dalgarno sequence helps the ribosome find the right start codon, and the first amino acid is N-formylmethionine. Then the ribosome moves on codon by codon, adding amino acid after amino acid. When a **stop codon** reaches the A site, a release factor frees the finished chain. Often several ribosomes read the same mRNA at the same time; they form a polysome.

Because the ribosomes of bacteria and humans are different, **antibiotics** can disturb translation in bacteria in a targeted way. **Tetracycline**, for example, prevents tRNA from binding to the bacterial ribosome. Streptomycin and erythromycin also act on the ribosome. Research into the structure of the ribosome was awarded the Nobel Prize in Chemistry in 2009.

begriffe.erklaerung: A small building block from which proteins are made.
A tiny protein factory in the cell.
Three bases in a row on the mRNA that stand for an amino acid.
A small RNA molecule that brings amino acids to the ribosome.
The link that holds two amino acids together in a chain.

gewusst: A single cell can contain millions of ribosomes.
Bacterial ribosomes add about 15 to 20 amino acids to the chain per second.
The fact that RNA and not a protein makes the peptide bond is regarded as a clue to an early RNA world at the beginning of life.

teile.einleitung: A pond is a small, fairly shallow body of still water that has often been made by people. Despite its small size, it is a paradise for animals and plants, from frogs and newts to dragonflies and water lilies. If you sit quietly on the bank, you can discover a lot there.
wichtigste: A pond is smaller and shallower than a lake.
Many ponds were made by people, for example as fish ponds, fire ponds or garden ponds.
Reeds and other tall plants often grow on the bank, and water lilies float on the water.
Tadpoles turn into frogs, and young dragonflies first live in the water.
Pond skaters can walk over the water without sinking.
In spring newts come to the pond, and mallards often swim on it.
When it is very cold, a pond freezes over on top in winter.

abschnitte.text: A pond is a body of **still water**, that is, water without a strong current. It is smaller and shallower than a lake, often only one to two metres deep. Because the light usually reaches the bottom, plants can grow almost everywhere. Ponds are often made by people, while small natural bodies of still water are often called **“Weiher”** in German. In everyday language, though, both words are used in a similar way.

abschnitte.titel: Plants by and in the water
abschnitte.text: On the bank grow tall plants such as **reeds**, bulrushes and rushes. Further out, the large round leaves of the **water lily** float on the surface. Underwater grow plants such as Canadian waterweed, which release oxygen into the water. The plants form different zones, from the damp bank to the deeper water.

In spring, frogs and toads lay their spawn in the pond. **Tadpoles** hatch from it; at first they breathe with gills, and later they turn into little frogs. **Newts** with their long tails also come into the water in spring. Young dragonflies, the larvae, live in the pond for one to several years and hunt there before they emerge as flying dragonflies. Mallards swim on the water, and fish such as carp or sunbleak live in it.

The **pond skater** has fine, water-repellent hairs on its legs. Because of this, the **surface tension** of the water carries it, and it can dart around on it. Whirligig beetles spin in fast circles on the surface. The backswimmer, as its name says, swims on its back just below the surface of the water.

In summer the shallow water can get warm, and algae sometimes grow strongly. In winter, when it is very cold, the pond freezes over on top. Because ice is lighter than water, it floats on top, and underneath the water stays liquid at about four degrees. In this way fish and many animals can spend the winter at the bottom. Frogs and newts often spend the winter in the mud or on land under leaves.

In Switzerland, many wetlands and small bodies of water disappeared in the last century because land was drained. That is why newly made **ponds** are very important for amphibians such as the tree frog or the great crested newt. Nature conservation organisations and municipalities therefore create new ponds. Even a natural garden pond without fish can help frogs and dragonflies.

begriffe.erklaerung: A body of water in which the water hardly flows, for example a pond or lake.
The larva of a frog or toad, which lives in the water.
The eggs of frogs, toads or fish in the water.
A force that holds the surface of water together like a thin skin.
An animal such as a frog or newt that lives in water and on land.

gewusst: A pond skater can feel through the tiny ripples on the surface when an insect has fallen into the water.
Dragonfly larvae catch their prey with a catching mask that shoots out lightning fast.
Fish in garden ponds often eat the spawn and tadpoles of frogs.

teile.einleitung: Self-organisation means that small building blocks come together by themselves into ordered structures without any plan from outside. This happens in snowflakes, in soapy water, in living cells and even in modern nanotechnology.
wichtigste: In self-organisation, building blocks arrange themselves spontaneously into structures without outside control.
It belongs to the bottom-up approach to making things, that is, from small to large.
It is driven by the system reaching a state with lower free enthalpy.
In water, phospholipids form double layers by themselves, as in cell membranes.
Above a certain concentration, surfactants form micelles.
In DNA origami a long DNA strand is folded with short staple strands.
The coat proteins of many viruses assemble by themselves into the capsid.

abschnitte.text: Self-organisation means that many small parts form an order by themselves. Nobody controls them from outside, and there is no building plan as with a Lego model. The order arises through the **forces** between the parts. Examples from nature are snow crystals, sand dunes or flocks of birds that change direction together.

Molecules attract or repel each other. They keep moving until they have found a particularly favourable arrangement. Chemists say the system reaches a state with lower **free enthalpy**. You can imagine this like marbles in a bowl that roll down into the hollow by themselves.

Soap molecules, called **surfactants**, have a water-loving head and a water-repelling tail. Above a certain amount in water they form small spheres, the **micelles**, with their tails pointing inwards. In a similar way, phospholipids form double layers by themselves in water, because their tails turn away from the water. The membranes of all living cells are made of such double layers.

Self-organisation plays a big role in living things. The coat proteins of many viruses assemble quite by themselves into a regular shell, the **capsid**. DNA also forms its famous double helix by itself, because A always pairs with T and G always with C. This exact **base pairing** makes DNA an ideal building block.

In nanotechnology self-organisation is used to build tiny structures. This is called the **bottom-up** approach, because you go from the single molecule to the larger component. In **DNA origami** a long DNA strand is folded with many short staple strands into shapes such as smiley faces or little boxes. On gold surfaces, thiols form ordered layers by themselves that are only one molecule thick.

begriffe.erklaerung: A tiny sphere of soap molecules that forms by itself in water.
A way of building from small to large, in which building blocks join together.
The protective protein shell of a virus.
Technology with tiny structures only millionths of a millimetre in size.

gewusst: With DNA origami researchers have already folded a tiny map and smiley faces out of DNA, which can only be seen with special microscopes.
Every snowflake arises through the self-organisation of water molecules and so has six arms.

teile.einleitung: Thomas Alva Edison was an American inventor and businessman who is one of the most famous inventors in history. He developed the phonograph, improved the light bulb and built one of the first electricity networks. With more than 1000 patents he fundamentally changed people's everyday lives.
wichtigste: Thomas Alva Edison came from the USA.
He lived from 1847 to 1931.
He was taught mostly at home by his mother.
He invented the phonograph, which could record and play back sounds.
He turned the light bulb into a really usable light for homes.
So that the light bulbs could shine, he built an electricity network.
He held more than 1000 patents.
He was called “the Wizard of Menlo Park”.

abschnitte.text: Thomas Alva Edison was born in 1847 in Milan in the US state of Ohio. He only went to school for a short time and was then taught mostly at home by his **mother**. As a teenager he already sold newspapers on the train and experimented in a small laboratory. From his youth he was hard of hearing, but this did not stop him from inventing.

In 1876 Edison set up a large research laboratory in **Menlo Park** in the state of New Jersey. There many employees worked together on new inventions, which was completely new at the time. Because so many inventions came from there, he was called “the **Wizard of Menlo Park**”. Later he moved to an even larger laboratory in West Orange.

In 1877 Edison invented the **phonograph**, the first device that could record sounds and play them back. The sound waves were scratched with a needle into a cylinder covered with tin foil. For the first recording, Edison spoke a nursery rhyme into it. People were amazed that a machine could talk.

The light bulb already existed before, but it only burned for a short time. Edison and his team searched for a long time for a better filament and in 1879 found a carbon filament that glowed for many hours. So that the **light bulbs** could shine in homes, an **electricity network** was needed. In 1882 Edison opened one of the first power stations for a whole district of a city in New York.

During his life Edison registered more than 1000 **patents**. He also worked on film cameras, batteries and telegraphs. He argued with Nikola Tesla and George Westinghouse about whether direct current or **alternating current** was better, and alternating current won. Edison died in 1931; his company became part of the General Electric group, which still exists today.

begriffe.erklaerung: A person who thinks up and builds something new.
A right that secures an invention for the inventor for a certain time.
An early device for recording and playing back sounds on a cylinder.
A lamp in which a thin wire becomes so hot from electricity that it glows.
Electric current that keeps changing its direction, as in our sockets today.

gewusst: For the light bulb, Edison's team tested thousands of materials, even bamboo fibres.
Edison said something like: genius is one per cent inspiration and ninety-nine per cent perspiration, in other words hard work.
The electricity in Swiss sockets is alternating current, the very type of current Edison fought against for a long time.

teile.einleitung: Animal tracks are all the signs that animals leave behind in nature, for example footprints, droppings, feeding remains or feathers. If you can read them, you know which animal has passed by, even if you never see it yourself. Reading tracks is like detective work in the woods.
wichtigste: Animal tracks are especially easy to see in snow and mud.
The print of a single foot is called a footprint.
Roe deer leave prints of cloven hooves.
In a fox's print you can see four toe pads, usually with claws.
Cats pull in their claws when walking, so they are missing from the track.
The droppings of wild animals are called scat, and pellets are balls coughed up by owls.
When a hare hops, its hind feet land in front of its front feet.

abschnitte.text: Animal tracks include **footprints**, that is, prints of single feet, and whole **trails**, which form a row of prints. But droppings, feeding remains, hair, feathers, scratch marks and burrows are also tracks. Prints are easiest to see in fresh snow, in mud or in damp sand. Hunters, foresters and researchers use tracks to find out which animals live in an area.

Dogs and **foxes** show four toe pads and usually the claws in their print. The fox puts its feet exactly one behind the other, so that the track looks like a string of beads. **Cats** pull in their claws when walking, which is why you see no claw marks with them. The badger has five toes and long claws with which it digs.

Even-toed hoofed animals such as **roe deer**, red deer, chamois and wild boar have cloven hooves. The print of a roe deer is small and heart-shaped. With a wild boar you can often also see two small dewclaws behind the main print. A red deer print is much larger than that of a roe deer.

The **hare** moves by hopping. In doing so it puts its long hind feet down in front of its front feet, which lie one behind the other. This creates a typical pattern of two large and two small prints. Squirrels also jump and leave prints that usually begin or end at a tree.

The **squirrel** leaves behind gnawed cones with frayed remains, while mice gnaw the cones neatly. Squirrels split hazelnuts, while mice gnaw a round hole into them. The droppings of wild animals are called **scat**, and you can often recognise the animal from their shape. Owls cough up indigestible remains such as bones and fur as **pellets**. Researchers study pellets to find out which mice live in an area.

In winter you can discover many tracks in Swiss forests and mountains, for example of fox, roe deer, hare, chamois or ptarmigan. With a bit of luck you may even find tracks of lynx or wolf, which live in Switzerland again. If you go looking for tracks, you should not disturb the animals and should stay on the paths. Many nature conservation organisations and parks offer guided tracking walks for families.

begriffe.erklaerung: The print of a single animal foot; in German “Trittsiegel”.
A whole row of an animal's footprints.
The droppings of wild animals.
A coughed-up ball of bones, hair and feathers made by owls and birds of prey.
Animals with cloven hooves such as roe deer, red deer or wild boar.

gewusst: A single owl pellet can contain the bones of several mice.
A lynx puts its hind feet almost exactly into the prints of its front feet, so that you only see one track.
Dinosaurs also left footprints; in Switzerland such tracks are preserved in the Jura, for example.

teile.einleitung: The Swiss Light Source, SLS for short, is a large research facility at the Paul Scherrer Institute in Villigen in the canton of Aargau. In a ring, electrons race round almost at the speed of light and produce extremely bright X-ray light as they do so. With this light, researchers can look into the tiniest structures, right down to individual atoms.
wichtigste: The SLS is located at the Paul Scherrer Institute (PSI) in Villigen in the canton of Aargau and started operating in 2001.
Its storage ring has a circumference of about 290 metres.
Synchrotron radiation is produced when fast electrons are deflected by magnets.
Undulators with many magnets of alternating polarity produce especially bright light.
The light is led to the measuring stations through beamlines.
There is an ultra-high vacuum in the storage ring, so that the electrons do not collide with gas molecules.
With the upgrade project SLS 2.0, the facility received a new storage ring from 2023 with much more brilliant X-ray light.

abschnitte.text: The SLS stands on the site of the **Paul Scherrer Institute** on the River Aare, between Brugg and Zurzach. The round building is easy to recognise from outside and looks like a giant UFO. The PSI is Switzerland's largest research institute for natural sciences and engineering. Every year researchers from many countries come here to carry out their experiments.

First, electrons are produced and brought to high energy in a **linear accelerator** and a pre-accelerator. Then they circle in the **storage ring**, where strong magnets keep them on their path. Every time the electrons are steered round a bend, they give off light, the synchrotron radiation. Until the rebuild in 2023, the electrons had an energy of 2.4 gigaelectronvolts (GeV). Because hardly anything may disturb them, there is an **ultra-high vacuum** in the ring.

An **undulator** consists of many small magnets with alternating polarity. This makes the electrons fly back and forth as if on a slalom course, and they send out especially focused, bright light. This light is led through **beamlines** to the experimental stations around the ring. Each beamline specialises in certain kinds of study, for example X-ray images, spectroscopy or crystal measurements.

The SLS is used particularly often to **determine the structure of proteins**. In this way researchers from universities and the pharmaceutical industry find out how proteins are built and where a medicine can dock. New materials for batteries, computer chips or solar cells are also studied here. The X-ray light can even be used to look inside fossils and works of art without damaging them.

After more than 20 years of operation, the facility was modernised. In autumn 2023 it was switched off, and as part of **SLS 2.0** a completely new storage ring was installed. The electrons now circle at about 2.7 GeV, and the X-ray light is many times brighter and more finely focused. In 2025 the renewed facility started operating again.

begriffe.erklaerung: Very bright light that is produced when fast electrons are steered onto a curved path.
A ring-shaped tube in which electrons fly round and round for hours.
A row of magnets that makes electrons swing in a slalom and so produces especially bright light.
A space from which almost all the air has been removed.
A path with mirrors and instruments that leads the light from the ring to an experiment.

gewusst: The electrons in the SLS go round the ring about a million times a second.
The X-ray light of the SLS is billions of times brighter than that of an X-ray machine at the doctor's.
At the PSI there is a second large X-ray facility, SwissFEL, which produces extremely short flashes of light.

teile.einleitung: Tadeus Reichstein was a Swiss chemist who received the Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine in 1950. He was one of the first to produce vitamin C artificially, and he researched hormones that are still important in medicine today. He was born in Poland in 1897 and died in Basel in 1996 at the age of 99.
wichtigste: Tadeus Reichstein lived from 1897 to 1996 and reached the age of 99.
In 1933 he succeeded in producing vitamin C artificially.
He studied hormones of the adrenal cortex, which belong to the steroids.
The hormone cortisone was soon used against rheumatoid arthritis.
In 1950 he received the Nobel Prize together with Edward Kendall and Philip Hench.
From 1938 he was professor of pharmaceutical chemistry at the University of Basel.
In old age he studied ferns intensively.

abschnitte.text: Tadeus Reichstein was born on 20 July 1897 in Włocławek in what is now Poland. His family moved to Switzerland, and he grew up in Zurich. There he studied chemistry at **ETH Zurich** and completed a doctorate. Later he became a Swiss citizen.

In 1933 Reichstein succeeded in producing **vitamin C** in the laboratory, independently of its occurrence in fruit. His method, the Reichstein synthesis, was suitable for large quantities. The Basel company Roche used it to produce vitamin C cheaply. Vitamin C is important for the body's defences, and a lack of it can cause the disease scurvy.

From the 1930s, Reichstein studied the **adrenal cortex**, part of a small gland above the kidney. From it he isolated numerous hormones, all of which belong to the class of substances called **steroids**. One of them was **cortisone**, which soon proved to be an effective remedy for rheumatoid arthritis and inflammation. Today cortisone preparations are used, for example, for allergies, asthma and skin diseases.

For his research on the hormones of the adrenal cortex, Reichstein received the Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine in 1950. He shared it with the US researchers Edward Kendall and Philip Hench. From 1938 he was professor of pharmaceutical chemistry at the **University of Basel**. Later he headed the Institute of Organic Chemistry there.

After his retirement Reichstein continued his research, now mainly on **ferns**. He studied their substances and the cell nuclei of many species of fern. He went on publishing scientific papers into old age. He died in Basel on 1 August 1996.

begriffe.erklaerung: A substance that the body needs in small amounts and usually takes in with food.
A messenger substance in the body that controls important processes.
A group of chemical substances with a similar structure, which includes many hormones.
Making a substance in the laboratory from simpler substances.

gewusst: Reichstein lived through almost the whole of the 20th century; he reached the age of 99.
As well as chemistry, Reichstein was interested in plants all his life, especially ferns.
His method of producing vitamin C was used in industry around the world for decades.

teile.einleitung: The Stanford prison experiment was a famous and controversial psychology experiment from 1971. Students played guards and prisoners in a mock prison, and the situation quickly got out of control. Today it is discussed above all as an example of how research should not be carried out.
wichtigste: The experiment was led in 1971 by the psychologist Philip Zimbardo.
The prison was set up in the basement of the psychology building at Stanford University.
The roles of guards and prisoners were handed out by chance.
The experiment, planned for two weeks, was stopped after six days.
Christina Maslach got Zimbardo to end the experiment.
Critics today object that the guards were encouraged to behave harshly.
In his book “The Lucifer Effect” Zimbardo compared Stanford with the abuses at Abu Ghraib prison.

abschnitte.text: The experiment took place in August 1971 at **Stanford University** in California. It was led by the psychologist **Philip Zimbardo**, who himself took on the role of prison superintendent. The prison was set up in the basement of the psychology building, with cells, barred doors and a corridor as the yard. The participants were young men, mostly students, who had answered a newspaper advertisement and were paid.

The roles of **guards** and **prisoners** were handed out by chance. The prisoners were picked up at home by real police officers and given smocks and numbers instead of names. The guards wore uniforms and dark sunglasses. After only a short time some guards began to bully the prisoners, and several prisoners were under great strain.

Two weeks had been planned, but after **six days** the experiment was stopped. This was prompted by the young psychologist **Christina Maslach**, who saw what was going on and clearly objected. Zimbardo later admitted that he himself had slipped too far into his role as prison superintendent. He had changed from a researcher into part of what was happening.

Zimbardo interpreted the result as meaning that the **situation** can lead people to behave badly. Many experts today strongly doubt that it shows this. Recordings and reports show that the guards were encouraged to behave harshly. In addition there were only a few participants and no proper comparison group, and some participants later said that they had partly been acting.

In 2002 the British psychologists Stephen Reicher and Alexander Haslam recreated the experiment with the **BBC Prison Study** under strict ethical rules. There the guards did not automatically behave cruelly, and the groups developed quite differently. In his 2007 book “The Lucifer Effect”, Zimbardo compared his experiment with the abuses at **Abu Ghraib** prison in Iraq. Philip Zimbardo died in 2024.

The experiment helped to shape the rules for research with people. Today such studies have to be checked in advance by an **ethics committee**, in Switzerland too. Participants must be allowed to stop at any time and must not be put under unnecessary strain. In textbooks the experiment often serves as a warning and as an example of critical thinking.

begriffe.erklaerung: A planned test with which you want to check a question scientifically.
A group of experts who check whether an experiment with people is acceptable.
The part of psychology that studies how people behave in groups.
A task or character that someone takes on in a situation.

gewusst: Several films have been made about the experiment, including the German film “Das Experiment” from 2001.
The experiment was partly funded by the US Office of Naval Research.
Christina Maslach married Philip Zimbardo the year after the experiment.

teile.einleitung: The peeler is a kitchen tool with which you can peel potatoes, carrots and apples quickly and thinly. The most famous model, the “Rex”, was invented in Switzerland in 1947. To this day it is a classic of Swiss design and lies in countless kitchen drawers.
wichtigste: A peeler only takes off a thin layer, which is why in German it is called a “Sparschäler”, a saving peeler.
The best-known peeler is the Rex, invented in 1947.
Its blade lies across the handle and can move.
For decades the Rex was made by the company Zena in Affoltern am Albis.
In 2003 the Rex appeared on a Swiss postage stamp.
It consists of a simple, light metal frame.
The Rex is regarded as a Swiss design classic.

abschnitte.text: A peeler is a small hand tool for **peeling** vegetables and fruit. It has a short blade with a narrow slit and a sharp edge. If you pull it over a potato, it shaves off a very thin layer. In this way more of the potato is left than when peeling with an ordinary knife, so you **save** food.

On the Rex the blade lies **across** the handle, rather like on a razor. It is mounted so that it can **move** and so adapts to the round shape of a potato or an apple. The blade has two cutting edges, so you can peel in both directions. With the point at the side you can also dig eyes and bad spots out of potatoes.

The Rex was invented in **1947** in Switzerland by Alfred Neweczerzal. The device was simple, cheap and practical, and it quickly became popular. For decades it was made by the company **Zena** in **Affoltern am Albis** in the canton of Zurich. Many millions were sold, not only in Switzerland but also abroad.

The Rex is regarded as a typical example of good **design**: it has no unnecessary parts and does its job perfectly. In 2003 it appeared on a **postage stamp** of Swiss Post in a series on Swiss design classics. Together with the Swiss Army knife it is one of the best-known everyday objects from Switzerland. Many families have used the same model for generations.

You hold the vegetable in one hand and pull the peeler over it in short strokes with the other. It is safest to peel away from yourself. Besides potatoes and carrots you can also peel asparagus, cucumbers and apples. With the peeler you can even shave thin strips of vegetables or chocolate for decoration.

begriffe.erklaerung: Removing the outer skin of fruit or vegetables.
The sharp metal part of a knife or tool.
The careful shaping of the form and function of an object.
A small stamp that you stick on letters to pay for the postage.

gewusst: The Rex is so simply built that its shape has hardly changed since it was invented.
In many Swiss households there is more than one Rex in the drawer.
The German word “Sparschäler” explains the idea: because less is peeled off, less of the potato is lost.

teile.einleitung: SwissFEL is a huge research facility at the Paul Scherrer Institute in the canton of Aargau. It produces extremely short and bright X-ray flashes with which very fast processes in molecules can be observed. You can think of it as a super-fast camera for the tiniest world.
wichtigste: SwissFEL is located at the Paul Scherrer Institute in Villigen in the canton of Aargau.
The facility was officially inaugurated in 2016.
It is about 740 metres long in total.
The electrons are accelerated in a linear accelerator.
SwissFEL produces at most 100 X-ray pulses per second.
The pulses last only a few to several dozen femtoseconds.
The two beamlines are called Aramis and Athos.
The facility cost about 275 million francs.

abschnitte.text: SwissFEL is a **free-electron laser** that produces X-ray light. The abbreviation FEL stands for Free Electron Laser. The facility is located at the **Paul Scherrer Institute** in Villigen in the canton of Aargau, Switzerland's largest research institute for natural sciences and engineering. It was officially inaugurated in 2016 and cost about 275 million francs.

First, electrons are brought almost to the speed of light in a straight **linear accelerator**. Then they fly through long rows of magnets called **undulators**. The magnets force the electrons onto a wavy path, and as they move they send out X-ray light. This light builds up into an extremely bright, laser-like flash.

The whole facility is about **740 metres** long, roughly as long as seven football pitches one after another. It is housed in a long, low building that is partly hidden in the forest floor. There are two beamlines with names from a famous novel: **Aramis** for hard and **Athos** for soft X-rays. Soft X-rays have less energy than hard ones.

The X-ray pulses last only a few to several dozen **femtoseconds**. A femtosecond is one quadrillionth of a second. SwissFEL can produce at most 100 such pulses per second. Because the flashes are so short, they can be used like a camera to capture individual moments of **molecular processes**.

With SwissFEL, researchers observe how chemical reactions take place or how proteins change their shape. This helps, for example, in developing new **medicines**. New materials for electronics or solar cells are also studied. There are only a few such **X-ray lasers** in the world, so researchers come to Villigen from many countries.

begriffe.erklaerung: Invisible, high-energy light that can pass through many substances.
A straight facility in which tiny particles such as electrons are made very fast.
