A row of magnets that forces electrons onto a wavy path so that they send out light.
An unimaginably short period of time: one quadrillionth of a second.

gewusst: In one femtosecond, even light travels only about a third of a thousandth of a millimetre.
The names Aramis and Athos come from two characters in the novel “The Three Musketeers”.
Because the facility is in such demand, researchers have to apply with their ideas and are given only a few days of measuring time.

teile.einleitung: Starfish are star-shaped sea animals that crawl slowly over the seabed. Although they have “fish” in their name and live in the sea, they are not fish but belong to the echinoderms. They have amazing abilities: they can regrow lost arms and turn their stomach inside out to eat.
wichtigste: Starfish are echinoderms and are related to sea urchins and sea cucumbers.
Most starfish have five arms, but some kinds have many more.
If a starfish loses an arm, it can grow it back.
It moves along with many small tube feet.
Instead of blood, seawater flows through its body in many tubes.
It has simple eyes at the tips of its arms.
Many starfish like to eat mussels.

abschnitte.text: A starfish has a flat body with a **central disc**, from which usually five arms branch off. Some kinds, such as the sunstar, have more than ten arms. Starfish come in many colours, from orange and red to blue and violet. Their skin is covered with small plates of lime and spines, which is why they are counted among the **echinoderms**. There are about 1,600 species worldwide.

Starfish live in all the oceans of the world, from shallow coasts to the deep sea. They are found on rocks, on sand and in coral reefs. They do not occur in fresh water, so there are no starfish in Swiss lakes. On the coasts of the North Sea and the Baltic the **common starfish** is frequent and often lies between the stones at low tide.

Instead of blood, seawater flows through the starfish in many fine tubes, the **water vascular system**. With this water pressure it moves hundreds of small **tube feet** on the underside of its arms. In this way it crawls slowly forward and holds on to rocks. Simple eyes at the tips of the arms can tell light from dark and see rough outlines. The starfish has no brain but a network of nerves.

Many starfish like to eat **mussels**. They wrap their arms around the mussel and pull with their tube feet until the shells open a crack. Then they push their stomach out of their mouth and into the mussel. There they digest the soft flesh and afterwards pull their stomach back in. Other kinds eat snails, dead animals or tiny particles.

If a starfish loses an arm, for example to an enemy, it grows back over time. This ability is called **regeneration**. In some kinds a whole new starfish can even grow from a separated arm with a piece of the central disc. The **crown-of-thorns starfish** eats corals and can badly damage reefs when it multiplies in huge numbers. Other starfish, on the other hand, keep mussel beds in balance.

begriffe.erklaerung: A group of animals with plates of lime in their skin, which includes starfish and sea urchins.
Small feet on the underside with which a starfish moves and holds on.
Tubes in the starfish through which seawater flows.
The regrowing of lost body parts.

gewusst: Starfish have neither heart nor brain and still work amazingly well.
Today experts often call starfish sea stars, because they are not fish.
A starfish can push its stomach out so far that it can digest mussels through a very narrow gap.

teile.einleitung: Training data are the examples from which an artificial intelligence learns. Just as a child has to see many dogs to recognise dogs, an AI needs thousands or millions of examples. How well an AI works later depends greatly on this data.
wichtigste: Training data are examples from which an AI learns.
Labelling data, for example writing “cat” under a picture of a cat, is called annotation.
Part of the data is held back as test data in order to check the AI on unfamiliar examples.
Bias means that the data shows reality in a one-sided way.
“Garbage in, garbage out” means: bad data leads to bad results.
The practice dataset MNIST contains 70,000 images of handwritten digits.
ImageNet, with over 14 million labelled images, gave a big boost to image recognition.
When training with texts and images from the internet, the question of copyright arises.

abschnitte.text: In **machine learning**, nobody writes all the rules by hand. Instead, the computer is shown many examples, the **training data**. The program looks for patterns in them by itself, for example which shapes are typical of a cat. A language model learns from huge amounts of text which words often appear together. The more good and varied examples there are, the better the AI learns.

A lot of data first has to be labelled; this is called **annotation**. Under a picture of a cat you write “cat”, and for an email you note “spam” or “not spam”. These descriptions are also called labels. People often do this work by hand, which takes a lot of time. When we click on traffic lights in a picture puzzle on the internet, we are sometimes helping with labelling too.

The data is usually split into **training data** and **test data**, for example 80 to 20 per cent. The AI learns with the larger part, and it is tested with the smaller part. This shows whether it can also solve examples that it has never seen before. It is like a test with new questions instead of the ones from the exercise book. If the AI has only learned things off by heart, it does badly on the test data.

The dataset **MNIST** contains 70,000 images of handwritten digits from 0 to 9 and is often used for practice. The image database **ImageNet** was built up from 2009 by the researcher Fei-Fei Li and her team and contains over 14 million labelled images. In 2012 a neural network in an ImageNet competition recognised images much better than all previous programs. This success is regarded as the start of today's AI boom.

When training data shows reality in a one-sided way, it is called **bias**. If a face recognition system learns almost only with photos of light-skinned people, it recognises other faces less well. Experts say “garbage in, garbage out”, meaning that bad data leads to bad results. Incorrect labels or duplicated data also make an AI worse. That is why training data is checked carefully before it is used.

Many AI systems are trained with texts and images from the internet. This raises the question of whether the **copyright** of authors, photographers or artists is being infringed. This is being argued about in many countries, including in court. Personal data such as photos or names are also protected. If you put pictures online yourself, you should know that they might be used for training.

begriffe.erklaerung: Examples from which an AI learns patterns.
Labelling data with the correct answer.
Examples that are held back and used to check how good an AI is.
A distortion when data shows reality in a one-sided way.
An organised collection of a lot of data.

gewusst: Some of the digits in the MNIST dataset come from school pupils in the USA.
Large language models are trained with so many texts that a person could not read them in a whole lifetime.
Sometimes artificial training data is created when real examples are missing.

teile.einleitung: Spinach is a green leafy vegetable that can be eaten raw as a salad or cooked. It is famous because it supposedly contains especially large amounts of iron, but that is exactly a well-known mistake.
wichtigste: With spinach you eat the leaves.
Spinach contains plenty of vitamins.
The idea that spinach contains much more iron than other vegetables is a mistake.
In the past dried spinach was probably measured instead of fresh.
Our body is rather bad at absorbing the iron from spinach.
Liver contains much more iron than fresh spinach.
The cartoon character Popeye becomes strong through spinach.

abschnitte.text: Spinach is an annual plant with dark green, soft leaves. It belongs to the **amaranth family**, which also includes chard and beetroot. Spinach originally comes from western Asia, probably from the area of present-day Iran. Arab traders brought it to Spain in the Middle Ages, from where it spread throughout Europe.

Spinach grows quickly and likes cool weather, so it is sown in spring or autumn. The **leaves** are eaten, young leaves raw as a salad, larger ones mostly cooked. If it gets too warm and the days too long, the spinach shoots up and forms flowers. Spinach is also grown in Switzerland, and you can buy it fresh or frozen.

For a long time people believed that spinach contained especially large amounts of **iron**. In the 19th century dried spinach was probably measured and the value was taken for fresh spinach. But fresh spinach contains no more iron than many other vegetables. It also contains **oxalic acid**, which hinders the absorption of iron in the gut. Liver, meat, pulses or oat flakes often supply the body with iron better.

Spinach is still a healthy vegetable, because it contains plenty of **vitamins**, for example vitamins A, C and K, as well as folic acid. Our body needs iron for the blood, because it helps transport oxygen. If you eat spinach together with foods rich in vitamin C, such as orange juice, more iron is absorbed. Cooked spinach may be warmed up again if it was cooled quickly and kept in the fridge, because otherwise harmful nitrite can form from **nitrate**.

The sailor **Popeye** is an American cartoon character who was invented in 1929. When Popeye eats a tin of spinach, he gets huge muscles and wins every fight. The cartoons made spinach more popular with children in the USA. So a mistake about iron helped people to eat more vegetables.

begriffe.erklaerung: A mineral that the body needs for the blood and for transporting oxygen.
A substance in spinach and rhubarb that makes it harder to absorb iron and calcium.
A substance from the soil that plants take up and that can turn into nitrite.
A vegetable of which you mainly eat the leaves.

gewusst: In the American town of Crystal City there is a statue of Popeye, because a lot of spinach was grown there.
After eating spinach your teeth sometimes feel rough; that comes from the oxalic acid.

teile.einleitung: A telescope is an instrument with which you can observe distant things such as stars, planets and galaxies. It collects much more light than our eyes and makes distant objects appear bigger and brighter. Telescopes have completely changed our picture of the universe.
wichtigste: With a telescope you observe distant stars.
There are lens telescopes and mirror telescopes.
The first telescopes were built around 1608 in the Netherlands.
In 1609 Galileo Galilei was one of the first to point a telescope at the sky.
Large telescopes often stand high up on mountains, where the air is clear.
Space telescopes such as Hubble and James Webb observe from outside the atmosphere.

abschnitte.text: The word telescope comes from Greek and means “looking into the distance”. A telescope collects light with a large lens or a mirror and focuses it. The larger the opening, the more light is collected and the fainter the objects you can see. You then look at the enlarged image through an **eyepiece**.

A **lens telescope**, also called a refractor, bends the light with glass lenses. A **mirror telescope** or reflector collects the light with a curved mirror. Isaac Newton built one of the first mirror telescopes in 1668. The largest telescopes in the world today are mirror telescopes, because it is easier to build huge mirrors than huge lenses.

Around 1608 the spectacle maker Hans Lipperhey in the Netherlands applied for a patent for a telescope. As early as 1609, **Galileo Galilei** in Italy built his own, better telescopes and pointed them at the sky. He saw craters on the Moon and in 1610 discovered four moons of Jupiter. These observations showed that not everything revolves around the Earth.

The Earth's atmosphere blurs and swallows part of the light. That is why telescopes are sent into space. The **Hubble Space Telescope** has been orbiting the Earth since 1990 and has delivered thousands of famous pictures. The James Webb Space Telescope was launched at the end of 2021 and observes mainly in infrared light.

Large telescopes are housed in **observatories**, often in dry deserts or on high mountains, as in Chile or on Hawaii. In Switzerland there are many public observatories where you can look through a telescope yourself. On the Gornergrat near Zermatt there are observatories at over 3100 metres. The University of Bern built the space telescope CHEOPS, which has been studying planets around other stars since 2019.

To start with, a good pair of **binoculars** is often enough to see craters on the Moon and the moons of Jupiter. It is best to observe on a dark night, far from city lights. You must never look at the Sun through a telescope or binoculars, because that can make you blind immediately. For the Sun you need special protective filters.

begriffe.erklaerung: The lens that you look into on a telescope.
A telescope that focuses light with lenses.
A telescope that collects light with a curved mirror.
A building with telescopes for observing the sky.

gewusst: The main mirror of the James Webb telescope is 6.5 metres wide and consists of 18 gold-coated segments.
Radio telescopes do not capture visible light but radio waves from space.
The further a telescope looks into space, the further it looks into the past, because the light has been travelling for so long.

teile.einleitung: The deep sea is the deep, dark part of the oceans below about 200 metres. It is cold and pitch dark there, and the water pressure is enormous. Even so, amazing animals live in the deep sea, and many of them are still unknown to anyone.
wichtigste: It is dark and cold in the deep sea.
The deepest point of the seas is the Mariana Trench, about 11 kilometres deep.
The water pressure is especially great in the deep sea.
Black smokers are hot springs on the deep seabed.
In 1960 the Swiss Jacques Piccard was one of the first to dive to the deepest point.
The sperm whale dives very deep to hunt squid.
Many animals of the deep sea are still unknown.

abschnitte.text: From a depth of about 200 metres, hardly any sunlight gets through, and from about 1000 metres it is completely **dark**. That is why no plants that need light can grow there. The water is usually only 2 to 4 degrees, almost like in a fridge. The deep sea is the largest habitat on Earth, because it covers more than half of the Earth's surface. Yet it has been explored much less than the surface of the Moon.

With every 10 metres of water depth, the **water pressure** rises by about one bar. In the Mariana Trench, about 11 kilometres down, it is therefore more than a thousand times as great as at the surface. That is as if a lorry were standing on an area the size of a thumbnail. Submersibles therefore need very thick walls of steel or titanium. Deep-sea animals have no air bubbles in their bodies that could be squashed, and so they can withstand the pressure.

On the seabed there are hot springs from which dark, mineral-rich water pours out. They are called **black smokers**, because the water looks like smoke. They were discovered at the end of the 1970s and greatly surprised researchers. Around these springs live bacteria that get energy from chemical substances instead of from sunlight. Tube worms, mussels and crabs feed on them.

Many deep-sea animals can produce their own light; this is called **bioluminescence**. The anglerfish lures prey with a glowing fishing rod on its head. Other animals have huge eyes or are almost transparent. The **sperm whale** dives more than a thousand metres deep to hunt squid, even giant squid. Many animals feed on marine snow, that is, remains that slowly sink down from above.

On 23 January 1960 the Swiss **Jacques Piccard** and the American Don Walsh dived into the Mariana Trench in the submersible “Trieste”. They reached the deepest point, the Challenger Deep. Only in 2012 did a crewed dive go that deep again, this time with the film director James Cameron. Today the deep sea is often explored by remote-controlled robots. On almost every expedition, researchers find new, previously unknown species.

begriffe.erklaerung: The part of the sea below about 200 metres.
The force with which water presses from all sides.
The ability of a living thing to produce its own light.
A hot spring on the seabed with dark water.
Small remains of living things that slowly sink into the depths.

gewusst: If you put Mount Everest into the Mariana Trench, its summit would still be more than 2000 metres under water.
For a long time, more people had been on the Moon than at the deepest point of the sea.
The water at black smokers can be hotter than 300 degrees, but because of the high pressure it does not boil.

teile.einleitung: A funnel is a device that is wide at the top and narrow at the bottom. With it you can fill liquids or powders into a narrow opening without spilling anything. Together with filter paper, you can even use it to separate substances from each other.
wichtigste: With a funnel you pour liquid into a narrow opening.
A funnel is wide at the top and narrow at the bottom.
When filtering cloudy sandy water, the sand stays in the filter paper.
The clear liquid that runs out at the bottom is called the filtrate.
A coffee filter works in a similar way to a funnel and filter paper.
If you lift the funnel slightly in the neck of the bottle, air can escape.
Powder funnels have an especially wide spout.
With a separating funnel you separate liquids such as oil and water.

abschnitte.text: A **funnel** has the shape of a cone that turns into a narrow tube at the bottom. The tube is called the **spout**. At the top, the wide opening catches everything you pour in and directs it down into the narrow opening. In this way you can fill juice into a bottle, oil into an engine or water into a watering can. Funnels are made of plastic, metal or glass.

If the funnel fits exactly in the neck of the bottle, the air in the bottle cannot escape. Then the liquid builds up in the funnel and hardly runs through. If you lift the funnel slightly, the **air** can escape and the liquid flows again. Some funnels have small grooves on the spout for this purpose. For flour, sugar or other **powders** there are funnels with an especially wide spout, so that nothing gets blocked.

If you put a folded **filter paper** into the funnel, you can remove solid particles from a liquid. If you pour in cloudy sandy water, the sand gets caught in the paper; this is called the **residue**. Clear water drips out at the bottom; this is the **filtrate**. A filter coffee machine works in exactly the same way: the coffee grounds stay behind and the coffee runs through. Filtering is a simple experiment that you can also do at home.

In the laboratory there are many special funnels. A **separating funnel** looks like a pear with a tap at the bottom. You fill it, for example, with oil and water, which do not mix, and wait until two layers form. When you open the tap, the lower, heavier layer runs out first, in this case the water. With a porcelain **Büchner funnel**, a pump sucks the liquid through the filter more quickly.

There are funnel shapes in nature too. The larva of the **antlion** builds a funnel in the sand into which ants slide. A tornado often shows itself as a funnel cloud that reaches from the sky to the ground. The German expression “auf den Trichter kommen” (to come onto the funnel) means that you have finally understood something. And in the past, a gramophone had a large horn shaped like a funnel that made the music louder.

begriffe.erklaerung: A cone-shaped device for filling things into narrow openings.
The clear liquid that has run through a filter.
What stays behind in the filter paper when filtering.
A laboratory funnel with a tap that is used to separate liquids.

gewusst: The “Nuremberg funnel” is a German saying for the idea that you could simply pour knowledge into someone.
With its outer ear, the human ear also works a little like a sound funnel.
On some musical instruments, such as the trumpet, the wide end is also called the bell, or in German “Trichter” or “Schalltrichter”.

teile.einleitung: Sunscreens are creams, lotions or sprays that protect the skin from the Sun's UV rays. They prevent sunburn and lower the risk of skin damage and skin cancer. In Switzerland in particular, with its high mountains, good sun protection is especially important.
wichtigste: Sunscreens protect the skin from ultraviolet radiation, UV radiation for short.
UV-B radiation mainly causes sunburn.
UV-A radiation goes deep into the skin and makes it age.
The sun protection factor shows how much longer you can in theory stay in the Sun: with 10 minutes of natural protection and SPF 20, it is at most 200 minutes.
Mineral sunscreens use titanium dioxide and zinc oxide as filters.
Putting on more cream keeps up the protection but does not extend it.
Sun protection is recommended from a UV index of 3.
In the mountains and on snow the UV radiation is especially strong.

abschnitte.text: Besides light and heat, the Sun also sends out invisible **UV radiation**. **UV-B** is high in energy and mainly causes sunburn. **UV-A** goes deeper into the skin and makes it age faster, with wrinkles and spots. Both kinds of radiation can damage the genetic material in skin cells and so encourage skin cancer. The even more dangerous UV-C radiation is caught by the ozone layer.

Sunscreens contain **UV filters**. Chemical filters absorb the radiation and turn it into heat. **Mineral filters** such as titanium dioxide and zinc oxide consist of tiny particles that reflect and absorb the UV light. Good products protect against both UV-B and UV-A. Waterproof creams last better when swimming but still lose some of their effect.

The **sun protection factor**, SPF for short, shows how much longer you can in theory stay in the Sun. If your skin turns red after 10 minutes without protection, a cream with SPF 20 protects for at most 200 minutes. In reality the protection is usually less, because people put on too little cream or rub it off. That is why you should apply plenty and put more on after swimming or sweating. Reapplying keeps up the protection but does not extend the time.

abschnitte.titel: Mountains, snow and the UV index
abschnitte.text: The higher you climb, the thinner the air and the stronger the UV radiation. In the Swiss Alps it is therefore much more intense than in the Central Plateau. Fresh **snow** reflects most of the UV radiation, so when skiing it comes from above and below. How strong the radiation is at the moment is shown by the **UV index**, which MeteoSwiss gives every day. Sun protection is recommended from a value of 3.

In the 1940s the Swiss chemist **Franz Greiter** developed a well-known sun cream. It is said to have been prompted by a bad sunburn on a mountain climb up Piz Buin, after which the brand is named. Greiter also made the idea of the sun protection factor known. By the way, Switzerland is one of the countries in Europe with an especially large number of cases of melanoma, the dangerous black skin cancer.

It is best to avoid the strong midday sun between about 11 a.m. and 3 p.m. **Clothes**, a hat and sunglasses protect more reliably than any cream. Sun cream is put on about 20 to 30 minutes before going out in the Sun. Do not forget your ears, nose, neck and feet either. Babies should not be in direct sunlight.

begriffe.erklaerung: Invisible, high-energy radiation from the Sun that causes sunburn.
A number that shows how much longer a cream protects the skin from sunburn in theory.
A number that shows how strong the UV radiation is at the moment.
A layer high in the air that catches a large part of the UV radiation.

gewusst: A well-known sun cream brand is named after Piz Buin, a mountain on the border between Switzerland and Austria.
Even when the sky is cloudy, a large part of the UV radiation comes through the clouds.
For every 1,000 metres of height, UV radiation increases by about 10 per cent.

teile.einleitung: The Swiss National Park in the Engadine is the only national park in Switzerland and one of the oldest in Europe. Since 1914 nature here has been allowed to develop freely without human interference. If you visit it, you can watch red deer, chamois, ibexes and, with a bit of luck, bearded vultures.
wichtigste: The Swiss National Park was founded in 1914 and is the oldest national park in the Alps.
It lies in the canton of Grisons in the Lower Engadine and Val Müstair; the visitor centre is in Zernez.
Nature is left to itself there, and fallen trees stay where they lie.
Hikers must stay on the marked paths.
Dogs are banned in the park, even on a lead.
Red deer are often seen in the meadows, as well as chamois, ibexes and marmots.
The bearded vulture was reintroduced here from 1991.

abschnitte.text: The national park lies in the east of Switzerland in the canton of **Grisons**, between the Lower Engadine, the Ofen Pass and the Val Müstair. It covers about 170 square kilometres, almost twice the size of Lake Zurich. The area lies between about 1,400 and over 3,100 metres above sea level. The Ofen Pass road runs through the park, and the visitor centre is in **Zernez**.

The park was founded on 1 August **1914** and is a strict **nature reserve**. There is no hunting, logging, mowing or fertilising here. Fallen trees stay where they lie and provide a habitat for fungi, beetles and woodpeckers. For over a hundred years researchers have been observing how former pastures and forests change without people. In this way the national park is a large open-air laboratory for science.

**Red deer** are seen especially often; they graze in the meadows in summer and bellow in autumn. Chamois and ibexes live among the rocks, and marmots whistle on the alpine pastures. The huge **bearded vulture** was wiped out in Switzerland at the beginning of the 20th century. From 1991 young bearded vultures were released in the national park, and today they breed in the Alps again. Wolves and bears also occasionally roam through the area.

So that the animals are not disturbed, strict **park rules** apply. You must stay on the marked hiking paths, and dogs are banned, even on a lead. Picking plants, taking stones, making fires and camping are not allowed. Cycling is also only permitted on a few roads. You can stay overnight in the Chamanna Cluozza hut or in inns on the edge of the park.

With **binoculars** you can watch animals from a safe distance, especially early in the morning and in the evening. A popular walk is into the Val Trupchun, where you often see large herds of deer. The visitor centre in Zernez has an exhibition showing how the park works. The national park is also part of the UNESCO Biosfera Engiadina Val Müstair.

begriffe.erklaerung: A large protected area in which nature comes first.
An area in which animals and plants are strictly protected.
Setting animals that have been bred free in nature.
A large bird of prey of the Alps that feeds mainly on bones.

gewusst: The Swiss National Park is the only park in Switzerland that bears the name national park.
The bearded vulture eats mainly bones and drops large bones from the air onto rocks to break them.
The strictest protection rules in Switzerland apply in the park; you may not even take a stone.

teile.einleitung: Transfer RNA, tRNA for short, is a small molecule found in all cells. It brings the right building blocks, the amino acids, to the cell's protein factories. You can think of it as a translator that turns the language of the genes into the language of proteins.
wichtigste: tRNA brings the right amino acids to the ribosome.
In a two-dimensional drawing it looks like a clover leaf.
In three-dimensional space it has the shape of an L.
The amino acid is attached to the 3' end with the sequence CCA.
The anticodon of the tRNA pairs with the codon of the mRNA.
The enzyme aminoacyl-tRNA synthetase loads the tRNA with the correct amino acid.
A typical tRNA consists of about 70 to 90 nucleotides.
In 1965 Robert Holley was the first to fully sequence an alanine tRNA from yeast.

abschnitte.text: **Transfer RNA** is a short chain of about 70 to 90 building blocks, the **nucleotides**. Like the genetic material DNA, it is a nucleic acid. Each cell has many different tRNAs, at least one kind for each of the 20 amino acids. Their task is to bring amino acids to the **ribosome**. There the amino acids are joined into long chains, the proteins.

If you draw a tRNA flat on paper, it looks like a **clover leaf** with three leaves and a stem. This is because parts of the chain lie against each other and form small loops. In space, the clover leaf folds further into an **L shape**. At one end of the L sits the amino acid, at the other end the anticodon. This shape was worked out in 1974 with the help of X-rays.

The instructions for a protein are written on the messenger RNA, the mRNA, in groups of three bases, the **codons**. Each tRNA also carries three bases in one of its loops, the **anticodon**. If the anticodon fits the codon like a key in a lock, the tRNA attaches to the mRNA. In this way exactly the right amino acid ends up in the right place. The ribosome then joins it to the growing protein chain.

The amino acid hangs on the so-called 3' end of the tRNA, which always ends with the bases **CCA**. To make sure each tRNA carries the right amino acid, there are special enzymes, the **aminoacyl-tRNA synthetases**. Each of these enzymes recognises a particular amino acid and the matching tRNAs. It works very precisely and even corrects its own mistakes. Without this precision, many wrong proteins would be made.

In the 1950s the researcher Francis Crick suspected that there must be a translating molecule and called it an adaptor. Shortly afterwards tRNA was indeed discovered. In 1965 **Robert Holley** was the first to determine the complete base sequence of a nucleic acid, namely an alanine tRNA from yeast. For this he received the Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine in 1968, together with two other researchers. The work took several years and needed large amounts of yeast.

begriffe.erklaerung: A building block from which proteins are made.
The protein factory in the cell.
Three bases on the mRNA that stand for an amino acid.
Three bases on the tRNA that match the codon.
A single building block of DNA or RNA.

gewusst: Because codons sometimes only have to match exactly at two positions, one tRNA can read several similar codons.
tRNA contains unusual bases that are modified afterwards and are hardly found in other RNAs.
To sequence the first tRNA, Holley's team needed about 140 kilograms of yeast.

teile.einleitung: In microbiology, sterilisation means completely freeing objects, liquids or rooms of all living microorganisms. It is essential in hospitals, in laboratories and in the food industry, so that no germs cause diseases.
wichtigste: Sterilisation kills all microorganisms, including tough spores.
Disinfection, by contrast, only kills most pathogens.
In its standard programme an autoclave usually works at 121 °C.
Because of the increased pressure, the steam becomes hotter than 100 °C.
Bacterial endospores are especially resistant to heat.
Heat-sensitive solutions are filtered with filters of about 0.2 micrometres.
Many disposable syringes are sterilised with gamma radiation.

abschnitte.text: Sterile means free of germs, so without any living bacteria, fungi or viruses. In **sterilisation**, all microorganisms are killed, including their tough resting forms. **Disinfection**, on the other hand, only kills most pathogens, for example when you disinfect your hands. Sterile instruments are needed for operations, injections and a lot of laboratory work.

The most important device is the **autoclave**, a kind of large pressure cooker. Inside it, steam is heated under increased pressure so that it becomes hotter than 100 °C. In its standard programme an autoclave usually works at 121 °C for about 15 to 20 minutes. The hot steam gets deep into the objects and reliably kills the germs. The autoclave was invented around 1879 by Charles Chamberland, a colleague of Louis Pasteur.

Some bacteria form **endospores**, which are especially tough resting forms. They survive boiling water, dryness and many chemicals. That is why pasteurisation, as used for milk, does not count as sterilisation, because heat-resistant germs and spores survive it. How quickly germs die is described by the **D-value**, the time in which 90 per cent of the germs are killed at a certain temperature. With 1 million spores and a D-value of 2 minutes, statistically 100 spores are still left after 8 minutes.

Not everything can cope with steam, so there are other methods. Glass and metal can be sterilised in dry hot air at about 180 °C. Heat-sensitive liquids such as some medicines are pushed through fine **filters** with pores of about 0.2 micrometres, which hold back bacteria. Many disposable medical products such as syringes are sterilised in the factory with **gamma radiation**, often when they are already packed.

In the past, many people died of infections after operations. Only in the 19th century did researchers such as Louis Pasteur and Joseph Lister realise that germs cause diseases. Since then, sterilising instruments has been one of the most important rules in hospitals. Tins of food are also heated so that no dangerous bacteria can multiply inside them.

begriffe.erklaerung: Tiny living things such as bacteria and fungi that you can only see under a microscope.
A device that makes objects free of germs using hot steam under pressure.
A very tough resting form of some bacteria.
Killing most pathogens, but not necessarily all germs.

gewusst: A pressure cooker in the kitchen works on the same principle as an autoclave.
Some bacterial spores can survive for decades or even longer and then become active again.

teile.einleitung: The thermohaline circulation is a huge ocean current that spans the globe and is driven by the temperature and salt content of the water. It is often compared to a gigantic conveyor belt that carries water through all the oceans. In doing so it spreads heat around the Earth and so also affects the climate in Europe.
wichtigste: Temperature and salt content determine the density of seawater and drive the circulation.
In the Greenland Sea and the Labrador Sea, surface water sinks into the depths.
Wallace Broecker coined the image of the global conveyor belt.
AMOC stands for Atlantic Meridional Overturning Circulation.
Antarctic Bottom Water is the densest body of water in the world ocean.
A complete circuit takes about 1000 years.
Meltwater from Greenland could weaken the Atlantic circulation.

abschnitte.text: The name is made up of **thermo** for heat and **haline** for salt. Cold and salty water is heavier than warm or fresh water; we say it has a higher **density**. Heavy water sinks, light water stays at the top. These differences set huge masses of water in the oceans in motion.

In the North Atlantic, warm surface water cools down a lot, especially in the **Greenland Sea** and the **Labrador Sea**. When sea ice forms there, salt is pushed out as brine, and the water beneath becomes even saltier. The cold, salty water sinks into the depths and slowly flows south. Around Antarctica, **Antarctic Bottom Water** forms; it is the densest body of water in the world and fills the deepest ocean basins.

The American geochemist **Wallace Broecker** coined the image of a worldwide **conveyor belt**. Deep water travels through the Atlantic, the Indian Ocean and the Pacific and rises back to the surface somewhere. Then it flows back as warm surface water. A particle of water needs about 1000 years for a complete circuit.

The Atlantic part of the current is called the **AMOC**, which stands for Atlantic Meridional Overturning Circulation. It includes the Gulf Stream, which carries warm water from the Caribbean northwards. Because of this, western and northern Europe are much milder than areas at the same latitude in Canada. The climate in Switzerland is also influenced by this supply of heat.

Because of global warming, a lot of ice is melting on **Greenland**. The meltwater is fresh water and lowers the density of the surface water, so that it sinks less strongly. Researchers fear that this could weaken the AMOC. How strongly and how quickly this could happen is being studied intensively, including at Swiss universities such as the University of Bern.

begriffe.erklaerung: How heavy a substance is in relation to its volume.
How much salt is dissolved in seawater; also called salinity.
Cold, heavy seawater that flows at great depth.
The great overturning current in the Atlantic, which includes the Gulf Stream.

gewusst: The currents in the deep sea are so slow that they often move only a few centimetres per second.
A particle of water that sinks in the North Atlantic today may only come back to the surface in about 1000 years.
According to researchers, the Atlantic circulation changed strongly several times at the end of the last ice age.

teile.einleitung: The Swiss Science Center Technorama in Winterthur is a science centre where you can experience natural sciences with your own hands. Instead of just looking at things, you can try out hundreds of experiments yourself. It is one of the largest science centres in Switzerland and a popular destination for school classes and families.
wichtigste: The Technorama is in Winterthur in the canton of Zurich.
It is a science centre, not a traditional museum.
You are allowed to try out the exhibits yourself.
You can experiment with light, magnets, water and much more.
It is meant above all for marvelling and discovering.
A glass prism shows that white light is made of the colours of the rainbow.

abschnitte.text: The **Technorama** is a **science centre** in Winterthur in the canton of Zurich. In a science centre you do not learn by reading signs but by trying things out yourself. The Technorama started as a technology museum and later became a house of experiments. Today its official name is Swiss Science Center Technorama.

In the section about light you can experiment with mirrors, lenses and prisms. A **glass prism** splits white light into the colours of the rainbow. With a mirror you explore how light is **reflected** and why the mirror image appears the wrong way round. Optical illusions show how easily our brain can be tricked.

With a **magnet** you can try out which things are attracted, for example an iron nail. Other experiments show invisible magnetic fields with iron filings. In a show you experience how high electrical **voltage** creates flashes of lightning. It is also explained why you need to be careful of lightning.

Many experiments show how water and air move. You can create whirls, watch waves or make currents visible. Other stations explain gravity, balance and chance. Outside in the park there are also large experiments, for example with **water** and sound.

For school classes there are **workshops** and laboratories in which children and young people do their own research. Many classes from all over Switzerland visit the Technorama on a school trip. The aim is to awaken curiosity and enjoyment of science and technology. If you discover something yourself, you often understand it and remember it better.

begriffe.erklaerung: A place where you discover natural sciences by experimenting yourself.
A piece of glass that splits white light into its colours.
An object that attracts things made of iron.
A test in which you try something out and observe it.

gewusst: There are almost no “Do not touch” signs in the Technorama, because touching is expressly encouraged.
White light is actually a mixture of all the colours of the rainbow.
A rainbow forms because raindrops split sunlight like little prisms.

teile.einleitung: Spontaneous generation was a very old idea: living things such as maggots, worms or even mice were thought to arise by themselves from mud, rot or rubbish. For over 2,000 years many scholars believed in it. Only careful experiments showed that life only comes from life.
wichtigste: The Latin technical term for spontaneous generation is generatio spontanea.
The ancient philosopher Aristotle taught that some animals arise from mud or rot.
In the 17th century Jan Baptist van Helmont thought that mice could arise from dirty laundry and wheat.
In 1668 Francesco Redi showed with covered meat that maggots hatch from flies' eggs.
Lazzaro Spallanzani proved that broths boiled for a long time and sealed stay free of germs.
Louis Pasteur disproved spontaneous generation around 1860 with his swan-neck flasks.
The principle that living things only come from living things is called biogenesis.

abschnitte.text: In ancient Greece **Aristotle** already held the view that some animals arise from mud or rot. After all, people saw that maggots suddenly appeared on rotten meat, or frogs in puddles. Without a microscope they could not see how this really happened. This idea was called **generatio spontanea**, spontaneous generation.

In the 17th century the Flemish scholar **Jan Baptist van Helmont** described a recipe for mice. You were to put dirty laundry and wheat in a container, and after a few weeks mice would appear. Today we know that the mice were simply attracted by the food. The example shows how important exact and controlled experiments are.

In 1668 the Italian doctor **Francesco Redi** put meat into several jars. He left some open and covered others with gauze. Maggots appeared only on the open meat, because flies could lay their eggs there. This was one of the first experiments with a **control group** in biology.

After the microscope was invented, people saw tiny living things everywhere, and the argument started again. In 1748 the English naturalist **John Needham** boiled mutton broth only briefly and still found microbes in it afterwards, which he took as proof of spontaneous generation. The Italian **Lazzaro Spallanzani**, on the other hand, boiled broths for a long time and sealed the containers, and they stayed free of germs. Critics, however, said that the long boiling destroyed a mysterious life force.

Around 1860 **Louis Pasteur** built glass flasks with a long, curved neck, the so-called swan-neck flasks. Air could get in, but dust and germs got caught in the bend, and the boiled broth stayed clear. Only when the neck was broken off did it go cloudy. In the 1870s the physicist **John Tyndall** explained why some hay infusions went cloudy despite boiling: some bacteria form spores that are very resistant to heat.

From these experiments came the principle of **biogenesis**: life only comes from life. This knowledge is the basis for hygiene, tinned food, the pasteurisation of milk and germ-free operations. The question of how the very first life on Earth arose billions of years ago is a separate one. It is still being researched today and has nothing to do with mice from laundry.

begriffe.erklaerung: The old idea that living things arise by themselves from non-living matter.
The principle that living things only come from living things.
Part of an experiment in which nothing is changed, so that you can compare.
A tiny living thing that can only be seen under a microscope, such as a bacterium.
A very resistant resting form of some bacteria or fungi.

gewusst: Some of Pasteur's swan-neck flasks are said to be still free of germs today at the Pasteur Institute in Paris.
For disproving spontaneous generation Pasteur received a prize from the French Academy of Sciences in 1862.
Heating food to kill germs is called “pasteurising” after Pasteur.

teile.einleitung: A streamlined shape is round at the front and narrow at the back, which is why it glides especially easily through air or water. Fish, penguins and birds have it naturally. Engineers build cars, trains and aeroplanes on this model so that they use less energy.
wichtigste: A streamlined shape is round at the front and narrow at the back.
The teardrop shape is considered especially good for gliding through air.
Vehicles with a streamlined shape use less energy.
When cycling fast, it is mainly air resistance that slows you down.
Racing cyclists crouch low over the handlebars so that less air slows them down.
Penguins and tuna swim very fast thanks to their streamlined shape.
In a wind tunnel, engineers test how strongly a car is slowed down by the wind.

abschnitte.text: When something moves through air or water, it constantly has to push it aside. This slows it down; this is called **drag**, or in air **air resistance**. A streamlined shape is round at the front and gets narrower towards the back, so that the air or water can flow smoothly around it. The **teardrop shape** is considered especially good.

With an angular shape, the flow breaks away and forms eddies at the back. These eddies, as it were, suck at the object and slow it down a lot. With a streamlined shape, the flow stays close to the body for longer and hardly forms any eddies. How good a shape is, is described by the **drag coefficient**: the smaller it is, the less resistance.

The **penguin** cannot fly, but thanks to its streamlined body it swims very fast underwater. The **tuna**, with its spindle-shaped body, is also a fast swimmer. Dolphins, trout and seals have similar shapes. Birds fold in their wings when diving so that they are slowed down less.

Cars, trains and aeroplanes are often built with a streamlined shape, because then they use **less energy**. In a **wind tunnel**, air is blown at a car or a model and engineers measure how strongly it is slowed down. A Japanese high-speed train was given a long nose modelled on the beak of the kingfisher, so that it does not make a loud bang when entering tunnels. Racing cars are also tested in wind tunnels for a long time, for example by the Sauber Formula 1 team in Hinwil in the canton of Zurich.

When cycling fast, it is mainly **air resistance** that slows you down, and it grows strongly with speed. That is why racing cyclists crouch low over the handlebars so that less air slows them down. Time trial riders wear smooth suits and teardrop-shaped helmets. Ski racers also go into a low crouch in the downhill, which is called the egg.

begriffe.erklaerung: The braking force that air exerts on something that is moving.
A facility in which air is blown against vehicles or models to measure the resistance.
A number that shows how streamlined a shape is; in German it is called the “cw-Wert”.
A swirling flow that forms behind angular shapes.

gewusst: If you double the speed, the air resistance becomes about four times as large.
A drop falling from a tap actually has a rather round shape and not the typical teardrop shape.
The kingfisher dives head first into the water with hardly any splash.

teile.einleitung: A stopwatch is a watch that you use to measure how long something takes. You start it at the press of a button and stop it again when something is over. Whether in a race during PE, when boiling eggs or in a ski race: stopwatches help to measure time precisely.
wichtigste: With a stopwatch you measure how long something takes.
In a race, you press the stopwatch for the first time at the start.
The display 01:30 means one minute and 30 seconds when the minutes are shown first.
The “Reset” button sets the time back to zero.
Whoever needs less time for the same distance is faster.
In ski races, time is measured to the hundredth of a second.
Today a stopwatch is often found in your mobile phone.

abschnitte.text: A stopwatch does not show the time of day, but how **long** something lasts. At the start you press a button and the watch begins to count. At the finish you press again and the time stops. With the **Reset** button you set the time back to zero.

Many stopwatches show minutes, seconds and hundredths of a second. If the minutes are shown first, 01:30 means one minute and 30 seconds, so 90 seconds. One second has 100 **hundredths of a second**. So at 12.45 seconds, 12 whole seconds and 45 hundredths have passed.

Lina runs a distance in 12 seconds, Tim the same distance in 15 seconds. Lina is faster, because she needs **less time**. If Lea needs 20 seconds for one lap, three laps at the same speed take 60 seconds, so exactly one minute. Many stopwatches have a button for **split times**, so that you can see each lap separately.

In ski races, time is measured to the **hundredth of a second**, and often a tiny difference decides who wins. There, nobody presses a button; instead the time is measured electronically with **light barriers** and start gates. A person, with a reaction time of about two tenths of a second, would measure too inaccurately. Swiss watch companies such as Omega and Longines have long been official timekeepers at big sporting events, for example at the Olympic Games.

abschnitte.titel: From pocket watch to mobile phone
abschnitte.text: The first watches for timing were built at the beginning of the 19th century. Mechanical stopwatches have clockwork with a spring and a large hand that moves over a dial. Later came **digital stopwatches** with a number display, which work with a vibrating quartz crystal. Today there is a stopwatch in almost every **mobile phone** and in many sports watches.

Stopwatches are not only used in sport. In the kitchen a timer helps to make sure eggs do not get too hard. In lessons you might measure, for example, how long a pendulum takes for one swing. In scientific experiments, too, accurate timing is often crucial.

begriffe.erklaerung: The length of time between the beginning and the end of something.
The hundredth part of a second.
The time that has passed up to a certain point during a run.
A beam of light that triggers a time measurement when it is interrupted.
A wristwatch with a built-in stopwatch function.

gewusst: In a photo finish, a picture of the finish line decides who arrived first.
A watch with a stopwatch function is called a chronograph, after the Greek words for “time” and “write”.
In swimming pools, athletes stop their own time by touching a touch pad at the finish.

teile.einleitung: Animal sounds are all the noises animals use to communicate, from birdsong to the croaking of frogs. Animals warn, attract, call their young or show who owns a territory. If you listen carefully, you can recognise many animals by their call without seeing them.
wichtigste: The cuckoo calls its own name.
The tawny owl calls “hoo-hoo” in the woods at night.
In the Alps the marmot warns with a loud whistle.
In spring, frogs croak at the pond.
The field cricket chirps by rubbing its wings together.
In spring, birds sing especially often early in the morning.
The echolocation calls of bats are too high for our ears.
Roe deer make barking sounds when there is danger.

abschnitte.text: Animals use their voices to send **messages**. Many birds sing to mark out their **territory** and show others: I live here. Alarm calls report danger, for example when a bird of prey is coming. Young animals beg for food with calls, and parents find their young again by the sound of their voice. Some animals keep their group together with contact calls.

Birds make their sounds with a special organ, the **syrinx**, which sits deep in the chest. In spring they sing especially often, most of all at dawn. This concert is called the dawn chorus. The **cuckoo** is easy to recognise, because it calls its own name. At night in the woods you hear the **tawny owl** with its “hoo-hoo”.

In the Alps the **marmot** warns its family with a shrill whistle when an eagle or fox is coming. Then they all disappear into the burrow in a flash. The **roe deer** barks loudly when it is startled, which surprises many walkers. In autumn you can hear red deer roaring in some mountain valleys. The fox can also bark and scream.

In spring the **frogs** croak at the pond, often in a chorus. Some frogs have **vocal sacs**, which swell like little balloons and make the sound louder. Crickets and grasshoppers have no voice. The field cricket rubs its wings together, so that a scraper runs over a row of teeth. This produces its typical chirping on warm summer evenings.

Humans only hear sounds in a certain range. Bats make very high calls, **ultrasound**. The echo tells them where obstacles and insects are, even in complete darkness. Elephants, on the other hand, also communicate over long distances with very low sounds, infrasound. Whales sing songs underwater that can be heard many kilometres away.

Researchers record animal sounds with microphones and make them visible as a picture, a so-called sonogram. In this way species can be identified and counted without disturbing them. The **Swiss Ornithological Institute** in Sempach studies, among other things, which birds occur where. Today there are also apps that recognise bird calls on a mobile phone.

begriffe.erklaerung: An area that an animal defends against others of its kind.
The voice organ of birds in the chest.
Sounds that are so high that humans cannot hear them.
A stretchy skin in frogs that makes the croaking louder.
A sound with which an animal warns others of danger.

gewusst: Some birds, such as the jay, can imitate the voices of other animals.
Some species of bird can sing two notes at the same time with their syrinx.
Young songbirds learn their song by listening to adult birds.

teile.einleitung: Sadness is a feeling that everyone knows, children just as much as adults. You feel low and heavy when you have lost something or someone, or when something does not go as you had hoped. Sadness is part of life, and it usually passes again.
wichtigste: Sadness is a basic feeling that all people all over the world know.
Many people cry when they are very sad, and tears flow from their eyes.
When people are sad, the corners of their mouth often turn down.
Children are sad, for example, when their pet dies or when they are homesick at camp.
The sadness after the death of a loved one is called grief.
A hug or a conversation often helps when someone is sad.
Sadness usually passes again.

abschnitte.text: Sadness is one of the **basic feelings**, like joy, fear, anger and disgust. You feel low, tired or empty and often have less desire to do things that are usually fun. A sad person is also described as **downhearted** or dejected. The feeling is completely normal and shows us that something matters to us.

You can often recognise sadness in the face by drooping **corners of the mouth** and inner eyebrows pulled upwards. Many people **cry**, and tears flow from the tear glands down their cheeks. Some withdraw and want to be alone, while others look for closeness. The voice often becomes quieter and slower too. Researchers have found that sad faces look similar all over the world.

Sadness often comes from a **loss**, for example when a pet dies or a friend moves away. An argument, a bad mark or a disappointment can also make you sad. If you miss your family at camp, you are **homesick**. When a loved one has died, it is called **grief**, which often lasts longer and comes in waves.

It helps to talk about your feelings, for example with your parents, friends or a teacher. A **hug**, a listening ear or simply being there often does sad people good. Exercise in the fresh air, music, drawing or writing can also help. Crying is allowed and can even bring relief. You do not have to hide sadness.

Sadness shows other people that we need help or comfort. It gives us time to think about something difficult and to **come to terms** with it. After that, you can often gather new strength. Anyone who has been sad themselves can understand others better; this is called **compassion**.

Usually sadness becomes weaker after a while. But if it lasts a very long time and you hardly enjoy anything any more, you should get help. A doctor or a psychology specialist can then give support. Children and young people in Switzerland can contact the **Pro Juventute** helpline on 147 free of charge at any time.

begriffe.erklaerung: Something you sense inside, for example joy, fear or sadness.
The deep sadness after losing a loved person or animal.
Sadness because you miss your home and your family.
When you sense and understand how another person is feeling.
Another word for sad and low.

gewusst: Tears shed when crying from sadness are made up differently from tears when chopping onions.
In the animated film “Inside Out”, Sadness is a character of her own who becomes very important at the end.
Humans are the only living things known for certain to cry tears because of their feelings.

teile.einleitung: A spin-off is a new company that grows out of an existing organisation, for example a university. Researchers take their invention out of the laboratory and turn it into a product that can be bought. In Europe ETH Zurich is especially well known for its many successful spin-offs.
wichtigste: A university spin-off is a company that uses a university's research results commercially.
The word comes from English and means something like an offshoot or a split-off.
A spin-off usually gets the rights to a university patent through a licence agreement.
Climeworks filters CO2 directly from the air and runs large plants in Iceland.
Sensirion is known internationally for sensors, for example for humidity and gases.
Scandit develops software with which you can scan barcodes with a smartphone.
With the Pioneer Fellowship, ETH Zurich supports researchers with a business idea before they found a company.

abschnitte.text: A spin-off forms when part of a larger organisation breaks away and becomes independent. In a **university spin-off**, researchers found a company to bring an invention from their research to the market. Often they are doctoral students or young researchers who take the knowledge from their project with them. The word spin-off is also known from film and television, where it is a new series that has grown out of a well-known one.

When something is invented at a university, the university often has the invention protected by a **patent**. A patent means that only the owner may use the invention commercially for a certain time. A spin-off therefore makes a **licence agreement** with the university and may then use the patent. In return the company pays the university, for example, a fee or a share of the profits.

Founding a company is difficult and needs money, time and courage. ETH Zurich helps with the **Pioneer Fellowship**, a support programme that gives researchers financial help before they found their company. On top of that there is advice, rooms and contacts with investors. The EPFL in Lausanne and other Swiss universities also have such programmes.

**Climeworks** was founded in 2009 by two ETH graduates and builds plants that filter CO2 directly from the air. In Iceland the collected CO2 is pressed deep underground, where it turns to stone in the rock. **Sensirion** from Stäfa on Lake Zurich makes tiny sensors that measure, for example, humidity or gases and are found in cars, appliances and mobile phones. Scandit from Zurich turns smartphones into barcode scanners, which are used, for example, in shops and logistics.

The ETH Domain includes the two universities ETH Zurich and EPFL as well as four research institutes. These are called the **PSI**, WSL, Empa and Eawag. The Paul Scherrer Institute researches, for example, materials and energy, the WSL forests, snow and landscape, Empa materials and technology, and Eawag water. Spin-offs keep coming out of these institutes too.

Spin-offs bring knowledge from research into everyday life so that society benefits from it. They create new jobs and strengthen **innovation** in Switzerland. In international rankings Switzerland is regularly among the most innovative countries in the world. Not every new company succeeds, but the founders learn a lot even from failures.

begriffe.erklaerung: A new company that grows out of a university or another company.
A protective right that allows a person or company alone to use an invention for a certain time.
Permission to use something that belongs to someone else, usually in return for payment.
A young company with a new idea that wants to grow quickly.

gewusst: ETH Zurich counts dozens of new spin-offs every year, many of them in technology, medicine and computer science.
In Iceland the CO2 stored by Climeworks turns into solid rock in the basalt within a few years.
Many of Sensirion's sensors are smaller than a grain of rice.

teile.einleitung: A seismograph is a measuring instrument that records shaking of the ground, above all earthquake waves. It even detects earthquakes that happen thousands of kilometres away. In this way researchers can find out where, when and how strongly the Earth has shaken.
wichtigste: A seismograph measures shaking and earthquake waves.
The record made by a seismograph is called a seismogram.
Modern instruments work electronically and are very sensitive.
From the measurements of several stations the location of an earthquake can be determined.
The strength of an earthquake is given as its magnitude.
In Switzerland the Swiss Seismological Service at ETH Zurich monitors earthquakes.

abschnitte.text: A seismograph is a device that measures and records movements of the ground. The word comes from Greek: **seismos** means shaking, and graphein means to write. In the past a pen drew a zigzag line on a paper drum. Today computers store the data, and the actual measuring instrument is often called a **seismometer**.

Inside it a heavy mass hangs or rests that, because of its **inertia**, stays almost still when the ground shakes. The casing moves with the ground, but the mass hardly moves. The difference between the two movements is measured and recorded. This produces a picture of the shaking, the **seismogram**.

In an earthquake different waves spread through the Earth. First the fast **P waves** arrive, then the slower **S waves**. From the time difference between the two you can calculate how far away the earthquake was. With three or more measuring stations the location of the earthquake, the epicentre, can be determined precisely.

As early as AD 132 the Chinese scholar Zhang Heng built a **seismoscope**. It was a bronze vessel with dragon heads, from which a ball fell into the mouth of a toad during an earthquake. In the 19th century the first real seismographs were made that could record movements. In 1935 Charles Richter in California developed the famous **Richter scale**.

Switzerland is also an earthquake country, especially Valais, the Grisons and the Basel region. The **Swiss Seismological Service** (SED) at ETH Zurich runs a network of over a hundred measuring stations. Each year it records about 1,000 to 1,500 mostly very weak earthquakes in Switzerland and neighbouring areas. The strongest known earthquake destroyed large parts of the city of Basel in 1356.

Seismographs help to report earthquakes quickly and to organise help. They are important for warnings of **tsunamis**, the huge waves after undersea earthquakes. Researchers also use the waves to look inside the Earth; this is how the Earth's core was discovered, for example. In addition, seismographs can detect nuclear tests or volcanic eruptions.

begriffe.erklaerung: The recorded curve that shows how strongly the ground shook.
The point on the Earth's surface directly above the origin of an earthquake.
A number that tells you how much energy an earthquake released.
The property of bodies to stay in their state of motion.

gewusst: Modern seismographs even detect the shaking of trains, lorries and full football stadiums.
With seismographs it was found out that the Earth has a liquid outer core.
Seismometers have even been set up on the Moon and on Mars.

teile.einleitung: Svante Pääbo is a Swedish researcher who studies ancient DNA from bones and mummies. With his team, he was the first to decode large parts of the genetic material of the Neanderthal. For this he received the Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine in 2022.
wichtigste: Svante Pääbo was born in 1955 in Stockholm, Sweden.
He is regarded as a co-founder of palaeogenetics, the study of ancient genetic material.
As early as the 1980s he obtained DNA from an Egyptian mummy.
His team was the first to decode large parts of the Neanderthal genome.
He does research at the Max Planck Institute for Evolutionary Anthropology in Leipzig.
In 2022 he received the Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine.
His father Sune Bergström had also received a Nobel Prize.

abschnitte.text: Svante Pääbo was born in **Stockholm** in 1955. His mother was a chemist from Estonia, and his father was the Swedish biochemist **Sune Bergström**. At Uppsala University, Pääbo first studied Egyptology and then medicine. The link between ancient cultures and modern biology shaped his whole career.

Even as a young researcher, Pääbo wondered whether genetic material was still preserved in ancient bodies. In the 1980s he succeeded in obtaining DNA from an **Egyptian mummy**. This was a sensation, because after death DNA slowly breaks down into tiny pieces. This gave rise to a new field of research, **palaeogenetics**.

The Neanderthal lived in Europe and western Asia from about 400,000 to 40,000 years ago. Pääbo's team examined bone remains and put the genetic material together like a huge puzzle. In 2010 they published a first draft of the **Neanderthal genome**. It showed that many people today outside Africa carry a small share of Neanderthal genetic material.

The team also obtained DNA from a tiny finger bone from the **Denisova Cave** in Siberia. The genetic material matched neither modern humans nor Neanderthals. In this way a previously unknown form of human was discovered, the **Denisovan**. It was the first time that a form of human had been identified only through its genetic material.

The biggest difficulty with ancient DNA is **contamination** with modern DNA. Even a flake of skin or a breath from a researcher can spoil a sample. That is why Pääbo's team works in especially clean clean rooms with protective suits and masks. Today experts from all over the world, including Switzerland, work according to these strict rules.

Since 1997 Pääbo has headed a department at the **Max Planck Institute for Evolutionary Anthropology** in Leipzig. In 2022 he alone received the **Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine**. His father had already been awarded a Nobel Prize in the same category in 1982. Pääbo's research helps us understand what distinguishes modern humans from their extinct relatives.

begriffe.erklaerung: The building plan in every cell in which a living thing's hereditary information is stored.
All the DNA of a living thing, that is, all its hereditary information together.
The science that studies ancient genetic material from bones, teeth or mummies.
An extinct form of human that lived in Europe until about 40,000 years ago.
When foreign, modern DNA gets into an ancient sample and spoils the result.

gewusst: At first Pääbo did his mummy experiments secretly at night and at weekends, because they were not part of his actual studies.
The finger bone from which the Denisovan was discovered was smaller than a fingernail.
Father and son both received a Nobel Prize in the same category, which is very rare.

teile.einleitung: The Swiss National Supercomputing Centre, CSCS for short, is Switzerland's national centre for high-performance computers. It is located in Lugano in Ticino and belongs to ETH Zurich. Some of the fastest computers in Europe work here for science and weather forecasting.
wichtigste: The CSCS is located in Lugano in the canton of Ticino.
It belongs to ETH Zurich.
The computers are cooled with water from Lake Lugano.
Its long-serving supercomputer was called Piz Daint, after a mountain in the Grisons.
In 2024 the new Alps infrastructure, which replaces Piz Daint, was inaugurated.
MeteoSwiss calculates its weather models on CSCS computers.
Computing power is measured in FLOPS.

abschnitte.text: The CSCS was founded in 1991 and is part of **ETH Zurich**. Since 2012 it has been housed in a modern building in **Lugano**. Researchers from universities all over Switzerland can apply for computing time there. This means that not every university has to buy its own expensive giant computers.

A **supercomputer** consists of thousands of processors that work on one task at the same time. It is millions of times faster than an ordinary laptop. Its performance is measured in **FLOPS**, that is, calculations with decimal numbers per second. The **TOP500** ranking compares the fastest supercomputers in the world twice a year.

The best-known computer at the CSCS was called **Piz Daint**, named after a mountain in the canton of the Grisons. For many years it was one of the fastest computers in Europe. In 2024 the new research infrastructure **Alps** was inaugurated. It uses modern graphics processors and is particularly well suited to artificial intelligence and climate research.

Supercomputers get very hot when they compute, a bit like a laptop on your lap, only much more so. For this, the CSCS pumps cold water from the depths of **Lake Lugano** through a long pipe. The lake water absorbs the heat and then flows back. In this way the centre saves a lot of electricity for air conditioning and protects the **environment**.

**MeteoSwiss** has its weather models for Switzerland calculated on CSCS computers. Researchers there simulate, for example, the climate, earthquakes, new materials or processes in the human body. Training large AI models also needs enormous computing power. Such **simulations** would be far too slow on normal computers.

begriffe.erklaerung: A huge computer made of thousands of processors that calculates extremely fast.
The unit of computing power: how many calculations with decimal numbers are possible per second.
A ranking that compares the 500 fastest computers in the world twice a year.
A copy of a real process in the computer, for example of the weather.

gewusst: The water for cooling is taken from a depth of about 45 metres in Lake Lugano, where it is cool all year round.
A supercomputer like Alps fills a whole hall with many cupboard-sized computer racks.
For a weather forecast, the computer calculates the weather for millions of small cubes of air above Switzerland.

teile.einleitung: A table is an arrangement of data in rows and columns. In this way a lot of information can be shown clearly and you can quickly look something up. We come across tables every day, from the school timetable to the train timetable.
wichtigste: A table arranges data in rows and columns.
The horizontal lines are called rows.
The vertical lines are called columns.
A single box is called a cell.
The first row usually contains the headings.
The school timetable is a table.
With tables you can easily compare and add up numbers.

abschnitte.text: A **table** is a grid of boxes in which you enter words or numbers. The horizontal lines are called **rows**, the vertical ones **columns**. Where a row and a column cross, there is a **cell**. Each cell holds exactly one piece of information.

At the very top, in the first row, there are usually the **headings**, also called the header row. They say what is in each column, for example “Name”, “Age” or “Favourite fruit”. Often the first column also has labels, such as the days of the week. So you know straight away where to find a particular piece of information.

A survey shows: apple 7 children, banana 5 children, pear 3 children. If you add them up, that is 7 plus 5 plus 3, so 15 children. If a weather table shows Monday 3 degrees and Tuesday 7 degrees, it was 4 degrees warmer on Tuesday. So tables help with **comparing** and **adding up**.

The **school timetable** shows the days of the week in columns and the lessons in rows. The SBB train timetable, the league table of a football league or the nutritional information on a packet are also tables. In maths there is the times table. In chemistry, the **periodic table** arranges all the elements in one big table.

On the computer you create tables with a **spreadsheet** program, for example Excel or LibreOffice Calc. There the computer can automatically add up numbers in the cells or calculate averages. With one click, the data can be turned into charts. As long as about 4000 years ago, people in Mesopotamia wrote tables of numbers on clay tablets.

begriffe.erklaerung: A horizontal line in a table.
A vertical line in a table.
A single box where a row and a column cross.
A computer program with which you create tables and calculate in them.

gewusst: The word table comes from the Latin “tabula”, meaning board or tablet.
The periodic table of the elements is one of the most famous tables in the world.
In a spreadsheet, a single table can have more than a million rows.

teile.einleitung: In biology, transcription is the first step with which a cell uses the information in its genes. In it, a section of DNA is copied and rewritten into a message made of RNA. You can imagine it like copying a recipe out of a valuable cookery book that has to stay in the library.
wichtigste: In transcription, a section of DNA is rewritten into RNA.
The enzyme that does this work is called RNA polymerase.
The new RNA strand is always extended from 5' to 3'.
In RNA, the base uracil replaces the thymine of DNA.
In eukaryotes, transcription takes place in the cell nucleus.
In eukaryotes, RNA polymerase II copies the genes for proteins.
The poison alpha-amanitin from the death cap mushroom blocks RNA polymerase II.

abschnitte.text: The instructions for all the proteins of a living thing are stored in the **DNA**. But DNA is valuable, and in plants, animals and fungi it stays in the **cell nucleus**. That is why a copy of a gene is made from **RNA**, the so-called messenger RNA or mRNA. This copy travels to the ribosomes, where a protein is then built during translation. Transcription means “rewriting”.

The **RNA polymerase** attaches to a starting region in front of the gene, the **promoter**. It opens the DNA double helix a little way, like a zip. One of the two strands serves as a template; it is called the **template strand**. For each base on the template, the polymerase adds the matching RNA base, and the strand grows from 5' to 3'. Instead of thymine, **uracil** is put in.

In bacteria such as E. coli, transcription ends at a section of DNA called the **terminator**. For some genes, a protein called the **Rho factor** helps: it follows the RNA polymerase along the RNA and releases it. Eukaryotes have three different RNA polymerases with different tasks. RNA polymerase II is responsible for the genes that contain instructions for proteins.

In eukaryotes, the freshly copied RNA is not yet finished. It is given a protective cap at one end and a tail at the other. In addition, sections that are not needed are cut out; this process is called **splicing**. Only then does the finished mRNA leave the nucleus through small pores.

Without transcription, no cell could make proteins and live. This is shown by the poison **alpha-amanitin** from the death cap mushroom, which blocks RNA polymerase II. That is why this mushroom is deadly, and you should never eat mushrooms you do not know. In Switzerland you can have mushrooms you have picked checked at an official mushroom inspection. Some antibiotics also work by blocking transcription in bacteria.

begriffe.erklaerung: The hereditary molecule in which the instructions of a living thing are stored.
A molecule similar to DNA that, among other things, serves as a copy of genes.
The enzyme that makes the RNA during transcription.
A section in front of a gene where transcription begins.
A base of RNA that replaces the thymine of DNA.

gewusst: An RNA polymerase can add dozens of bases per second.
Many RNA polymerases can make copies of a single gene at the same time.
The word transcription is also used in music and language, for example for rewriting a piece of music.

teile.einleitung: Self-healing materials are materials that can repair small damage such as cracks or scratches themselves. Their model is nature: just as a graze on your knee heals, plastic, concrete or paint should also recover. This saves repairs and makes things last longer.
wichtigste: The model for self-healing materials is wound healing in nature.
In some plastics, built-in microcapsules burst when a crack forms and fill the crack.
In self-healing concrete, bacteria form lime that closes cracks.
The sleeping bacteria become active through water that gets into a crack.
In 2023 researchers showed that lumps of lime in Roman concrete can close cracks by themselves.
Some self-healing plastics heal when they are warmed.
Self-healing coatings already exist for car paint against small scratches.
Such materials last longer and need fewer repairs.

abschnitte.text: **Self-healing materials** can repair damage completely or partly without help from outside. Usually this is about tiny cracks that can hardly be seen with the naked eye. Such **microcracks** are dangerous because they grow over time and finally make a component break. If a crack is closed early, the material stays stable for longer. The model is **wound healing** in people, animals and plants.

A well-known method comes from researchers at the University of Illinois in the USA, who presented it around 2001. Inside the plastic there are tiny **microcapsules** filled with a liquid glue. If a crack forms, the capsules burst and the liquid flows in. There it meets a substance that makes it harden, rather like a two-part glue. The drawback: at the same spot it usually only works once.

In other plastics the bonds between the molecular chains can be broken and made again. If you warm them, the particles become mobile and join up again across the crack. In this way, for example, **coatings** for car paint are made in which fine scratches disappear in the warmth of the sun. Some phone cases and screen protectors also use such effects.

Over time concrete gets cracks through which water gets in and makes the steel inside rust. That is why researchers in the Netherlands developed **bacterial concrete**. In it, special bacteria sleep together with nutrients in small capsules. If water gets into a crack, the bacteria wake up and form **lime**, which closes the crack. In this way bridges, tunnels and buildings can last longer.

Many Roman buildings are still standing after almost 2,000 years, for example the Pantheon in Rome. In 2023 researchers found out that small white lumps of lime play an important role in **Roman concrete**. If water gets into a crack, it dissolves lime from these lumps. The lime crystallises again in the crack and closes it. So the Romans built with self-healing concrete without knowing it.

Self-healing materials last **longer** and need to be repaired or replaced less often. This saves money, raw materials and energy, which also helps the environment. They are especially useful where repairs are difficult, for example in aircraft, satellites or pipes deep underground. Many of these materials are still expensive or have only been tested in the laboratory. Researchers are working to make them ready for everyday use.

begriffe.erklaerung: A tiny crack that can often only be seen under a microscope.
A tiny ball in which a substance is enclosed.
