A substance made of very long molecular chains, from which plastics are made.
A building material made of cement, water, sand and gravel that becomes rock-hard.

gewusst: In some concrete mixtures bacteria sleep for years until water wakes them.
The Pantheon in Rome has a dome of unreinforced concrete almost 2,000 years old.
With some car paints, fine scratches disappear when the sun warms the car.

teile.einleitung: Scientifica is a large science festival in Zurich, organised jointly by the University of Zurich and ETH Zurich. Researchers show experiments there, give talks and answer questions. Entry is free, and children and teenagers are especially welcome.
wichtigste: Scientifica is a science festival for the public.
The organisers are the University of Zurich and ETH Zurich.
Entry is free.
The events take place mainly in the main buildings of UZH and ETH in the centre of Zurich.
Each edition has a shared main theme.
As well as adults, Scientifica is aimed especially at children and teenagers.
Relaxed discussion rounds such as the Science Café are also typical.

abschnitte.text: **Scientifica** is the Zurich science days. For several days the universities open their doors to anyone who is interested. Hundreds of researchers show what they are working on and explain it in an understandable way. There are exhibitions, hands-on experiments, talks and discussions. Visiting is **free**, and you usually do not have to register.

Most events take place in the **main buildings** of the University of Zurich and ETH Zurich. These two large buildings stand right next to each other above the old town. From there you look out over the city and Lake Zurich. You can reach them, for example, with the Polybahn, a small funicular railway from Central.

Each edition of Scientifica has a shared **main theme**. Researchers from very different subjects then show what their field contributes to this theme. In this way, for example, medicine, computer science, history and physics come together. This shows how varied research is and how the subjects are connected.

Scientifica is also aimed especially at **children and teenagers**. For them there are special lectures, workshops and hands-on experiments. You can, for example, control robots, do research under the microscope or talk to researchers. Many school classes visit the festival, and some young people discover their favourite subject there.

A popular format is the **Science Café**, in which researchers discuss things with the audience in a relaxed setting. Science should not only be explained but also questioned. Throughout Switzerland the foundation **Science et Cité** works for this dialogue between science and society. There are similar festivals in other Swiss cities too.

begriffe.erklaerung: A large event over several days with many different activities.
The Swiss Federal Institute of Technology, one of the best-known universities in the world.
Abbreviation for the University of Zurich, the largest university in Switzerland.
A relaxed conversation between researchers and the public, often over coffee or drinks.

gewusst: At Scientifica you can ask world-class researchers questions without paying any entry fee.
The main buildings of ETH and the University of Zurich stand right next to each other.
For each edition the universities choose a shared theme on which all subjects show something.

teile.einleitung: “Science” is one of the most famous scientific journals in the world, in which researchers publish their new discoveries. It is published every week in the USA and reports on all areas of the natural sciences. Anyone who is allowed to publish an article in “Science” is regarded as particularly successful.
wichtigste: “Science” is a weekly scientific journal from the USA.
It was founded in 1880, with support from the inventor Thomas Edison.
It is published by the AAAS, which has its headquarters in Washington, D.C.
As well as research articles it carries news and comments on science.
Every year it names the most important discovery as its “Breakthrough of the Year”.
Its freely available sister journal is called “Science Advances”.
Together with “Nature”, “Science” is regarded as the most important general science journal.

abschnitte.text: “Science” is a **scientific journal**, that is, a magazine in which researchers publish their results for other experts. It covers many fields, from biology and medicine to physics and chemistry, and climate and space. Only a few selected research papers appear in each issue. In addition there are news items, comments and book reviews. The journal appears in print and online.

“Science” was founded in New York in **1880**. The inventor **Thomas Edison** supported its founding with money. The first years were difficult, and the journal nearly closed several times. Around 1900 the **AAAS**, the American Association for the Advancement of Science, took over the journal. Since then “Science” has been its official journal.

abschnitte.titel: How does an article get in?
abschnitte.text: Researchers send their work to the editors, but only a small proportion is accepted. First experts check anonymously whether the work is careful and new. This process is called **peer review**, that is, assessment by colleagues in the field. Often the researchers then have to improve their work. Only then does the article appear.

How often other researchers cite articles from a journal is measured with the **impact factor**. It gives the average number of times the articles are cited. “Science” has a very high impact factor and is therefore regarded as especially prestigious. Its most important rival is the British journal **“Nature”**. However, critics argue that such figures alone do not show how good an individual piece of research is.

Every year in December the editors choose the **“Breakthrough of the Year”**. Examples of what has been honoured are advances in vaccines or discoveries about the universe. Since 2015 there has also been the sister journal **“Science Advances”**, whose articles can all be read free of charge. Researchers from Switzerland, for example from ETH Zurich, also regularly publish in “Science”.

begriffe.erklaerung: A magazine in which experts publish new research results.
The checking of a research paper by other experts before it is published.
A number that tells you how often articles in a journal are cited on average.
The American Association for the Advancement of Science, the publisher of “Science”.

gewusst: The inventor of the light bulb, Thomas Edison, helped to found “Science”.
Only a small proportion of the research papers submitted to “Science” are accepted.
The AAAS is one of the largest scientific organisations in the world.

teile.einleitung: A straw man argument is a trick in discussions in which you distort the other person's opinion and then attack this false version. So you fight against a straw dummy instead of the real opponent. If you know the trick, you can argue more fairly and defend yourself better.
wichtigste: In a straw man argument, you refute a distorted version of the opposing position.
The image probably comes from a straw dummy, which is easy to defeat.
You can recognise a straw man when the opposing position is exaggerated.
A good counter-strategy is to repeat your own position precisely.
The opposite of a straw man is the steel man, in which you examine the strongest form of the opposing position.
The principle of charity requires you to interpret other people's statements as reasonably as possible.
The straw man argument is regarded as a fallacy.

abschnitte.text: A **straw man argument** is a fallacy in reasoning. Instead of responding to what someone really said, you present their opinion in an exaggerated or twisted way. Then you refute this weak version and pretend that you have refuted the real opinion. The name probably comes from a **straw dummy**, which is easy to knock over because it does not fight back.

A says: “We should build more cycle paths.” B replies: “So A wants to ban all cars!” That is a straw man, because A said nothing about banning cars. It is similar when a researcher suggests testing a medicine further and a critic says: “So she claims it cures everything!” The critic is building up an **exaggerated** claim that is easy to attack.

A warning sign is when someone sums up the opposing position in an **exaggerated** way or with words like “so” and “always”. Often a small suggestion is turned into an extreme demand. Sometimes someone only picks out the weakest point and ignores the good reasons. You should ask yourself: did the person really say that?

abschnitte.titel: What you can do about it
abschnitte.text: If someone answers with a straw man, it helps to repeat **your own position** calmly and precisely. You can also say in a friendly way: “That is not what I claimed; what I meant was this.” The other way round, you can ask whether you have understood someone correctly. That way the discussion stays on the actual topic.

The opposite of the straw man is the **steel man**. Here you present the opposing position in its strongest form before you examine it. This goes well with the **principle of charity**, which requires you to interpret other people's statements as reasonably as possible. People who discuss like this learn more and often end up being more convincing.

In the 19th century, the philosopher **Arthur Schopenhauer** already described similar tricks in his work on the art of being right. One of them consists of exaggerating and stretching the opponent's claim. You come across straw man arguments in discussions in the playground, on social media and in politics. In Switzerland, with its many popular votes, it is especially important to present arguments fairly.

begriffe.erklaerung: A mistake in thinking in which a conclusion is not properly justified.
A reason that you use to support an opinion.
The strongest and fairest presentation of an opposing position.
Understanding other people's statements in a way that makes them as reasonable as possible.

gewusst: In German the fallacy is called “Strohmann-Argument”, and the steel man is called “Stahlmann”.
In the past, soldiers practised fighting on dummies made of straw, which of course put up no resistance.
Scarecrows are a kind of straw man too: they look like people but are harmless.

teile.einleitung: Soap is a cleaning product that loosens fat and dirt from skin and objects. It is made by boiling fats or oils with an alkali. The secret of how it works is tiny particles that can bind to water and to fat at the same time.
wichtigste: Soap is made from fat or oil and an alkali; this process is called saponification.
For hard soaps such as household soap, caustic soda is used.
A soap particle has a water-loving head and a long, water-repelling tail.
Soap particles trap droplets of fat in small spheres called micelles.
Soap destroys the fatty envelope of flu viruses and coronaviruses.
In hard water insoluble lime soap forms.
Soap lowers the surface tension of water.
A solution of household soap and water is alkaline.

abschnitte.text: **Soap** is a cleaning product that has been known for thousands of years. Chemically speaking, soaps are salts of fatty acids. They belong to the **surfactants**, substances that place themselves between water and fat. There are hard soaps such as household soap, soft soap and liquid soaps. Many of today's shower gels and shampoos contain other, artificially made surfactants.

Soap is made when fats or oils are heated together with an **alkali**. In the process the fats are split, and soap and glycerine form. This process is called **saponification**. With caustic soda, hard soaps such as household soap are made; with caustic potash, soft soap. Olive oil, coconut oil or animal fat, for example, are used as the fat.

Every soap particle has a **water-loving head** and a long, water-repelling tail. The tail holds on to the fat, and the head stays in the water. In this way many soap particles surround a droplet of fat and form a small sphere, a **micelle**. These spheres can easily be rinsed away with water. Without soap, water and fat would simply stay separate.

Many viruses, such as flu viruses and coronaviruses, are surrounded by a thin **fatty envelope**. Soap breaks this envelope down, and the virus is destroyed as a result. That is why washing your hands thoroughly with soap is so effective. Experts recommend soaping your hands for about 20 to 30 seconds. Bacteria and dirt are washed away at the same time.

Soap lowers the **surface tension** of water. A paper clip carefully laid on the water therefore sinks as soon as you add a little soap. In very hard water, as found in many parts of Switzerland, soap forms insoluble **lime soap**. This shows up as a grey deposit in washbasins and baths. Soap solutions are slightly alkaline, which can dry out the skin.

More than 4,000 years ago the Sumerians in ancient Mesopotamia already knew soap-like mixtures of oil and ash. In the Middle Ages cities such as **Aleppo** in Syria and Marseille in France became famous for their soaps. For a long time soap was a luxury. Only in the 19th century did it become cheap and available to everyone, which greatly improved hygiene.

begriffe.erklaerung: The chemical reaction in which soap is made from fat and an alkali.
A substance that can link water and fat together.
A tiny sphere of soap particles that traps fat inside.
A kind of thin skin on the surface of water, caused by water particles holding together.
A basic liquid, for example caustic soda solution.

gewusst: Soap bubbles shimmer in many colours because their skin is only a few thousandths of a millimetre thick.
Simply washing your hands with soap can literally take apart viruses with a fatty envelope.
The grey ring in the bath is often lime soap from hard water.

teile.einleitung: Why does a huge steel ship float, while a small glass marble sinks straight away? Whether something floats or sinks does not simply depend on its weight but on how heavy an object is compared with its size. The secret is called buoyancy.
wichtigste: A cork, an apple and an ice cube float in water.
A glass marble or a stone sinks.
If you put a stone in water, the water level rises because the stone displaces water.
If you shape a sinking ball of modelling clay into a little boat, it can float.
Cooking oil floats on top of water.
Armbands full of air help children to stay up.
Density is what matters: anything lighter than the same amount of water floats.

abschnitte.text: **Density** tells you how much a substance weighs for the same size. A litre of water weighs about one kilogram. If an object is lighter than the same amount of water, it floats; if it is heavier, it sinks. Cork and wood are lighter than water; glass, stone and iron are heavier. Cooking oil is also a little lighter than water and therefore collects on top.

Water pushes from below against everything that dips into it. This force is called **buoyancy**. The Greek scholar **Archimedes** found out more than 2,000 years ago that the buoyancy is as great as the weight of the water displaced. That is why the water level rises when you put a stone in a glass: the stone pushes water aside. If the buoyancy is greater than the weight of the object, the object floats.

A ball of modelling clay sinks because it displaces little water. If you shape it into a flat **little boat** with a high edge, the same clay displaces much more water. Then the buoyancy is enough, and the boat floats. Large steel ships work in just the same way: their hull is hollow inside and filled with air. If you load too much into it, the ship sinks deeper, and in the worst case it goes down.

An **ice cube** floats because frozen water is a little less dense than liquid water. However, only a small part sticks out; with icebergs it is about a tenth. An apple floats because a lot of air is trapped inside it. **Armbands** and life jackets are also filled with air or light foam and so increase buoyancy.

In salt water the buoyancy is greater than in fresh water, because salt water is denser. That is why it is easier to float in the sea than in Lake Zurich. In the very salty **Dead Sea** you can even lie on the water and read a newspaper. An egg that sinks in tap water starts to float if you stir a lot of salt into the water.

A submarine can sink or surface on purpose. To do this it fills tanks with water or blows them empty again with air. Fish do something similar with their **swim bladder**, which they fill with more or less gas. In this way they can hover in the water without sinking or rising.

begriffe.erklaerung: How heavy a substance is in relation to its size.
The force with which water pushes an object that is dipped into it upwards.
The water that an object pushes aside when it dips into it.
A gas-filled organ with which many fish hover in the water.

gewusst: A steel ship weighing thousands of tonnes floats because its hollow hull displaces a great deal of water.
Only about a tenth of an iceberg can be seen above the water.
An egg sinks in tap water but floats in very salty water.

teile.einleitung: A voice assistant is a computer program with which you can communicate by speaking instead of typing. You ask it a question or give it a task, and it answers with a computer voice. Well-known examples are Siri, Alexa and Google Assistant.
wichtigste: A voice assistant listens with a microphone and answers through a loudspeaker.
Usually you first say a particular wake word so that it listens.
It is often in a smartphone, but also in speakers, cars and televisions.
For most questions it needs an internet connection.
It can, for example, set an alarm, play music or tell you the weather.
Recordings can be stored, which is why you should not tell it any secrets.
Behind voice assistants there is artificial intelligence.

abschnitte.text: A **voice assistant** is a program that understands spoken language and reacts to it. Well-known ones are Siri from Apple, Alexa from Amazon and Google Assistant. They can be found in smartphones, in **smart speakers**, in cars or in televisions. Instead of typing on a screen, you simply talk to the device.

First the device waits for the **wake word**, for example “Hey Siri” or “Alexa”. Then the microphone records the question and usually sends it over the internet to large data centres. There **speech recognition** turns the sounds into text, and a program tries to understand what is meant. The answer is then read out with an artificial voice through the loudspeaker.

Voice assistants set alarms and timers, do sums, translate or tell you the weather. You can use them to play music and audiobooks or to dictate messages. In a **smart home** they switch lights, heating or blinds on and off. For people with visual impairments or other disabilities they are a great help in everyday life.

As early as the 1960s there were the first computers that recognised single spoken words. In 2011 Apple brought the first well-known voice assistant to a smartphone with **Siri**. Amazon followed in 2014 with Alexa and its own speaker, and Google in 2016 with Google Assistant. Newer voice assistants use large language models and can therefore answer much more naturally.

A voice assistant is constantly listening for its wake word and can sometimes mishear. Recordings are often stored on the companies' servers and can be analysed. That is why you should not tell it any **secrets**, passwords or addresses. In the settings you can switch off the microphone and delete stored recordings. Many voice assistants do not yet understand Swiss German as well as Standard German.

begriffe.erklaerung: A word with which you wake up the voice assistant, for example “Alexa”.
Technology that turns spoken words into written text.
A house or flat in which devices can be controlled over the internet.
Computer programs that solve tasks which would otherwise need human thinking.

gewusst: The name Siri comes from Norwegian.
The name Alexa is meant to recall the famous ancient library of Alexandria.
The artificial voices are often created from many hours of recordings of real speakers.

teile.einleitung: The tree of life shows how all living things on Earth are related to one another. As in a family tree, the branches lead back to common ancestors. Right at the bottom, at the root, stands an original form from which all life today descends.
wichtigste: All life is divided into three domains: bacteria, archaea and eukaryotes.
The division into three domains was proposed by the researcher Carl Woese.
In 1837 Charles Darwin drew a first tree in his notebook, together with the words “I think”.
In the 19th century Ernst Haeckel drew famous, artistic trees of life.
A branching point means that two lines arise from one ancestral species.
According to today's tree of life, birds belong to the dinosaurs.
Fungi are more closely related to animals than to plants.

abschnitte.text: The tree of life is a picture of the **relationships** between all living things. Each **branching point** means that two separate lines have developed from one ancestral species. The closer two branches lie to each other, the more closely the living things are related. The tips of the twigs are the species living today, but many branches also end in extinct species.

In the 18th century **Carl Linnaeus** sorted living things into groups and introduced two-part names such as “Homo sapiens”. But he did not yet see descent in this. Only **Charles Darwin** recognised that species change over a long time and come from one another. In 1837 he drew a first small tree in his notebook and wrote “I think” above it.

In the 19th century the German zoologist **Ernst Haeckel** spread Darwin's ideas in Germany. He drew large, artistic trees of life that look like real oak trees. Haeckel also coined terms such as ecology. Some of his groupings are now regarded as out of date, but his pictures are still famous.

In the 1970s **Carl Woese** compared the genetic material of microbes and in doing so discovered a group of its own, the **archaea**. Since then all life has been divided into three domains: bacteria, archaea and eukaryotes. The eukaryotes include all living things with a cell nucleus, that is animals, plants, fungi and many single-celled organisms. Today trees of life are made above all by comparing **DNA**.

The modern tree of life holds a few surprises. **Birds** are descendants of predatory dinosaurs and therefore count as dinosaurs themselves. Fungi are more closely related to animals than to plants. The closest living relatives of humans are chimpanzees and bonobos.

For bacteria and archaea the tree of life is sometimes more of a net. This is because they can swap genes with one another, even between quite different species. Besides, the mitochondria, the power stations of our cells, originally came from bacteria. That is why researchers today often draw the tree of life with cross-links between the branches.

begriffe.erklaerung: The largest group into which living things are divided; there are three of them.
Living things whose cells have a nucleus, such as animals, plants and fungi.
Single-celled microbes without a nucleus that form a domain of their own.
The slow change of living things over many generations.
A species from which two or more later species descend.

gewusst: In Darwin's famous book “On the Origin of Species” of 1859 there is only one single picture, and it is a tree of life.
A chicken is more closely related to Tyrannosaurus than a crocodile is.
A button mushroom is more closely related to you than to a fir tree.

teile.einleitung: Technology transfer means that knowledge from research is turned into products and services. In this way an invention from a university laboratory is meant to find its way into everyday life. Switzerland is regarded as one of the most innovative countries in the world.
wichtigste: Technology transfer is the transfer of research knowledge into commercial use.
At ETH Zurich, the office ETH transfer takes care of patents, licences and spin-offs.
Switzerland Innovation is a network of innovation parks at several locations.
Innosuisse funds projects in which universities and companies work together.
The Technology Readiness Level scale describes the stage of development of a technology from 1 to 9.
The “Valley of Death” means the funding gap between research and the market.
A confidentiality agreement protects an invention before it has been registered.

abschnitte.text: In **technology transfer**, knowledge moves from universities and research institutes into companies. In this way an idea in the laboratory becomes, for example, a new medicine, a sensor or a piece of software. This can happen through **licences**, in which a company is allowed to use an invention and pays for it. Researchers also often found their own company, a so-called **spin-off**.

Every large university has a transfer office; at ETH Zurich it is called **ETH transfer**. It helps with registering patents, granting licences and supporting spin-offs. The Confederation's funding agency, **Innosuisse**, supports innovation projects by universities and companies. Typically the research partner receives the funding, while the company makes its own contribution.

**Switzerland Innovation** is a network of innovation parks at several locations in Switzerland. There, researchers, start-ups and large companies work close to one another. One location is, for example, near the Paul Scherrer Institute in Aargau, another in Dübendorf near Zurich. Being close together is meant to help ideas become products more quickly.

abschnitte.titel: From the laboratory to the market
abschnitte.text: How far a technology has been developed is described by the **Technology Readiness Level** scale from 1 to 9. Level 1 is just a basic principle on paper, level 9 a proven system in real use. Between research and market launch there is often a lack of money; this gap is called the **Valley of Death**. Many good ideas fail at exactly this point.

An invention can only be patented if it is new and has not yet been published. That is why the university and the company often first sign a **confidentiality agreement**, NDA for short. In the USA, the **Bayh-Dole Act** of 1980 allowed universities to hold patents on research funded by the state. This law is regarded as a milestone of technology transfer worldwide.

begriffe.erklaerung: A right that gives a person or company sole ownership of an invention for a certain time.
Permission to use a protected invention in return for payment.
A new company that grows out of a university or research institute.
A new idea that is actually put into practice and used.

gewusst: Switzerland has been in first place in the worldwide innovation ranking, the Global Innovation Index, for many years.
Dozens of new spin-off companies come out of ETH Zurich every year.
A patent usually lasts at most 20 years; after that anyone may use the invention.

teile.einleitung: A lateral moraine is a long ridge of debris and stones at the edge of a glacier. The glacier brought the material along like a conveyor belt and dumped it at its sides. In the Alps such ridges are often seen high above today's ice, as witnesses of earlier, much larger glaciers.
wichtigste: A lateral moraine is a ridge of debris at the edge of a glacier.
Moraine material is unsorted: large and small stones lie mixed together.
Young lateral moraines often have a narrow, sharp crest.
Many lateral moraines today lie high above the ice, because the glaciers have shrunk greatly since about 1850.
The trimline on the valley slopes shows the highest level of the glacier around 1850.
Steep lateral moraines can slide and break away when the glacier shrinks.
Hardly any plants grow on moraines that have just become free of ice, because hardly any soil has formed yet.

abschnitte.text: A **moraine** is rock debris that a glacier carries and dumps. The **lateral moraine** lies at the edge of the glacier, along the valley slopes. It consists of boulders, gravel, sand and fine rock flour. The material comes from rockfalls and landslides on the mountainsides and from the ice grinding against the rock. Because the ice does not sort anything, large and small stones lie all mixed up.

Where the ice melts away at its lower end, a curved ridge forms, the **terminal moraine**. Under the glacier the ground moraine forms. When two glaciers flow together, their inner lateral moraines join to form a **medial moraine**, which lies on the ice as a dark stripe. Such stripes can be seen especially well on the Great Aletsch Glacier. Ice Age glaciers also shaped moraine material into long hills called drumlins, such as those found in the Zurich Oberland.

Around **1850**, at the end of the so-called Little Ice Age, the Alpine glaciers were especially large. Since then they have shrunk greatly and become thinner. That is why the lateral moraines from that time today often lie dozens to hundreds of metres above the ice. Above them you can see a light line on the valley slopes, the **trimline**. Below it the ice has ground the rock smooth.

Young lateral moraines often have a narrow, sharp **crest** and very steep sides. As long as the glacier lay next to them, the ice supported the debris. When the ice shrinks, this support is missing, and parts of the moraine can slide or break away. That is why mountain paths to huts have to be moved again and again. Hikers should be careful on moraine crests and not leave the marked paths.

On moraines that have only recently become free of ice, hardly any plants grow at first. There is no fertile **soil**, which only forms over many decades. The first to settle are lichens, mosses and tough pioneer plants such as the glacier buttercup. Older moraines, on the other hand, are covered with larches and alpine roses. In this way researchers can watch on moraines how new life arises.

begriffe.erklaerung: Debris of stones, gravel and sand dumped by a glacier.
A boundary line on a slope up to which a glacier once ground down the rock.
A cool period from about 1300 to 1850 in which the Alpine glaciers grew.
A long, streamlined hill shaped by an Ice Age glacier.

gewusst: The dark stripes on the Aletsch Glacier are medial moraines formed from lateral moraines that have joined.
From the height of a lateral moraine you can tell how thick the glacier used to be.
Some hiking paths to mountain huts had to be moved because the moraine below them slid away.

teile.einleitung: Tesafilm is a well-known transparent adhesive tape that is sticky on one side. The name is actually a brand of the Hamburg company Beiersdorf, but it is often used for any transparent sticky tape. In Switzerland people also often call it “Klebstreifen” or “Scotch”.
wichtigste: Tesafilm is a transparent adhesive tape that is sticky on one side.
The company Beiersdorf brought it out in Hamburg in the 1930s.
Sticky tape is usually wound onto a roll.
A dispenser has a small serrated, sharp edge for tearing it off.
It is used, for example, to close wrapping paper or to mend a torn sheet of paper.
For sealing boxes there is wide, brown parcel tape.
When you pull sticky tape off a wall, a piece of paint or paper often comes off with it.

abschnitte.text: Tesafilm consists of a thin, transparent **plastic film**. An **adhesive** is applied to one side, and the other side is not sticky. This means the tape can be rolled up without sticking to itself. The adhesive is a pressure-sensitive adhesive, which sticks as soon as you press on it lightly.

The Hamburg company **Beiersdorf** was already making plasters and adhesive tapes around 1900. The brand name tesa came from the name of an employee, Elsa Tesmer. In the 1930s the transparent Tesafilm came onto the market. At about the same time, Richard Drew at the company 3M in the USA invented Scotch tape. Today tesa is a separate company that belongs to Beiersdorf.

Sticky tape is kept on a **roll** made of cardboard or plastic. To cut it easily, there is a **dispenser**. It has a small serrated edge on which the tape tears off when you pull it. Careful: this edge is sharp enough for you to hurt yourself on it easily.

Sticky tape is very handy at school, in the office and at home. You use it to close wrapping paper, put up drawings or mend a torn sheet of paper. For boxes there is wide brown **parcel tape**, and painters use masking tape, which is easy to remove again. With posters on the wall, normal sticky tape can tear off paint or paper when you pull it off.

Sticky tape has even become famous in research. The physicists **Andre Geim** and Konstantin Novoselov used ordinary sticky tape to peel wafer-thin layers off graphite. In this way they obtained **graphene**, a layer of carbon only one atom thick. For this they received the Nobel Prize in Physics in 2010.

begriffe.erklaerung: A strip of film or paper that is coated with adhesive on one side.
A holder with a serrated edge with which you tear off sticky tape.
An adhesive that sticks with light pressure and does not need to dry.
A protected name under which a company sells its product.

gewusst: If you pull sticky tape quickly off the roll in the dark, a faint glow can appear.
Using a piece of sticky tape, researchers were able to make the material graphene and won the Nobel Prize for it.
Many people say Tesa even though they are using sticky tape of a different brand.

teile.einleitung: Swissmedic is the Swiss authority that authorises and monitors medicines and medical devices. Before a new medicine may be sold in Switzerland, Swissmedic checks whether it is well made, safe and effective. In this way the authority protects the health of people and animals.
wichtigste: Swissmedic is the Swiss Agency for Therapeutic Products, based in Bern.
The authority has been carrying out its tasks since 2002.
Its work is based on the Therapeutic Products Act.
Before authorisation, Swissmedic checks quality, safety and effectiveness.
Even after authorisation, Swissmedic evaluates reports of side effects.
As well as medicines, Swissmedic also monitors medical devices.
Swissmedic is a federal public-law institution assigned to the Department of Home Affairs.

abschnitte.text: Swissmedic is the **Swiss Agency for Therapeutic Products**, that is, the national supervisory authority for therapeutic products. It is based in **Bern**. Legally it is a **federal public-law institution** and is assigned to the Federal Department of Home Affairs. This means it belongs to the Confederation but can work fairly independently.

Swissmedic started its work on 1 January 2002. At the same time, the **Therapeutic Products Act**, which governs the authority's work, came into force. Before that, the main responsibility lay with the **Intercantonal Office for the Control of Medicines**, which was run by the cantons. With Swissmedic, supervision was brought together at federal level for the whole of Switzerland.

A company that wants to sell a new medicine submits an **application for authorisation** to Swissmedic. Experts then check the documents for **quality, safety and effectiveness**. For example, they look at whether the medicine is made cleanly and whether the benefit is greater than the risks. Only after this check may the medicine be sold in Switzerland.

Even after authorisation, Swissmedic stays alert. Doctors, pharmacists and patients can report **side effects**, and Swissmedic evaluates these reports. If necessary, the authority can issue warnings or have a medicine taken off the market. It also inspects manufacturing companies and monitors **medical devices** such as plasters, syringes or pacemakers.

Swissmedic only decides whether a medicine may be sold. Whether the **basic insurance** of the health insurance fund pays for it is decided by the **Federal Office of Public Health**. For this, the medicine is added to the so-called list of pharmaceutical specialities. Swissmedic also works with authorities in other countries, for example to fight fakes.

Medicines from unknown online shops can be **fake** and contain dangerous substances. That is why Swissmedic warns against ordering medicines from unsafe websites. It is safe to buy medicines at a pharmacy or chemist's. If you have questions, the staff at the pharmacy will be happy to help.

begriffe.erklaerung: The general term for medicines and medical devices.
Official permission to sell a medicine.
An unwanted effect of a medicine.
An aid for health that does not work chemically, such as a plaster or a thermometer.

gewusst: Swissmedic also checks medicines for animals, for example for dogs, cats and cows.
A medicine needs its own authorisation in Switzerland, even if it is already allowed abroad.

teile.einleitung: The standard deviation is a number from statistics that shows how much values are spread around their mean. If it is small, the values lie close together; if it is large, they are widely spread. It helps to compare measurements, marks or people's heights better.
wichtigste: The standard deviation measures the spread of values around the mean.
It has the same unit as the measured values, so for heights in centimetres it is centimetres.
The variance is the square of the standard deviation, so with a standard deviation of 3 it is 9.
If all values are multiplied by 2, the standard deviation doubles.
If the same number is added to all values, the standard deviation stays the same.
For a sample you divide by n minus 1 to make up for underestimating the spread.
The coefficient of variation is the standard deviation divided by the mean.

abschnitte.text: The **mean** tells you where values lie on average, but not how much they differ. That is what the **standard deviation** is for. It shows how far the values typically are from the mean. It is often written with the Greek letter sigma, σ.

First you calculate the mean. Then for each value you find the distance from the mean, square it and take the mean of these again; that is the **variance**. Finally you take the square root of it. For the values 2, 4, 4, 4, 5, 5, 7, 9 the mean is 5, the variance 4 and the standard deviation 2.

Two classes both have an average mark of 4.5. In class A the standard deviation is 0.3, in class B 1.2. This means that in class A almost everyone has similar marks, while the marks in class B are much more **spread out**. The average alone would not have shown this difference.

If 5 is added to all values, everything just moves up, and the standard deviation stays the same. If all values are multiplied by 2, the standard deviation doubles. Anyone who wants to compare spreads with different means uses the **coefficient of variation**. With a mean of 40 and a standard deviation of 6 it is 6 divided by 40, that is 15 per cent.

Many measured quantities, for example people's heights, roughly follow a **normal distribution**, which looks like a bell. In it about 68 per cent of the values lie at most one standard deviation away from the mean. Within two standard deviations lie about 95 per cent of the values. The normal distribution is closely linked with the mathematician Carl Friedrich Gauss.

If you know all the values of a group, you divide by the number n when calculating the variance. If you only have a **sample**, that is part of it, you divide by n minus 1. Otherwise you would usually underestimate the spread of the whole group a little. The English name “standard deviation” was coined at the end of the 19th century by the British statistician Karl Pearson.

begriffe.erklaerung: The sum of all values divided by how many there are, the average.
How far apart the values lie.
The average of the squared distances from the mean.
A distribution of values that looks like a bell.
The standard deviation in relation to the mean, often as a percentage.

gewusst: Almost all values of a normal distribution, about 99.7 per cent, lie within three standard deviations.
The quality method “Six Sigma” in factories is named after the standard deviation.
If all the values are the same, the standard deviation is exactly zero.

teile.einleitung: Simpson's paradox is an astonishing trap in statistics: a result that holds in every single group can reverse when you add all the groups together. Anyone who is not careful draws completely wrong conclusions from it. Well-known examples come from medicine and from university admission figures.
wichtigste: In Simpson's paradox a trend found in all subgroups reverses in the overall result.
It is named after the British statistician Edward H. Simpson.
In a kidney stone study, method A was better for small and for large stones, but method B was better overall.
The reason: method A was used more often for the difficult large stones.
A well-known example is the admission figures of the University of California, Berkeley, from 1973.
Behind the paradox there is usually a hidden confounding factor.
Whether the subgroups or the totals are what matters is decided with knowledge about the causes.

abschnitte.text: A **paradox** is something that seems impossible at first sight. In **Simpson's paradox** something does better in every subgroup but worse overall. That sounds like a calculation error, but it is not one. It is because the groups are of different sizes and different difficulty. The British statistician **Edward H. Simpson** described the phenomenon in 1951.

In a well-known study two treatments for kidney stones were compared. Method A cured 81 of 87 cases with small stones, about 93 per cent, and 192 of 263 with large ones, about 73 per cent. In total that was 273 of 350 cases, about **78 per cent**. Method B was worse in both groups but reached about 83 per cent overall. The reason: method A was used much more often for the **difficult large stones**, which are cured less often.

In 1973 it was noticed at the **University of California, Berkeley**, that overall far fewer women than men were admitted. Looking at the individual subjects, however, women were mostly admitted just as often or even more often. Women had applied much more often for subjects in which almost everyone was turned down. A worked example shows this: in subject X, 18 of 20 women and 80 of 100 men are admitted, in subject Y 20 of 100 women and 3 of 20 men. Women do better in both subjects, but overall only 38 of 120 women, about **32 per cent**, and 83 of 120 men are admitted.

Behind the paradox there is usually a **confounding factor**, also called a confounder. It affects both which group someone ends up in and the result. For the kidney stones it is the size of the stone, for the admissions the choice of subject. Anyone who overlooks the confounder is really comparing apples with oranges.

Mathematics alone does not tell you whether to believe the subgroups or the totals. You need **knowledge about the causes** behind the data. For the kidney stones, the comparison within the stone sizes makes more sense, because the size of the stone influenced the choice of treatment. Simpson's paradox shows how important critical thinking is when looking at statistics in newspapers, advertising and politics.

begriffe.erklaerung: A statement that seems contradictory but can still be true.
The science of collecting and analysing data.
A hidden influence that can distort the result of a comparison.
A proportion, for example how many out of a hundred cases were successful.

gewusst: A treatment can be better for mild and for severe cases and still look worse overall.
The same paradox can also occur in sport, for example with the scoring rates of two players over two seasons.
Simpson was not the first to notice the phenomenon, but it was named after him.

teile.einleitung: The nitrogen cycle describes the path of the element nitrogen through the air, soil, water and living things. Nitrogen is found in every protein and in genetic material, but most living things cannot use the nitrogen from the air directly. Only certain bacteria, and humans with their technology, can convert it.
wichtigste: Dry air consists of about 78 per cent nitrogen.
Rhizobia fix nitrogen from the air in the root nodules of legumes.
The enzyme nitrogenase splits the stable triple bond of the nitrogen molecule.
The reddish leghaemoglobin keeps the oxygen level low in the nodules and so protects the nitrogenase.
Cyanobacteria fix a lot of nitrogen from the air in waters and rice fields.
Lightning during thunderstorms turns nitrogen from the air into a reactive form without any living things.
Since the beginning of the 20th century, the Haber-Bosch process has produced ammonia from nitrogen in the air.
In Switzerland, most ammonia emissions come from farming.

abschnitte.text: Dry air consists of about **78 per cent** nitrogen, chemically N₂. In it, two nitrogen atoms are joined by a very strong **triple bond**. That is why this nitrogen is very unreactive, and plants and animals cannot use it directly. Yet all living things need nitrogen to build proteins and genetic material.

Some microbes can turn nitrogen from the air into ammonium; this is called **nitrogen fixation**. In this process, the enzyme **nitrogenase** splits the triple bond. In the root nodules of legumes such as clover, peas, beans and soya live **rhizobia**, which do this for the plant. The reddish leghaemoglobin keeps the oxygen low there, because oxygen would destroy the nitrogenase.

**Lightning** during thunderstorms also turns some nitrogen from the air into a reactive form, which reaches the soil with the rain. In waters and rice fields, **cyanobacteria** fix a large part of the nitrogen from the air. Plants then take up the nitrogen through their roots, mainly as nitrate or ammonium. Animals and humans get it by eating plants or other animals.

When living things die or excrete faeces and urine, bacteria break the remains down into ammonium again. Other bacteria turn ammonium into nitrate; this is called **nitrification**. In **denitrification**, yet other bacteria turn nitrate back into nitrogen gas. So the nitrogen is back in the air, and the cycle starts all over again.

At the beginning of the 20th century, the German chemists Fritz Haber and Carl Bosch developed the **Haber-Bosch process**. In it, **ammonia** is produced from nitrogen in the air and hydrogen under high pressure and heat. It is used to make artificial fertiliser, which has greatly increased harvests around the world. Experts estimate that without this fertiliser about half of today's humanity could not be fed.

abschnitte.titel: Too much of a good thing
abschnitte.text: When too much nitrogen gets into the environment, problems arise. Nitrate can get into the groundwater, and in lakes nutrients encourage too much algae growth. In Switzerland, most **ammonia emissions** come from farming, especially from the slurry and manure of farm animals. Ammonia harms forests, moors and species-rich meadows because it over-fertilises them.

begriffe.erklaerung: Turning nitrogen from the air into a form that living things can use.
An enzyme in some bacteria that can split nitrogen from the air.
Bacteria that live in the root nodules of legumes and fix nitrogen.
A sharp-smelling gas made of nitrogen and hydrogen.
A nitrogen compound that plants can easily take up as a nutrient.

gewusst: Farmers sow clover or beans to fertilise the soil with nitrogen in a natural way.
Fritz Haber received the Nobel Prize in Chemistry in 1918, and Carl Bosch in 1931.
If you cut open a root nodule of a pea, it is often pink inside.

teile.einleitung: The Swiss Polar Institute is a Swiss organisation that supports research in the coldest regions on Earth. It was founded in 2016 and funds projects in the Arctic, in Antarctica and in high mountains. Although Switzerland has no sea, it is very strong in ice and glacier research.
wichtigste: The Swiss Polar Institute was founded in 2016.
It funds Swiss research in the Arctic, Antarctica and high mountain regions.
Its founders include EPFL and ETH Zurich.
The businessman Frederik Paulsen played a major part in supporting its foundation.
Its first big expedition was the Antarctic Circumnavigation Expedition.
Switzerland has observer status in the Arctic Council.
Switzerland has joined the Antarctic Treaty.

abschnitte.text: The Swiss Polar Institute, SPI for short, was founded in **2016**. Its founding institutions include **EPFL** in Lausanne and **ETH Zurich**, as well as other research institutes. The Swedish businessman and polar traveller **Frederik Paulsen**, who lives in Switzerland, played a major part in supporting its foundation. The institute is based in Sion in Valais.

One of the SPI's main tasks is to fund Swiss **research projects** in polar and high mountain regions. It gives money to researchers and helps plan difficult journeys into the ice. It also brings together experts from different universities. Training young polar researchers is important to it as well.

Its first big undertaking was the **Antarctic Circumnavigation Expedition**, ACE for short. From December 2016 to March 2017, a Russian research ship sailed all the way round Antarctica. On board were researchers from many countries with more than 20 projects. They studied the sea, islands, animals, air and ice around the **southern continent**.

The SPI expressly also studies **high mountain regions** such as the Alps or the Himalayas. Glaciers and permafrost in the mountains react to climate change just as sensitively as the ice of the polar regions. That is why people sometimes speak of the **Third Pole**. With its glaciers, Switzerland has a lot of experience in this field.

As early as 1912, the Swiss researcher **Alfred de Quervain** and his team crossed the Greenland ice sheet. Switzerland has joined the **Antarctic Treaty**, which reserves Antarctica for peace and science. In the **Arctic Council**, where the countries around the North Pole work together, Switzerland has observer status. This allows it to contribute its knowledge without being an Arctic state itself.

begriffe.erklaerung: The region around the North Pole with a lot of sea ice and the Arctic Ocean.
The region around the South Pole with the ice-covered continent of Antarctica.
A planned research journey to an area that is hard to reach.
Ground that stays frozen all year round, including in high mountains.

gewusst: Switzerland has no sea, but it is one of the leading countries in glacier and ice research.
On the ACE expedition, the research ship sailed once all the way round Antarctica.
Because of its huge amounts of ice, the high mountain region is sometimes called the Third Pole.

teile.einleitung: Spitsbergen is a group of islands far to the north in the Arctic Ocean that belongs to Norway. In Norwegian it is called Svalbard, and it lies closer to the North Pole than almost any other inhabited place on Earth. More polar bears live here than in many other areas, and researchers from all over the world study the Arctic.
wichtigste: Spitsbergen, Svalbard in Norwegian, belongs to Norway.
The Dutch seafarer Willem Barentsz sighted the islands in 1596 and gave them their name.
The largest settlement is Longyearbyen, with the university centre UNIS.
Ny-Ålesund is almost entirely an international research village.
In the Svalbard Global Seed Vault seed samples from all over the world are stored.
An offshoot of the warm North Atlantic Current makes the sea on the west coast warmer.
In 1926 the airship Norge set off from Ny-Ålesund for the North Pole.

abschnitte.text: Spitsbergen lies between the Norwegian mainland and the North Pole, roughly between latitudes 74 and 81 degrees north. The largest island is also called Spitsbergen. More than half of the area is covered by **glaciers**, with pointed mountains rising between them. In summer the **midnight sun** shines for weeks, and in winter the dark **polar night** lasts for months.

On Spitsbergen live polar bears, Arctic foxes, walruses, seals and the small Svalbard reindeer. In summer millions of seabirds breed on the cliffs. Because of the polar bears you may only leave the settlements with protection, often with a rifle to scare them off. The animals are strictly protected, and large parts of the islands are national parks.

In 1596 Willem Barentsz saw the pointed mountain peaks and therefore called the land Spitsbergen, “pointed mountains”. After that whalers from many countries hunted in the waters, and later coal was mined. The **Svalbard Treaty** of 1920 gave the islands to Norway but allows citizens of the treaty countries to live and work there. That is why there is also a Russian mining settlement, Barentsburg. In 1926 the airship Norge with Roald Amundsen and Umberto Nobile set off from Ny-Ålesund for the North Pole.

In **Ny-Ålesund** scientists from many countries research the climate, ice and the atmosphere. In Longyearbyen there is the University Centre in Svalbard (UNIS), one of the northernmost universities in the world. Spitsbergen is warming much faster than the Earth's average, which is why it is especially important for climate research. The warm water of an offshoot of the **North Atlantic Current** often keeps the west coast free of ice for longer.

Since 2008 there has been the **Svalbard Global Seed Vault** near Longyearbyen, a vault deep inside the mountain. In it are stored seed samples of crops from all over the world, for example rice, wheat and beans. The permanent frost keeps the seeds cool even without electricity. In this way the variety of crop plants is to be preserved in case a disaster happens somewhere.

begriffe.erklaerung: The Norwegian name of the Spitsbergen group of islands.
A time in winter when the Sun does not rise all day.
A time in summer when the Sun does not set even at night.
Ground that stays frozen all year round.

gewusst: On Spitsbergen there are more snowmobiles than cars.
The name Svalbard means roughly “cold coast”.
Longyearbyen has a supermarket, a church and a school, although the town lies in the high Arctic.

teile.einleitung: The spallation neutron source SINQ is a large research facility at the Paul Scherrer Institute PSI in Villigen in the canton of Aargau. It produces neutrons with which researchers can look inside materials without destroying them.
wichtigste: SINQ is located at the Paul Scherrer Institute in Villigen in the canton of Aargau.
In spallation, fast protons knock neutrons out of heavy atomic nuclei.
The protons are supplied by a ring cyclotron with 590 MeV.
Unlike a research reactor, SINQ does not need a chain reaction.
SINQ supplies a continuous stream of neutrons.
A moderator slows down the fast neutrons.
Neutron radiography is used, for example, to make water in fuel cells visible.

abschnitte.text: SINQ stands for Swiss Spallation Neutron Source. It belongs to the **Paul Scherrer Institute**, the largest research institute for natural sciences and engineering in Switzerland. The facility has been in operation since the 1990s. Researchers from all over the world come to Villigen to experiment with **neutrons** here.

A large particle accelerator, the **ring cyclotron**, brings protons to an energy of 590 MeV. These very fast protons hit a target made of heavy atoms, for example lead. The atomic nuclei are smashed, and many neutrons fly out. This process is called **spallation**, from the English word for chipping off. Unlike in a nuclear reactor, no chain reaction is needed, and the facility stops at once when the beam is switched off.

The neutrons from spallation are much too fast for most experiments. That is why they fly through a **moderator** that slows them down, rather like a ball that bumps into other balls many times. At SINQ heavy water and very cold, liquid deuterium are among the materials used for this. A special feature is that SINQ supplies a **continuous** stream of neutrons, whereas many other spallation sources work in short pulses.

Neutrons are electrically neutral and can therefore get deep into materials. They are strongly scattered by **hydrogen**, so water or plastics can be made clearly visible with them. Because neutrons have a magnetic moment, they are also suitable for researching **magnetism**. In neutron radiography objects are scanned in a similar way to X-rays, but with a different result.

With **neutron radiography** you can see how water spreads in fuel cells or batteries. The inside of cultural treasures such as old bronze figures or swords can also be examined without damaging them. The proton beam at the PSI also produces **muons**, unstable elementary particles that are also used for materials research. In this way SINQ helps in the development of new materials, medicines and energy technology.

begriffe.erklaerung: An electrically neutral particle in the atomic nucleus.
The smashing of a heavy atomic nucleus by a very fast particle, which releases neutrons.
A material that slows down fast neutrons.
A particle accelerator in which particles get faster and faster on a spiral path.

gewusst: SINQ is one of the few spallation sources in the world that supplies neutrons continuously without breaks.
The proton accelerator at the PSI is one of the most powerful of its kind in the world.

teile.einleitung: Spider silk is the material from which spiders make their threads and webs. It is wafer-thin and yet, measured against its weight, stronger than steel. Researchers all over the world are trying to copy this wonder material artificially.
wichtigste: Spiders build their webs from spider silk.
The threads are made in silk glands in the spider's abdomen.
Spider silk is made of protein.
Measured against its weight, spider silk is stronger than steel.
A spider thread can stretch a lot without breaking.
A spider does not stick to its web, because it walks on threads that are not sticky.
Artificial spider silk could be used, for example, for threads in medicine.

abschnitte.text: In the spider's abdomen there are several **silk glands**. There the silk is at first a thick liquid. It comes out through small tubes, the **spinnerets**. Only when the spider pulls the thread out does it become solid. Many spiders can make different kinds of thread with different glands.

Spider silk is made of **protein**, just like our hair. The long protein chains lie partly in order and partly loosely next to each other. The ordered parts make the thread strong, the loose ones make it stretchy. A thread from a garden spider is much thinner than a human hair.

Measured against its weight, spider silk is **stronger than steel**. At the same time a thread can stretch considerably before it breaks. In this way a web can stop a fly or a bee that flies into it at speed without breaking. This mixture of strength and stretchiness is what makes spider silk so special.

With its web the spider catches **insects**, for example flies and midges. An orb web like that of the European garden spider has dry spoke threads and a sticky **capture spiral**. The spider walks mainly on the dry threads and so does not get stuck. Many orb-weaving spiders eat their old web and use the protein for a new one.

Spiders are hard to keep like silkworms, because they live alone and may eat one another. That is why researchers get bacteria or yeasts to produce the protein of spider silk. Artificial spider silk could be used for **stitches in medicine**, for light fabrics or for protective clothing. Because the body tolerates it well, it is especially interesting for stitching wounds.

Spiders do not use their silk only for webs. They let themselves down on a safety line and make protective cases for their eggs from it. Young spiders let the wind carry them away on a thread; this is called **ballooning**. In autumn the glittering threads can often be seen on meadows; in German this time is also called “Altweibersommer”, in English gossamer season.

begriffe.erklaerung: An organ in the spider's abdomen in which the liquid silk is made.
Small tubes on the abdomen from which the thread comes out.
An important building material of living things.
A round spider's web with spokes and a spiral, like a wheel.

gewusst: Darwin's bark spider in Madagascar stretches its webs across whole rivers.
In Madagascar a golden cloth was woven from the silk of over a million golden silk orb-weavers.
Young spiders can let the wind carry them many kilometres on a silk thread.

teile.einleitung: A titanium implant is a part made of the metal titanium that doctors put into the body. It replaces, for example, a tooth root or a hip joint, or it stabilises a broken bone. Titanium is especially suitable for this, because the body tolerates it very well and the bone can even grow onto it.
wichtigste: A thin oxide layer protects the surface of titanium and makes it well tolerated.
The direct growing together of bone and implant is called osseointegration.
The alloy Ti-6Al-4V is used particularly often.
With about 60 per cent of the density of steel, titanium is much lighter.
Because titanium is less stiff than steel, the bone is shielded less from load.
Titanium is not ferromagnetic, so people with titanium implants can usually have an MRI scan.
Zirconium dioxide is a metal-free alternative for dental implants.

abschnitte.text: An **implant** is an artificial part that stays in the body permanently. Titanium is used, for example, for artificial tooth roots, hip and knee joints, and screws and plates for broken bones. The cases of pacemakers are also often made of titanium. A dental implant is a small screw that is put into the jawbone and later carries a crown.

In air, titanium immediately forms a wafer-thin layer of **titanium oxide**. This layer is very stable and protects the metal from rust and corrosion. The body hardly recognises it as a foreign body, so there are rarely defence reactions. Titanium is also strong, but with about 60 per cent of the density of steel it is much lighter. The alloy **Ti-6Al-4V** is often used; as well as titanium it contains about 6 per cent aluminium and 4 per cent vanadium.

In the 1950s and 1960s the Swedish researcher Per-Ingvar Brånemark discovered that bone can grow firmly together with titanium. This growing together is called **osseointegration**. To make it work better, the surfaces are often blasted and etched so that they become rough. Bone cells get a better hold on the rough surface. With dental implants, healing usually takes from a few weeks to a few months.

Titanium is less stiff than steel; we say it has a lower **modulus of elasticity**. This is an advantage, because the bone then continues to carry part of the load. If the implant carried everything by itself, the bone next to it could become weaker. Titanium is also not ferromagnetic, so it is not attracted by magnets. That is why people with titanium implants can usually go into an MRI scanner.

Switzerland is an important country for implants. The company **Straumann** in Basel is one of the largest manufacturers of dental implants in the world. As a metal-free alternative, there are dental implants made of the ceramic **zirconium dioxide**, which are white like teeth. Very rarely a person is sensitive to titanium, and then ceramic can be a solution.

begriffe.erklaerung: An artificial part that is put into the body permanently.
The firm growing together of bone and an implant.
A mixture of several metals.
Strongly attracted by a magnet, like iron.
A thin protective layer that forms on the surface of a metal.

gewusst: Titanium was named after the Titans, giant figures from Greek mythology.
Brånemark discovered osseointegration rather by chance, when a titanium chamber could no longer be removed from a bone.
Titanium is also used for aircraft, glasses frames and watches.

teile.einleitung: Stem cells are special cells that can divide again and again and in doing so become quite different types of cell. They are, so to speak, the body's spare parts store. Because they can replace lost tissue, they are very exciting for medicine.
wichtigste: A stem cell can renew itself and develop into specialised cells.
Pluripotent stem cells can form all the cell types of the body, but not a whole organism.
Multipotent stem cells such as blood stem cells only form the cell types of a particular tissue.
In adults the blood stem cells are found in the bone marrow.
In 2006 Shinya Yamanaka turned mature body cells back into pluripotent stem cells.
To do this he originally used four transcription factors.
In 2012 Yamanaka shared the Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine with John Gurdon.
Organoids are three-dimensional mini-organs grown from stem cells.

abschnitte.text: Our body consists of trillions of cells, most of which have a fixed job, for example as skin, muscle or nerve cells. Stem cells, on the other hand, are not yet fixed. They have two important properties: they can **renew themselves** and develop into **specialised cells**. When a stem cell divides, one daughter cell often stays a stem cell while the other becomes specialised.

Stem cells differ in how many cell types they can form. **Pluripotent** stem cells can form all the cell types of the body, but not a whole organism. **Multipotent** stem cells can only form the cells of a particular tissue. Blood stem cells, for example, become red and white blood cells and platelets.

Adults also have stem cells; they are called **adult stem cells**. In the **bone marrow** billions of new blood cells are made from blood stem cells every day. In the skin and the lining of the gut, too, stem cells make sure that old cells are constantly replaced. The innermost layer of the gut renews itself in this way within a few days.

For a long time it was believed that a specialised cell could not go back. As early as the 1960s the British researcher **John Gurdon** showed with frog cells that the nucleus of a specialised cell still contains all the building plans. In 2006 the Japanese researcher **Shinya Yamanaka** turned mature body cells back into pluripotent stem cells with four transcription factors. These are called induced pluripotent stem cells, iPS cells for short, and both researchers received the Nobel Prize in 2012.

The best-known treatment is **blood stem cell transplantation**, for example for leukaemia, a form of blood cancer. In it, a sick person receives healthy blood stem cells from a suitable donor. In Switzerland you can register as a blood stem cell donor from the age of 18. Researchers are also working on using stem cells to replace diseased heart, nerve or eye cells.

**Organoids** can be grown from stem cells in the laboratory. These are tiny, three-dimensional mini-organs, for example small models of the gut, the liver or the brain. They can be used to study how diseases develop and how medicines work. In this way fewer animal experiments may be needed in future.

begriffe.erklaerung: A cell that can divide and become different cell types.
Able to form all the cell types of the body.
Able to form only the cell types of a particular tissue.
Soft tissue inside bones in which blood cells are made.
A mini-organ grown from stem cells in the laboratory.

gewusst: Thanks to stem cells, flatworms called planarians can grow a whole new worm from a small piece.
Plants also have stem cells; they are found, for example, in the tips of roots and shoots.
The axolotl, a salamander from Mexico, can grow back lost legs completely.

teile.einleitung: The will of Alfred Nobel is one of the most famous wills in the world. In it, the Swedish inventor and businessman decided that almost all his fortune should be used for prizes. His last will gave rise to the Nobel Prizes, which are still awarded every December today.
wichtigste: Alfred Nobel signed his will in Paris in 1895.
He set aside about 94 per cent of his fortune for the prizes.
The prizes were to go to those who had brought the greatest benefit to humankind.
The nationality of the prizewinners was to play no role.
Nobel died in San Remo in Italy in 1896.
As executor, the young engineer Ragnar Sohlman carried out the last will, even though relatives resisted.
In 1900 the Nobel Foundation was set up to manage the fortune.

abschnitte.text: **Alfred Nobel** was born in Stockholm in 1833. He was a chemist and inventor and became famous above all for **dynamite**, which he patented in 1867. With factories in many countries he became very rich. He spoke several languages, wrote poems and lived in Paris for a long time.

In 1888 Alfred's brother Ludvig died in Cannes. A French newspaper mixed up the brothers and reported Alfred's death. In the **obituary** he was described as a man who had become rich through explosives. This story is said to have made Nobel think about his reputation. However, it is not completely certain whether it really was the reason for his will.

On 27 November 1895 Nobel signed his will in **Paris**. In it he set aside about 94 per cent of his fortune for five prizes: physics, chemistry, physiology or medicine, literature and peace. The prizes were to go to those who had brought the greatest benefit to humankind in the previous year. He wrote expressly that **nationality** must play no role. The peace prize was to be awarded by a committee of the Norwegian parliament.

Nobel died in **San Remo** on 10 December 1896. His will came as a surprise to many, and some of his relatives fought against it. There was also criticism in Sweden, because the prizes were to be international. The engineer **Ragnar Sohlman**, only 26 years old, was one of the executors. He collected the fortune from several countries and, after several years, made sure that Nobel's wishes were carried out.

In 1900 the **Nobel Foundation** was set up to invest and manage the money. In 1901 the first Nobel Prizes were awarded. The award ceremony takes place every year on 10 December, the anniversary of Nobel's death, in Stockholm and, for the peace prize, in Oslo. The prize in economic sciences was not in the will but was founded by the Swedish central bank in 1968. Many researchers from Switzerland have since received a Nobel Prize too.

begriffe.erklaerung: A document in which someone sets out what is to happen to their property after their death.
A person who makes sure that a will is carried out exactly as written.
An organisation that manages a fortune for a particular purpose.
A newspaper article about the life of a person who has died.

gewusst: Nobel wrote his will by hand and without the help of a lawyer.
Because Nobel had never married and had no children, he was free to decide what happened to his fortune.
The original of the will is kept today in the archive of the Nobel Foundation in Stockholm.

teile.einleitung: In ecology, succession is the natural sequence in which plants and animals settle in a habitat one after another. In this way, bare rock or an abandoned meadow can turn into a forest over many years.
wichtigste: Succession is the sequence over time of communities of living things in one place.
In primary succession, ground that previously had no life is colonised.
In secondary succession, a community forms anew, for example when a pasture becomes overgrown with bushes.
Lichens are among the first pioneers on bare rock.
On the Swiss Central Plateau, a beech forest would usually develop without humans.
Primary succession can be observed well in front of retreating glaciers.
The volcanic islands of Krakatoa and Surtsey are famous examples of resettlement.

abschnitte.text: The word **succession** comes from the Latin succedere, to follow. It means that plants and animals replace one another in a place. First come undemanding **pioneer species**, and later bigger and more demanding species follow. At the end there is often a stable **climax community**, which does not change much for a long time. On the Swiss Central Plateau, without human interference, this would usually be a beech forest.

In **primary succession**, life begins on ground where nothing grew before, such as bare rock or fresh lava. **Lichens** and mosses are the first to settle. They slowly break down the rock, and with dead plant remains a thin layer of soil forms. Later grasses, herbs, shrubs and finally trees can grow on it.

Because the glaciers in the Alps are retreating, new bare areas appear every year. In the **glacier foreland** you can observe primary succession as if along a timeline. Close to the ice only a few pioneer plants grow, further away small willows and larches, and further still a proper forest. At the Morteratsch Glacier in the Engadine, signs along the footpath show where the ice was in which year.

In **secondary succession**, the soil is already there, but the old plant cover has been destroyed or is no longer used. An example is an abandoned pasture that gradually becomes overgrown with bushes and turns into forest. After the storm **Lothar** in December 1999, large areas of forest in Switzerland were flattened. On some of these areas, researchers have since been observing how the forest grows back by itself. **Silting up**, in which a lake gradually fills with plants and mud, is also a form of succession.

In 1883 a huge volcanic eruption destroyed a large part of the island of **Krakatoa** in Indonesia, and all life there was wiped out. Researchers then observed how plants and animals settled on the island again. In 1963 the volcanic island of **Surtsey** rose out of the sea off Iceland. Only a few researchers are allowed to set foot on it, so that the natural colonisation can be followed undisturbed. Seeds and animals reached the island with the wind, with the sea and with birds.

begriffe.erklaerung: A living thing that is one of the first to settle in a new habitat.
A stable community of living things at the end of a succession, often a forest.
A partnership of a fungus and an alga that can grow even on bare rock.
The gradual filling of a lake with plants and sediment.

gewusst: Surtsey has been a UNESCO World Heritage Site since 2008, because the development of life on new land can be observed there.
Without mowing and grazing, most meadows in Switzerland would turn into forest within a few decades.

teile.einleitung: A robot vacuum cleaner is a small, round device that drives through the flat by itself and vacuums the floor. With sensors it recognises obstacles, stairs and walls. When its battery is flat, it drives back to its charging station on its own.
wichtigste: A robot vacuum cleaner vacuums the floor by itself.
Most robot vacuums are round and flat.
A side brush gets the dust out of corners and edges.
It collects the dirt in a dust container.
Sensors recognise steps, so it usually does not fall down the stairs.
Modern robot vacuums make a map of the flat.
An ordinary robot vacuum cannot climb stairs.

abschnitte.text: A robot vacuum cleaner is usually round and only about as high as a hand is wide, so that it fits under beds and sofas. Underneath, one or two **side brushes** turn and push dust from the corners to the middle. There a main brush picks up the dirt, and a fan sucks it into the **dust container**. The robot is driven by two wheels and a battery.

At the front the robot has a bumper that notices when it drives into a piece of furniture. Underneath, **cliff sensors** point downwards with invisible light and recognise when the floor suddenly ends, for example at a staircase. Many models also have a rotating laser or a camera. With these they measure distances and recognise walls, doors and obstacles.

Simple robots drive back and forth at random until they have covered the room often enough. Modern devices use their sensors to make a **map** of the flat. In this way they know where they have already been and drive neatly lane by lane. Using an app you can choose rooms or set no-go zones that the robot should not enter.

When the battery gets low, the robot looks for its **charging station** and docks there by itself. Some stations even empty the dust container automatically into a bigger bag. Even so, now and then you have to remove hair from the brushes and clean the filter. Some models can also mop.

One of the first robot vacuums on sale was the Trilobite from Electrolux in 2001; in 2002 came the well-known Roomba from the company iRobot. Today robot vacuums are found in many households, in Switzerland too. But they have limits: they cannot climb stairs, and cables, socks or toys lying around can block them. That is why it is best to tidy the floor before starting.

begriffe.erklaerung: A component that measures something in the surroundings, for example distance or light.
A sensor on the underside that recognises steps and edges.
The place where the robot recharges its battery.
A small, turning brush at the edge that gets dust out of corners.

gewusst: Electrolux's first robot vacuum was called Trilobite, after the prehistoric sea creatures.
Some cats like to ride around the flat on robot vacuums.
The company iRobot, which makes the Roomba, had earlier also developed robots for use in dangerous areas.

teile.einleitung: The sample size states how many people or things are included in a study. After all, you cannot always ask every person or test every screw in a factory. How large a sample has to be for the result to be reliable is one of the most important questions in statistics.
wichtigste: The sample size is abbreviated with the letter n.
With sample size planning, you calculate before a study starts how many participants are needed to prove an effect.
The smaller the effect you want to prove, the larger the sample has to be.
In clinical trials, researchers often aim for a statistical power of 80 per cent.
According to the law of large numbers, the mean approaches the expected value as the sample grows.
For a margin of error of 2 percentage points you need about 2400 respondents.
A biased selection is not repaired by a large sample.

abschnitte.text: A **sample** is a selection from a larger group, the population. The **sample size** n says how many elements this selection includes. From the sample you want to draw conclusions about the whole group, for example in surveys, medicine trials or quality checks. As a rule, the larger n is, the more accurate the result.

If you toss a coin only ten times, it can easily land on heads seven times. If you toss it a thousand times, the proportion is almost always close to half. This is described by the **law of large numbers**: as the sample grows, the mean approaches the expected value. Small samples, on the other hand, are prone to random outliers.

Surveys often state a **margin of error**. For a margin of error of 2 percentage points, with 95 per cent certainty and a proportion of around 50 per cent, you need about 2400 respondents. For 3 percentage points, roughly 1000 respondents are enough. If you want to halve the margin of error, you have to make the sample about four times as large.

Before a medical study, **sample size planning** is used to calculate how many participants are needed. The smaller the expected effect, the more participants are needed. Researchers often aim for a **statistical power** of 80 per cent, meaning a good chance of actually finding a real effect. Because some participants drop out, more are planned for: if you need 200 and expect 20 per cent to drop out, you include at least 250.

In 1936 the US magazine **Literary Digest** surveyed millions of people and received over two million replies. It still predicted the wrong winner of the election, because the people asked were mainly better-off. The pollster George Gallup got it right with a much smaller but well-chosen sample. The lesson: a biased selection is not repaired by size.
