Small studies that achieve a significant result often **overestimate** the size of the effect. With few participants, only effects that happen to be large reach the threshold of significance. Later, larger studies therefore often find smaller effects. That is why experts prefer to rely on several large studies rather than on a single small one.

begriffe.erklaerung: A selection from a larger group that is studied.
The whole group that you want to know something about.
The range in which the true value probably lies.
The probability of actually detecting an effect that really exists in a study.
A result that very probably did not come about just by chance.

gewusst: Whether you want to describe 10,000 or 10 million people makes hardly any difference to the sample size needed.
In the census, people used to try to count really everyone, a so-called full survey.
In Switzerland, the Federal Statistical Office today adds sample surveys to its register data.

teile.einleitung: Tim Berners-Lee is a British computer scientist and physicist who is regarded as the inventor of the World Wide Web. He developed it in 1989 and 1990 at the CERN research centre near Geneva. Thanks to his idea, today you can open web pages with a click.
wichtigste: Tim Berners-Lee is regarded as the inventor of the World Wide Web.
He was born in London in 1955.
The web was created at CERN near Geneva, that is, in Switzerland, on the border with France.
In 1989 he wrote a proposal for a linked information system.
He invented HTML, HTTP and web addresses.
In 1993 the web was released free of charge for everyone.
In 1994 he founded the World Wide Web Consortium, W3C for short.

abschnitte.text: Timothy Berners-Lee was born in London on 8 June 1955. His parents both worked on one of the first computers that could be bought. He studied physics at the University of Oxford. After that he worked as a software developer, among other places at **CERN**, the European Organization for Nuclear Research near Geneva.

Thousands of researchers from all over the world worked at CERN, and their information was scattered over many computers. In March 1989 Berners-Lee suggested linking documents with one another through **hyperlinks**. His boss is said to have written on it “vague but exciting”. In 1990 he developed the system further together with the Belgian Robert Cailliau.

Berners-Lee invented three important things: the language **HTML** for web pages, the transfer method **HTTP** and the web address, the URL. At the end of 1990, the first web server and the first browser, which was called “WorldWideWeb”, ran on his NeXT computer. The world's first web page was at the address info.cern.ch. It explained what the World Wide Web is and how to use it.

On 30 April 1993, CERN released the technology of the web **free of charge** for everyone. Berners-Lee never wanted to become rich from it but to share knowledge. That is exactly why the web spread very quickly all over the world. In 1994 he founded the **World Wide Web Consortium** (W3C), which still sets common rules for the web today.

In 2004 he was knighted by the British Queen, which is why he is also called Sir Tim Berners-Lee. In 2016 he received the **Turing Award**, a kind of Nobel Prize for computer science. He was honoured at the opening of the 2012 Olympic Games in London. The message “This is for everyone” appeared during the ceremony.

Berners-Lee campaigns for the web to remain open, free and accessible to everyone. He warns against fake news and against a few large companies collecting too much data. That is why he works on ideas that let people decide about their own **data**. It is important to know that the internet as a network of computers already existed before; he invented the web, which runs on it.

begriffe.erklaerung: The network of linked web pages that you look at with a browser.
A clickable reference that leads to another page.
The language in which web pages are written.
A program with which you can display web pages.
The European Organization for Nuclear Research near Geneva.

gewusst: On the first web server there was a note warning people not to switch the computer off.
You can still look at the world's first web page today at info.cern.ch.
So the World Wide Web was invented in Switzerland, more precisely at CERN in Meyrin near Geneva.

teile.einleitung: A tally chart is a simple way of keeping track while counting, by making a mark for each thing you count. Because you always group five marks into a bundle, you can quickly read off the result at the end.
wichtigste: With a tally chart you can count along quickly.
You make four upright marks and draw the fifth one across them.
This creates bundles of five, which you can count more quickly.
For the number 10 you need two bundles of five.
The number 7 is one bundle of five and two single marks.
Two bundles of five and three marks make 13.
Tally marks are among the oldest ways of recording numbers.

abschnitte.text: A **tally chart** helps you count things that come past one after another. For each thing you make an upright mark. After four marks you draw the fifth one **across** them, which creates a **bundle of five**. Then you start a new bundle next to it.

Instead of counting each mark separately, you count the bundles in steps of five: 5, 10, 15 and so on. Then you add the remaining single marks. So three bundles of five and one mark make 16. If Lea has four bundles of five while counting red cars, she has seen 20 red cars. Five is handy because we have five fingers on one hand.

Tally charts are used in traffic counts, for counting birds or for a vote in class. If Tim counts 8 blackbirds and 12 sparrows in the garden, he can see straight away in his chart that there are 4 more sparrows. When playing the card game Jass, points are often written down with marks too. A tally chart can then easily be turned into a **table** or a bar chart.

Tens of thousands of years ago, people were already carving notches into bones, probably to count something. A famous example is the **Ishango bone** from Central Africa with many carved notches. In the Middle Ages, people in Switzerland also used the **tally stick**, on which debts were recorded with notches. This is where the German saying “etwas auf dem Kerbholz haben” (to have something on the tally stick, meaning to have done something wrong) comes from.

Tally charts do not look the same everywhere. In China, Japan and Korea, people often write the character 正 when counting, which is made of exactly five strokes. In other countries, some people draw a square with a diagonal, which also makes five strokes. But the idea is the same everywhere: you combine marks into **groups**.

begriffe.erklaerung: A counting aid in which you make a mark for each thing you count.
Four upright marks with one mark across them, five altogether.
A wooden stick into which people used to carve notches to count debts.
A picture in which amounts are shown as bars of different heights.

gewusst: The Roman numerals I, II, III and V probably go back to old tally marks and notches.
Prisoners in films often count their days with tally marks on the wall.

teile.einleitung: A transistor is a tiny electronic component that can switch or amplify electric current. It was invented in 1947 and is regarded as one of the most important inventions of the 20th century. Without transistors there would be no computers, smartphones or games consoles as we know them.
wichtigste: The first working transistor was built in 1947 at Bell Labs in the USA.
It was made of the semiconductor germanium.
Bardeen, Brattain and Shockley received the Nobel Prize in Physics for it in 1956.
Transistors replaced the large, hot vacuum tubes.
A transistor can switch and amplify current.
The control terminal of a MOSFET is called the gate.
Doping creates n-type and p-type layers in silicon.
Today's computer chips contain billions of transistors.

abschnitte.text: A transistor is a component made of a **semiconductor**, usually silicon. It normally has three terminals. With a small current or a small voltage at one terminal, you can control a larger current between the other two. In this way it works like a switch without moving parts or like an amplifier.

Semiconductors conduct electricity less well than metal but better than an insulator. **Doping**, the targeted introduction of foreign atoms, creates n-type and p-type layers. In the most common type today, the **MOSFET**, the terminals are called gate, source and drain. A voltage at the gate opens or closes a conducting channel, similar to how a tap controls the flow of water.

In December 1947 John Bardeen and Walter Brattain built the first working transistor from germanium at **Bell Labs** in the USA. Their colleague William Shockley developed an improved design shortly afterwards. In 1956 the three received the Nobel Prize in Physics together. Bardeen later even received a second Nobel Prize in Physics for a different discovery.

Before that, electronic circuits needed **vacuum tubes**, which were large, used a lot of electricity and got hot. Transistors were much smaller and more reliable, and as early as the 1950s there were portable transistor radios. In 1958 Jack Kilby built one of the first **integrated circuits**, in which several components sit on one piece of semiconductor. For this he received the Nobel Prize in Physics in 2000.

Modern processors in computers and smartphones contain many billions of transistors on an area the size of a fingernail. The individual transistors are so small that they can only be seen with electron microscopes. Each one switches billions of times a second between on and off, that is, between 1 and 0. From this come all the calculations, images and games that a computer processes.

begriffe.erklaerung: A substance such as silicon whose conductivity can be controlled in a targeted way.
The targeted introduction of foreign atoms into a semiconductor.
An older, large glass component that was used for amplifying and switching before the transistor.
A chip on which many electronic components sit together.

gewusst: The transistor is the component that humanity has made in the greatest numbers.
The first transistor was about as big as the palm of a hand; today's are a thousand times thinner than a hair.
The name transistor is made up of the English words “transfer” and “resistor”.

teile.einleitung: A synapse is the point of contact between two nerve cells or between a nerve cell and a muscle cell. Here a signal is passed on from one cell to the next, usually with the help of chemical messengers. Without synapses we could neither think nor move nor learn anything.
wichtigste: A synapse connects two nerve cells or a nerve cell with a muscle cell.
Between the two cells there is a tiny gap, the synaptic cleft.
The messengers are called neurotransmitters and are stored in small vesicles at the end of the axon.
Acetylcholine transmits signals from the nerves to the skeletal muscles.
Dopamine is closely linked to the brain's reward system, while GABA mainly has an inhibiting effect.
The term “synapse” was coined by Charles Sherrington at the end of the 19th century.
There are about 100 trillion synapses in the human brain.

abschnitte.text: Nerve cells, also called **neurons**, pass on information as electrical signals. Every nerve cell has a long extension, the **axon**, through which it sends out signals. At the end of the axon is the synapse, where the signal is handed over to the next cell. A single nerve cell can be connected to other cells by thousands of synapses.

When an electrical signal arrives at the end of the axon, small **vesicles** merge with the cell wall. They release their messengers into the **synaptic cleft**. This gap is only about 20 to 40 millionths of a millimetre wide. On the other side, the messengers dock onto matching docking sites, the **receptors**, and trigger a new signal there. Afterwards the messengers are quickly broken down or taken back up.

There are dozens of different **neurotransmitters** with different tasks. **Acetylcholine** makes our muscles contract when the brain gives the command. **Dopamine** plays a role in joy, motivation and reward. GABA slows the nerve cells down and so makes sure that the brain is not overstimulated. Serotonin affects mood and sleep, among other things.

Synapses are not fixed but can become stronger or weaker. This ability is called **synaptic plasticity**. When you practise something often, the connections involved in the brain become stronger. Synapses that are rarely used, on the other hand, can be broken down again. This is how our memory is formed, and how we learn, for example, to ride a bike or learn vocabulary.

The British researcher **Charles Sherrington** gave the point of contact the name synapse in 1897, after a Greek word for “to join”. Before that, the Spaniard Santiago Ramón y Cajal had shown with the microscope that nerve cells are individual cells. Only with the **electron microscope** in the 1950s could the synaptic cleft really be seen. Several Nobel Prizes have been awarded for discoveries about the synapse.

Many medicines work directly at the synapses, for example medicines against pain, anxiety or depression. Some **poisons** also act here, for example the arrow poison curare, which blocks the transmission to the muscles. In Parkinson's disease, dopamine is lacking in the brain. That is why research into synapses is very important for medicine.

begriffe.erklaerung: A nerve cell that receives and passes on signals.
The long extension of a nerve cell through which it sends out signals.
A chemical messenger that transmits a signal at the synapse.
The tiny gap between two cells at a synapse.
A docking site to which only a matching messenger can bind, like a key in a lock.

gewusst: With about 100 trillion synapses, the brain has far more connections than there are stars in our Milky Way.
At a chemical synapse, a signal needs only about a thousandth of a second to cross the gap.
As well as chemical synapses, there are also electrical synapses, in which the current flows directly from cell to cell.

teile.einleitung: A vacuum cleaner is an electrical appliance that sucks dust and dirt off the floor with a stream of air. Today it can be found in almost every household. A good hundred years ago, vacuum cleaning was still an invention that amazed people.
wichtigste: A vacuum cleaner is driven by an electric motor.
The dust ends up in a bag or a container.
A filter makes sure that the dust does not fly out again.
Before there were vacuum cleaners, people cleaned with brooms and carpet beaters.
In 1901 the Englishman Hubert Cecil Booth built a large vacuum cleaner.
A robot vacuum is a small, round vacuum cleaner that drives through the flat by itself.
A small vacuum cleaner without a cable that you hold in your hand is called a handheld vacuum.

abschnitte.text: In a vacuum cleaner an **electric motor** drives a fast-turning fan. The fan pushes air out of the appliance, which creates **low pressure** inside. Air from outside flows in through the nozzle and hose, and as it does so it carries dust and crumbs with it. The dirt stays in a bag or container, and the air flows out again.

A **filter** also holds back fine dust so that it does not fly back into the air in the room. Especially fine filters, called HEPA filters, are important for people with allergies. Bagless vacuum cleaners make the air swirl round quickly, so that the dust is flung out by centrifugal force. The Briton James Dyson made such appliances well known in the 1990s.

In the past people swept the floor with a **broom** and hung carpets outside over a bar. There they beat them with a **carpet beater** until the dust flew out. That was hard work and stirred up a lot of dust. At the end of the 19th century there were the first carpet sweepers with brushes and devices with hand pumps.

In 1901 the English engineer **Hubert Cecil Booth** built a large motorised vacuum cleaner in London. The machine stood on a horse-drawn cart in the street, and long hoses led through the windows into the house. A little later the American James Murray Spangler invented a portable electric vacuum cleaner, and from 1908 the company Hoover made it famous. The Swedish company Electrolux also brought vacuum cleaners for households onto the market early on.

Today there are **robot vacuums** that drive through the flat with sensors and avoid obstacles. Cordless vacuum cleaners and small **handheld vacuums** work without a cable and are quickly to hand. For some years there have been rules in Europe that limit the electricity used by vacuum cleaners. That is why modern appliances clean almost as well as older ones with fewer watts.

Before vacuuming you should clear small **toys**, socks and cables off the floor. Otherwise they get sucked in or block the hose. If the bag is full or the filter is blocked, the appliance sucks less well and has to be emptied or cleaned. With a narrow crevice tool you can also reach corners and cracks.

begriffe.erklaerung: A state in which the air pressure is lower than in the surroundings.
A device that moves air quickly.
A sieve of fine material that holds back dust.
A small, self-driving vacuum cleaner with sensors.

gewusst: Hubert Cecil Booth is said to have tested his idea by sucking through a handkerchief on the cushion of a chair.
In English people often simply say “to hoover” for vacuuming, after the company Hoover.
Many robot vacuums use sensors to make a map of the flat so that they can find their way.

teile.einleitung: The sunflower is a large, bright yellow plant whose head is reminiscent of a sun. It comes from North America and is important worldwide today for oil, bird food and as decoration in the garden.
wichtigste: The sunflower originally comes from North America.
In the garden it often grows about 1 to 3 metres tall.
Its large head is made up of many small flowers.
The seeds are arranged in spirals in the head.
Young sunflowers turn their heads with the Sun.
Flowering sunflowers mostly face east.
Oil is pressed from the seeds.

abschnitte.text: The sunflower has a strong, hairy stem and large heart-shaped leaves. In the garden it often grows 1 to 3 metres tall. Its head is not really a single flower but an **inflorescence** made of many small flowers. Around the edge sit the large yellow ray florets, and in the middle hundreds of tiny **disc florets**, which later become the seeds. That is why it belongs to the daisy family, like daisies and dandelions.

The seeds are arranged in the head in **spirals** that run to the left and to the right. If you count the spirals, you often find numbers such as 34 and 55. These numbers belong to the **Fibonacci sequence**, in which each number is the sum of the two before it. In this way as many seeds as possible fit on the head without gaps.

During the day young sunflowers turn their heads from east to west and so follow the Sun. At night they turn back to the east again. This movement is called **heliotropism**. When the plant flowers, the head usually stays facing east. Researchers found out that in this way the flowers warm up faster in the morning and attract more bees.

The sunflower comes from **North America**, where Indigenous peoples grew it thousands of years ago. Spanish sailors brought it to Europe in the 16th century. At first it was only an ornamental plant; later it was grown above all in Russia as an **oil crop**. Today Russia and Ukraine are among the largest growing countries.

**Sunflower oil** is pressed from the seeds and used for cooking, frying and margarine. Roasted seeds are eaten as a snack or in bread. In winter tits and other birds like to eat sunflower seeds from the bird table. In Switzerland, too, you can see sunflower fields in summer, and many people pick flowers there themselves.

begriffe.erklaerung: Many small flowers that together look like one single large flower.
A plant family with basket-shaped flower heads, such as the sunflower and the dandelion.
The movement of a plant that follows the Sun.
The number sequence 1, 1, 2, 3, 5, 8, 13 and so on, in which each number is the sum of the two before it.

gewusst: A single large sunflower head can carry over a thousand seeds.
The scientific name Helianthus means sunflower in Greek.

teile.einleitung: Thermoluminescence dating is a method that can be used to determine the age of fired pottery, bricks or heated stones. It is based on the fact that certain crystals store radiation from the ground and give it off as a faint glow when heated. Archaeologists use it to date finds that are thousands of years old.
wichtigste: Thermoluminescence dating is used to determine the age of fired or heated finds.
The age is the palaeodose divided by the dose rate.
The radiation in the ground comes from uranium, thorium and potassium.
From about 500 degrees Celsius the signal is largely erased.
Unfired mud bricks can hardly be dated, because they were never strongly heated.
The water content of the soil must be taken into account, because water weakens radiation.
The accuracy is typically about 5 to 10 per cent of the age.

abschnitte.text: **Thermoluminescence** means “glowing through heat”. In minerals such as **quartz** and feldspar, natural radiation traps electrons in tiny defects of the crystal. When heated, they are released again and give off a faint light. The more radiation a crystal has absorbed, the more brightly it glows.

abschnitte.titel: The clock is set to zero
abschnitte.text: When a clay vessel is fired in a kiln, all the stored electrons are released. From about 500 degrees Celsius the signal is largely erased, and the **clock** is back at zero. After that, the shard may lie in the ground for thousands of years and collect new radiation. That is why unfired mud bricks can hardly be dated: they were never strongly heated.

The radiation that adds up in a buried shard comes from natural substances such as **uranium**, **thorium** and **potassium** in the ground. How much radiation arrives per year is called the **dose rate**. The water content of the soil also counts, because water weakens the radiation. That is why experts measure the surroundings of the find very precisely.

In the laboratory, the total stored radiation, the **palaeodose**, is determined by comparing the glow with samples that have been artificially irradiated. The age is then the palaeodose divided by the dose rate. Example: 15 grays divided by 2.5 milligrays per year gives 6000 years. The accuracy is typically about 5 to 10 per cent of the age.

The method was developed from the 1950s and 1960s, among other places at the University of Oxford. It is used to date **pottery**, fired bricks, hearths and heated flints from the Stone Age. Art dealers and museums also use it to detect **fakes** of ancient clay figures. A related method, optically stimulated luminescence, dates sand that was last exposed to sunlight.

begriffe.erklaerung: A glow that is not produced by heat, as in a flame, but by stored energy.
The total radiation that a sample has absorbed since it was last heated.
How much radiation a sample absorbs per year.
The unit for the absorbed dose of radiation, abbreviated Gy.

gewusst: Thermoluminescence has already exposed supposedly ancient clay figures as modern fakes.
The natural radiation in the ground is so weak that it is harmless to humans, but over thousands of years it leaves measurable traces.
Even flints that accidentally fell into a campfire tens of thousands of years ago can be dated in this way.

teile.einleitung: In German the word “teilen” has two meanings: in maths it means splitting an amount into equal parts, which is also called dividing. In everyday life it means sharing, giving others some of what you have. Both have to do with fairness and living together.
wichtigste: When you share fairly, everyone gets the same amount.
If you share 6 jelly babies fairly with a friend, each of you gets 3.
If you divide 12 cherries among 4 children, each one gets 3.
A toy that everyone wants can be shared by taking turns.
In a library, many people share the same books.
When several people share a car, it is called car sharing.
Some animals, such as vampire bats, also share their food.

abschnitte.text: In maths, dividing is also called **division**. The calculation 12 : 4 = 3 means: 12 cherries shared fairly among 4 children gives 3 cherries per child. The number being divided is called the **dividend**, the number you divide by is called the divisor, and the result is called the **quotient**. Dividing is the opposite of multiplying, because 3 times 4 makes 12 again.

abschnitte.titel: When it does not work out exactly
abschnitte.text: Not every division works out exactly. If you share 7 jelly babies between 2 children, each gets 3, and 1 jelly baby is left over; this is the **remainder**. You can also cut the last one in half, and then each gets three and a half. By the way, you cannot divide by zero at all; it is not allowed in maths.

In everyday life, sharing means giving others something or using something together. If everyone wants the same toy, you can **take turns**. It is fair when everyone gets the same amount or everyone gets a turn for the same length of time. The German saying “Geteilte Freude ist doppelte Freude” (shared joy is double joy) says that experiencing things together makes people happy.

In a **library**, many people borrow the same books one after another. In Switzerland there are also **toy libraries**, where you can borrow games and toys. In **car sharing**, several people share a car; in Switzerland the cooperative Mobility is well known for this. Using things together saves money, space and raw materials.

Animals sometimes share too. **Vampire bats** in Central and South America give some of their food to hungry members of their group. They mainly help those who have helped them in the past. Chimpanzees also share food, and ants feed one another. Researchers see in this the roots of cooperation and fairness.

begriffe.erklaerung: Calculating by dividing, for example 12 : 4 = 3.
The result of a division.
What is left over when a division does not work out exactly.
Several people use the same car together.
A place where you can borrow games and toys; in Switzerland it is called a “Ludothek”.

gewusst: A vampire bat can survive only a few nights without food, so sharing is vital for it.
The sign “:” for dividing is usual in Switzerland; in other countries people often write “÷” or a fraction line.
Even small children notice very clearly when something is shared out unfairly.

teile.einleitung: Synthetic biology is a young field of research between biology, chemistry and engineering. Researchers try to design and rebuild living things such as bacteria or yeasts in a targeted way so that they gain new properties. In doing so they often work like engineers who put a machine together from components.
wichtigste: The aim of synthetic biology is to design and build biological systems with new properties in a targeted way.
In 2010 Craig Venter's team was the first to run a bacterium with genetic material made entirely in the laboratory.
The minimal cell JCVI-syn3.0, presented in 2016, managed with only 473 genes.
Modified baker's yeast is used to produce a precursor of the malaria drug artemisinin.
The repressilator of 2000 was an artificial gene circuit that produces oscillations in bacteria.
Students from all over the world compete in the iGEM competition, including teams from ETH Zurich.
A kill switch is meant to make sure that artificially modified organisms die outside the laboratory.

abschnitte.text: In synthetic biology, genes are seen as **building blocks** that can be combined. A gene is a section of DNA that contains a set of instructions, usually for a protein. Researchers write new DNA sections on the computer and have them made in the laboratory. They then put these into cells so that the cells carry out new tasks. Unlike classic genetic engineering, whole **gene circuits** or even whole genomes are often newly designed.

In 2000 Michael Elowitz and Stanislas Leibler presented the **repressilator**. In it, three genes inhibit each other in a circle, so that the bacteria regularly blink on and off. At the same time, a genetic toggle switch was built that can switch between two states. Such circuits work in a similar way to electronic circuits in a computer.

In 2010 **Craig Venter's** team put genetic material assembled in the laboratory into a bacterium, and the cell lived and divided. In 2016 came the **minimal cell** JCVI-syn3.0 with only 473 genes, fewer than any other known free-living organism. In the international project Sc2.0, the entire genetic material of baker's yeast is being rebuilt. In 2019 researchers presented hachimoji DNA, which contains eight different bases instead of four.

A well-known example is the malaria drug **artemisinin**, which is originally obtained from sweet wormwood. Modified baker's yeast can produce a precursor of it, which makes the supply less dependent on harvests. Other aims are bacteria that detect diseases, break down pollutants or produce fuels and plastics. Insulin, too, has long been produced by modified microorganisms.

In the **iGEM** competition, students build their own biological systems from standardised building blocks. Teams from all over the world, including from ETH Zurich, present their projects every year. In Switzerland, for example, the ETH Department of Biosystems in Basel does research in synthetic biology. In this way young researchers learn how to plan biology like an engineering project.

Because new living things are created, **biosafety** is very important. A built-in **kill switch** is meant to make organisms die if they escape from the laboratory. Many people discuss how far we may change life and who sets the rules. In Switzerland, strict laws apply to work with modified organisms.

begriffe.erklaerung: A section of DNA that contains instructions for the cell.
The entire genetic material of a living thing.
Several genes that control each other like the parts of an electronic circuit.
A cell with as few genes as possible that can just about stay alive.
A built-in self-destruct switch that makes modified organisms die outside the laboratory.

gewusst: Watermarks with names and quotations in DNA code were even built into the artificial genetic material of Venter's bacterium so that it could be identified.
The minimal cell JCVI-syn3.0 has fewer genes than many natural bacteria that live as parasites.
Several hundred teams from dozens of countries take part in iGEM every year.

teile.einleitung: Table salt, also called cooking salt, is the salt we season our food with. Chemically it consists almost entirely of sodium chloride. In the past salt was so valuable that it was called “white gold”.
wichtigste: Table salt is also called cooking salt and consists mainly of sodium chloride.
It is obtained from the sea or from salt deposits deep in the Earth.
In Switzerland iodine is often added to table salt.
In the past people used salt to preserve meat, when there were no fridges yet.
Salt attracts water, which is why cucumber slices with salt give off water.
In the canton of Vaud you can visit a salt mine in Bex.
Too much salt is unhealthy, but the body needs a small amount.

abschnitte.text: Chemically, table salt consists almost entirely of **sodium chloride**, a compound of the elements sodium and chlorine. It forms small, cube-shaped **crystals** that can be seen well with a magnifying glass. Salt dissolves easily in water. Our body needs it for the nerves, the muscles and the water balance.

**Sea salt** is obtained by letting the Sun evaporate seawater in shallow basins. **Rock salt** comes from layers of salt in the ground that formed millions of years ago from seas that dried up. In Switzerland water is pumped down deep for this; the salt dissolves and the brine is brought back up. The Swiss salt works obtain salt in Riburg and Schweizerhalle near Basel and in Bex.

In the salt mine at **Bex** in the canton of Vaud salt has been mined since the 17th century. Visitors ride into the mountain on a small train and walk through long tunnels. Since 1922 **iodine** has been added to table salt in Switzerland, because many people had too little of it and got a goitre as a result. Swiss salt often also contains fluoride, which protects the teeth.

Salt makes food tastier and strengthens the flavour. It is added to the water for spaghetti mainly for the taste. If you sprinkle salt on cucumber slices, the salt crystals draw water out of the cells and the cucumbers go soft. For crafts you can knead a **salt dough** from flour, salt and water and bake it hard in the oven.

Before there were fridges, people preserved meat and fish with salt, because bacteria grow badly in salty surroundings. Salt was therefore very precious and was traded along long salt roads. The word **salary** for wages goes back to the Latin word for salt. In winter salt is spread on roads, because salt water only freezes at lower temperatures.

begriffe.erklaerung: The chemical name for cooking salt, a compound of sodium and chlorine.
A plant in which salt is obtained.
Water in which a great deal of salt is dissolved.
A substance the body needs in small amounts for the thyroid gland.

gewusst: Switzerland was one of the first countries in the world to add iodine to salt.
Experts recommend at most about 5 grams of salt a day for adults, roughly one teaspoon.
The Dead Sea is so salty that you float on the surface almost without moving.

teile.einleitung: The South Pole is the southernmost point on Earth. It lies in the middle of Antarctica on a huge sheet of ice, and from there every direction leads north. It is one of the coldest and loneliest places in the world.
wichtigste: The South Pole lies on the ice of Antarctica, about 2800 metres above sea level.
From the South Pole, you go north in every direction.
It is colder at the South Pole than at the North Pole, about minus 50 degrees on average over the year.
Roald Amundsen was the first to reach the South Pole, in 1911.
The Briton Robert Scott reached it in 1912 and died on the way back.
The marker is put in a new place every year, because the ice beneath it moves.
For photos there is a shiny ball surrounded by flags.

abschnitte.text: The geographic South Pole is the point where the imaginary **Earth's axis** passes through the surface in the south. It lies on a wide, flat plateau of **Antarctica**, far from the coast. Below the surface there is a layer of ice about 2700 metres thick, which is why the pole is about 2800 metres high. All lines of longitude meet here, and every step leads north.

It is much colder at the South Pole than at the North Pole, because it lies high up and is not surrounded by sea. On average over the year the temperature is about minus 50 degrees, and in winter often below minus 60 degrees. Very little snow falls, which is why Antarctica is regarded as a **cold desert**. For half the year the sun does not set, and for the other half it is dark.

In 1911 two expeditions tried to be the first to reach the South Pole. The Norwegian **Roald Amundsen** arrived with dog sledges on 14 December 1911. The Briton **Robert Scott** reached the pole about five weeks later, on 17 January 1912, and found Amundsen's tent there. Scott and his companions died on the way back from cold, hunger and exhaustion.

Since 1956 the USA has run the **Amundsen-Scott South Pole Station** right at the pole. In summer more than a hundred people work there, in winter only a small group that cannot leave for months. They study the weather, the ice, space and tiny particles from space. The station is supplied by aircraft that land on skis.

Next to the station is the **ceremonial South Pole**, a shiny ball on a stand surrounded by flags, where visitors take photos. The exact geographic pole is marked with a metal post. Because the ice moves about ten metres every year, this post is put in a new place at the beginning of each year. Every year the researchers design a new plaque for it.

begriffe.erklaerung: The ice-covered continent around the South Pole.
An imaginary line around which the Earth turns.
An imaginary line from pole to pole that is used to give the position of places on Earth.
An area where it is very cold and hardly any precipitation falls.

gewusst: The South Pole has no time zone of its own; the station uses New Zealand time.
The magnetic South Pole, which a compass reacts to, is not at the geographic South Pole.
Xavier Mertz from Basel took part in an Australian Antarctic expedition from 1911 to 1913 and lost his life on it.

teile.einleitung: Solar Impulse is a Swiss aircraft project that flies on solar energy alone. The adventurers Bertrand Piccard and André Borschberg flew around the whole Earth with Solar Impulse 2 in 2015 and 2016 without a single drop of fuel. In this way they wanted to show what clean energy can achieve.
wichtigste: Solar Impulse is a Swiss project by Bertrand Piccard and André Borschberg.
Solar Impulse 2 flew around the world in 17 stages in 2015 and 2016.
There was only room for one pilot in the cockpit, so the two took turns.
The wings were about 72 metres wide, wider than those of a jumbo jet.
The aircraft weighed roughly as much as a car.
The longest flight, from Japan to Hawaii, lasted almost 5 days without landing.
Thanks to batteries the aircraft also kept flying at night.

abschnitte.text: **Bertrand Piccard** from Lausanne is a psychiatrist and adventurer; in 1999 he was the first to fly around the Earth in a balloon without stopping. After that he wanted to build an aircraft that flies day and night on solar power alone. Together with the engineer and pilot **André Borschberg** he founded the Solar Impulse project. The Piccard family is famous for records; his grandfather Auguste and his father Jacques were already explorers.

On the wings, fuselage and tail of Solar Impulse 2 there were around 17,000 **solar cells**. They turned sunlight into electricity for four electric motors with propellers. During the day large **batteries** were also charged so that the aircraft could keep flying at night. It usually flew only about as fast as a car on a country road, which is slow for an aircraft.

With a wingspan of around 72 metres, the wings were wider than those of a Boeing 747. Nevertheless, the whole aircraft weighed only about 2.3 tonnes, roughly as much as a large car. It was made of very light materials such as **carbon fibre**. The cockpit was tiny and unheated, and the pilot slept only in short naps of a few minutes.

On 9 March 2015 Solar Impulse 2 took off in Abu Dhabi and returned there on 26 July 2016. The journey led in 17 **stages** across Asia, the Pacific, the USA, the Atlantic and Europe. André Borschberg flew alone for almost 5 days non-stop from Nagoya in Japan to Hawaii, a record for the longest solo flight. After that, damaged batteries had to be replaced, and the journey paused for several months.

The aircraft were developed in Switzerland, and test flights took place from the military airfield at **Payerne** in the canton of Vaud. The first model, Solar Impulse 1, flew through a whole night for the first time in 2010. Piccard later founded the Solar Impulse Foundation, which makes environmentally friendly technologies known. The project was meant to show that renewable energy makes great things possible.

begriffe.erklaerung: A component that turns sunlight directly into electric current.
A rechargeable store for electrical energy.
The distance from one wingtip to the other.
A section of a long journey.

gewusst: Solar Impulse 2 did not need a single litre of fuel to fly around the world.
The pilot could tip his seat back in the cockpit to do exercises against stiff muscles.
Bertrand Piccard used self-hypnosis to recover quickly during short breaks.

teile.einleitung: The Swiss National Science Foundation, SNSF for short, is the most important organisation that funds research in Switzerland. It was founded in 1952 and is based in Bern. Without it, many researchers at universities could not investigate their questions at all.
wichtigste: The Swiss National Science Foundation was founded in 1952.
It is based in Bern.
The SNSF is a foundation and gets its money mainly from the federal government.
Its main task is to fund research projects.
It awards about a billion francs a year (as of 2024).
Experts review the applications before a decision is made.
The topics of the National Research Programmes are set by the Federal Council.

abschnitte.text: The **Swiss National Science Foundation** is a **foundation** that was set up in Bern in 1952. It works on behalf of the federal government but is independent. This means that decisions on individual projects are made by experts, not by politicians. The SNSF funds research in all subjects, from medicine and physics to history and linguistics.

abschnitte.titel: Where does the money come from?
abschnitte.text: The SNSF's money comes almost entirely from the federal budget, that is, from taxes. It distributes about a billion francs a year (as of 2024). This pays, for example, for the salaries of young researchers, laboratory equipment, trips to excavations or surveys. This makes the SNSF the largest funder of **basic research** in Switzerland.

Researchers at Swiss universities and institutes can submit an **application** to the SNSF. In it they describe exactly what they want to find out and how. Then independent experts in Switzerland and abroad examine the application; this is called **peer review**. Only the best projects get money, because there are many more applications than funds.

In **project funding** the researchers choose the topic themselves. With “Ambizione” young researchers can lead their own project independently. The “Agora” scheme supports projects that bring science and the public into conversation. Until 2023, with “Sinergia”, there was a special programme for groups working together across subjects on one question.

For the **National Research Programmes** the Federal Council sets topics that are important for the country, for example health, energy or the environment. There are also the National Centres of Competence in Research, in which teams work on big topics for many years. When Switzerland was for a time not allowed to take full part in the EU research programme Horizon Europe, the SNSF created the SNSF Starting Grants as a temporary solution for researchers who could no longer receive ERC grants.

As well as the SNSF there is the funding agency **Innosuisse**. It supports mainly innovation projects in which universities work together with companies. The SNSF, on the other hand, funds mainly research that creates new knowledge, even if no product comes out of it yet. Together they help to make Switzerland one of the strongest research countries in the world.
